- THE BISHOP'S VISIT. Tell you about it? Of course I will! I thought %would be dreadful to have him come, For mamma said I must be quiet and still, And she put away my whistle and drum— And made me unharness the parlour chairs, And packed my cannon and all the rest Of my noisiest playthings upstairs, On account of this very distinguished guest. Then every room was turned upside down, And all the carpets hung out to blow; For when the Bishop is coming to town, The house must be in order, you know. So out in the kitchen I made my lair, And started a game of hide and seek ; Bat Bridget refused to have me there, For the Bishop was coming—to stay a week— And she must make cookies and cakes and pies, And fill every closet and platter and pan, Till I thought this Bishop, so great and wise, Mast be an awfully hungry man. Well ! at last he came ; and I do declare. Dear grandpa, he loosed just like you, With his gentle voice, and silvery hair, And eyes with a smile a-shining through. And whenever he read or talked or prayed, I understood every single word; And I wasn't the least bit afraid, Though I never once spoke or stirred ; Till, all of a sudden, he laughed right out, To see me sit quietly listening so ; And begun to tell us stories about SODA queer little fellows in Mexico. And all about Egypt and Spain—and then He wasn't disturbed by a little noise, Bat said that the greatest and best of men Once were rollicking, healthy boys. And he thinks it is no matter at all If a little boy runs and jumps and climbs ; And mamma should be willing to let me crawl Through the bannister-rails, in the hall, sometimes. And Bridget, air, made a great mistake, In stirring up each a bother, you see, For the Bi-hop—he didn't care for cake, And really liked to play games with me. • Bat though he's so honoured in word and act— (Stoop down, for this is a secret now)— He couldn't spell Boston! That's a fact! Bat whispered to me to tell him how. —Mrs. Nesoti, in Wide:Awake.

div.head: OLD LION AROUSED!
div.p: THE OLD LION AROUSED!

(Punch last week had a splendid cartoon—one of the happy hits" it makes oftenest amongst the comics." It represents John Bright as a Lion Bampant, with its foot on a coronet. The verses are given below.) • •• • -
Eh ? Dead or effete? Not a bit of it! Oldish, of course, But with wondrous reserves of elastic if slumbering force. There is spring in those sinews and strength in those pon-
- . deroas jaws. And they'd better be wary who come within clutch of his claws. May have fancied his fighting days over—and how he has fought But there probably lurked a dim doubt at the back of the

thought; For the leonine eye is undimmed, and the leonine pose, Even coachant, conveys a calm cave! to possible foes. Now Leo is up again, rampant, defiant, and dour, For he deems the occasion for fighting has come, and the
hour. Relcctant ? Not he ! Peace is pleasant, and welcome is
rest, And the chase of small every-day game is poor sport at the

best, Bat now the old quarry's afoot, the old foe is afield, And to skulk in one's den were as craven almost as to yield. Out, out in the open ! The days of stern fray are not o'er. And the forest once more shall re-echo that resonant roar, No Bctiont-like sham, the authentic reverberant thunder That forty years syne filled the foemen with awe and with
wonder. _ A hue leai loud it may 13A, bat lesa bellicose ? No ! The Old Lion always liked roaring, and loved a straighi

blow. Too tame 0 be toning that voice to the coo of the dove,. Or go with cut claws and drawn teeth, like the Lion in love. No ; like the old hunter who etira at the sound of the horn, Or like the old knight who in war time would hold it foal
scorn To skulk in retirement, and buckles on harness again, And is forth to the front of the battle to slay or be !Jahn-- Even so the Old Lion arouses at sound of the shout
Which. like that of the host which old Jericho compaesed

about, Bodes tumbling of ancient defences and tottering towers, And trembling of old domination and time-honoured towers. Ware Leo! His mane is afloat like a war-banner waving, As often of old, all the host of the hunters fierce braving. Uhl silvered with age. What of that ? They are vastly

mistaken Who fancy the Bing of the Forest is sluggish or shaken. Some promising cuss are afield. hut which one of the litter— Say Brummagem, Newcastle, Chelsea !—is fiercer or filter? The young lions roar, but their thunder is not as his thunder : It shakes not as his shakes, the ranks of the foemen asunder. S.) seeing big fighting at hand, he's once more to the front, Still game of the battle to bear, as aforetime the brunt, And the strength of the strongest, the pride of the proudest
may fail At the sound of the Old Lion's voice, and the wag of his tail

A Carious circumstance was lately witnessed by a gentle- man while on his tour through the West of England. A sailor had repaired to Plymouth Church with his lass, for the purpose of being married, when, arriving at the place appointed, the usual questions were put to him, and amongst the rest, the name of his fair one. "As for that," says Jack, "alt I know of her is that I took her in tow yes- terday afternoon, and that hr name is Bet." The result of many a bet is very doubtful. . _

The Abbe Reg-nier, Secretary of the French Academy, was collecting in his hat from each member a contribution for a certain purpose. The President, Roses, one of the forty, was a great miser, bat had paid his quota, which the Abbe not perceiving, he presented the hat a second time. Roses, as was to be expected, said he had already paid. "I believe it," answered Regnier, "although I did not see it." "And I," added Fontenelle, who was beside him, 'saw it, but I do not believe it." 0 fearful heart and troubled brain Take hope and strength from this, That Nature never hints in vain, Nor prophesies amiss. Her wild birds sing the same sweet stave, Her lights and airs are given Alike to playground and the grave; And over both is heaven.— Whittier.

"That certainly is not a pretty horse, but he looks gentle," said Mrs. Blank, who had some thought of buying the animal. "You need have no fear of him," answered the horse dealer. "A child could drive him anywhere." "But are you sure he will never run away ?" "I would stake my head on it," returned the dealer solemnly. "Bat," per- sisted the would•be purchaser, "what proof have you that he will never run away ?" "The very best of proof, madam. That horse was for three years owned by a cab- man, who always hired by the hour, and he has forgotten how to run."

"Well, my child," said a fond father to his little daughter, after she had been to church ", "what do you re- member of all the preacher said ?" Nothing," was the timid reply. " Nothing !" he exclaimed in a severe tone. "Now, remember, the next time you must tell me something of what he says, or you will have to be punished." Next Sunday the child came home with her eyes all wild with excitement. "I remember something to-day, Papa." she cried eagerly. "I am very glad Of it," said her father. "What did he say ?" "He said, 'A collection will now be male ! ' "—Chambers' Journal. De. A.- gentleman well Ilknown in the literary world was presented to a lady the ' other evening at a fashionable gathering. "Your name seems very familiar," remarked the lady. "Perhaps," in- timated the friend who made the presentation, "you have seen it in print." "Perhaps I have," replied the lady plaintively, "but I thought I might have seen it on a sign, I am so forgetful." BORROWING —Hive your own things. Accustom your. selves to be careful to keep on hand your own stock of writing paper, pens, pencils, and india-rubher. Do not de. 1 pend on mamma's workbasket for a thimble or needles, nor on her bureau drawer for ruffles and handkerchiefs. Do not consider that you have a right to borrow papa's knife, nor to make a foray on brother Tom's room for strings and wrapping-paper. Everybody should be independent of the home world, so far as some personal belongings are con- cerned. If yen allow yourselves to form the habit of going here and there with "Please lend me this" and "Do oblige me with that," you will often annoy people who are too polite to show their feelings, and you will sometimes incur mortifying refusals. It is usually much better to do with- out the use of an article than to borrow it. This is essen- tially true of things to wear. There are girls who put on their sisters' hats and aprons quite indiscriminately. There are boys who never have a collar in their box, nor a tie that isn't a perfect string and not fit to be seen. Remem- ber that a very wise man has told you "the borrower is ser- vant to the lender." This has many meanings, or rather the meaning of it makes itself plain in many ways as you go on in life. You will have a truer self-respect if you de. cide that you will, so far as you can, stand on your own feet and not borrow your neighbour's crutches. EQUINE DETECTITES.—A piece of detective work, rival- ling in professional acumen and dramatic effect some of the most astonishing achievements of Vidocq, has just been done in Philadelphia by Detective Hauser in connection with a recent murder. The bode of the victim was carried out of town in a waggon, and disposed of under a covered bridge. It occurred to the detective to drive an intelligent gray gelding, belonging to the butcher accused of the mur- der. over the ground that must hive been taken. The horse arrived at the spot where the different remains were found, stopped voluntarily at each place, and gave the most unmis- takable evidence of perfect familiarity with them. The detectives were perfectly convinced by his singular be- haviour that he knew all about the affair, and that they had arrested the right man. How this evidence is to be intro- duced into court it is difficult to say. This is not, how- ever, the first time that a horse has proved a valuable assist- ant in the detection of crime. A gentleman attended a church meeting, and left a valuable black horse tied up under a shed. When he came out of the meeting he found that his horse had been changed for a worthless old nag. He referred the matter to the detectives, who searched the neighbourhood in vain for the missing animal. At length some one suggested that the old nag should be allowed to go his way, which he did, and went directly to a barn some distance out of town, where the original steed was found. Dogs have frequently played important parts in connection with :criminal jurisprudence. In one celebrated case, the dramatieed version of which is doubtless familiar to many, a dog proved the principal witness for the prosecution. WOOLLEN UNDERCLOTIIING —lmong the many means by which we seek to guard ourselves from the effects of chill, there is one which hardly, even now, receives sufficient attention—the use of woollen underclothing. The majority of persons of the male max do, indeed, show their apprecia- tion of its wholesome qualities; but there remains a con- siderable moiety of these, and a far greater number of women and children, who prefer an undereuit of smooth but relatively meagre linen. Yet the superior advantages of wearing wool next the akin are easily apparent on refl.ction. They do not depend merely on its greater warmth and close. nen of application. It is further capable, according to its texture and in virtue of its composition, of better adapta- tion in respect of temperature to the needs of various cli- mates and the changes of seasons than any other dress material. Moreover, whether it be fine or rough, dense or light, woollen clothing, it is evident, exhibits a special faculty for absorbing and distributing moisture. It is this property especially which renders it the natural next cover- ing of the constantly' perspiring skin. If one be engaged, for example, in active exercise of limb, a linen fabric will absorb what products of transudation it can till it is wet, but will leave much moisture unabsorbed upon the clammy surface ; whereas a flannel, from its more spongy nature, will rest npon a ekin which it has nearly dried, and be but damp itself. It is obvious, then, that in the event of an after chill—and this occurs in summer as in winter—the body is, in the latter case, most favourably disposed to re- sist it. Flannel is not less cleanly than linen, though it may appear less white; and if the wearer bathe daily, it is surprising how long it will retain its purity. The disadvan- tage of skin irritation to which it sometimes gives rise is esually associated with coarseness of quality or freshness of manufacture, and is with nearly all who have experienced it a merely transient condition. Women, as well as men, we repeat, but above all children and the aged, who are alike particularly apt to take cold, should certainly adopt a woollen material for their customary undergarment It is easily possible to adjust the texture to the seasons so that it shall be warm enough in winter and not too warm in summer.—Lancet. How EMANCIPATION WAS RECEIVED IN THE WEST INDIES. —A work published many years ago, entitled 'Emancipa- tion in the West Indies," by Thome and Kimball, gives an exhibition of how the slaves received emancipation. This great event took place, as we know, in Antigua, on the lot of Aueust, 1834. The following is an account of the way in which the preceding night was kept:—" The Wesleyans kept' watchnight' in all the chapels on the night of the 31st July. One of the Wesleyan missionaries gave us an account of the watch•meeting at the chapel in St. John's. The spacious house was filled with the candidates for liberty. All was animation and eagerness. A mighty chorus of voices swelled the song of expectation and joy; and as they united in prayer, the voice of the leader was drowned in the universal acclamation of thanksgiving, and praise' and blessing, and honour, and glory to God, who had comedown for their deliverance. In such exercises the evening was spent until the hour of twelve approached. The missionary then proposed that when the clock on the cathedral should begin to strike, the whole congregation should fall upon their knees, and receive the boon of freedom in silence. Accordingly as the loud bell tolled its first note, the im- mense assembly fell prostrate on their knees. All VMS silence, save the quivering, half-stifled breath of the struggling spirit. The :aye notes of the clock fell upon the mul- titude; peal on peal, peal on peal, rolled over the prostrate throng, in tones of angels' voices, thrilling among the desolate chords and weary heart.etrings. Scarce had the clock sounded i's last, note when the lightning flashed vividly around, and a loud peal of thunder roared along the sky—God's pillar of fire and trump of jubilee! A moment of profoundest silence passed— then came the bust—they broke forth in prayer; they shouted, they sang " Glory! " " Hallelujah ! " they clapped their hands, leaped up, fell down, clasped each other in their free arms, cried, laughed, and went to and fro, tossing upward, their unfettered hands; but high above the whole there was a mighty sound which ever and anon swelled no. it was the utterings, in broken negro dialect, of gratitude to God. After this gush of excitement had spent itself, and the congregation became calm, the religious exercises were resumed, and the remainder of the night was occupied in singing and prayer, in reading the Bible, and in addresses from the missionaries, explaining the nature of the free- dom received, allel exhortine• the free ? t':: '.• A lndue- trous, steady, Obedient to the Taws and to show themselves r.,eonte in all things worthy of the high boon which God bad con- ferred upon them. The let of August came on Friday, and a release was proclaimed from all work until the next Mon- day. The day was chiefly spent, by the great mass of negroes, in the churches and chapels. Thither they flocked in crowds, and as doves to their windows. The clergy and missionaries throughout the island were actively engaged, seizing the opportunity in order to enlighten the people on all the duties and responsibilities of their situation. In every quarters we were assured that the day was like a Sab- bath. Work had ceased; the hum of business was still; and noise and tumult were unheard in the streets. Tran- quility prevaded the towns and country. A Sabbeth indeed! when the wicked ceased from troubling, and the weary were at rest, and the slave was freed from the master, The planters informed us that they went to the chapels where their own people were assembled, greeted them, shook hands with them, and exchanged most hearty good wishes.

The death is announced of the Rev Edward Stallybrass, whose name is intimately associated with the early opera- tions of the Lqndon Missionary Society. The deceased, who had passed his 90th year, was born at Ro:,ston, and educa- ted at Homerton College, under Dr Pye Smith. BISUOP CLarattvort died on Monday evening. He was the son of the late Mr Thomas Claughton. and brother of the Right Rev T L Claughton, Bishop of Rochester ; was born in 1814 at Haydock Lodge, Lancashire; and educated at Brasenose College, Oxford. He held the Bishopric of St. Helena from 1859 to 1862, when he was translate] to Co- lombo. He resigned the latter see in December, 1870, on being appointed Archdeacon of London and commissary to the Bishop of London. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &c. At a meeting of the London Executive Committee of the Jacob Wilson Testimonial Fund held last week it was an- nounced that the third list of subscriptions amounted to £1,450. THE HARVEST IN Essxx.—The sickle has now been put into all kinds of grain in different parts of Essex,—oats, wheat, and barley—and in a few days harvest operations will be quite general. The crops have rarely varied 80 much in quality as they do this year. In some districts there is a good yield, in others a moderate one, in others a poor one. The average, however, is expected to be very fair, and the quality of the grain is generally satisfactory. On some well-farmed heavy lands the wheat crop, it is said, will not fall below six quarters to the acre, and in a few instances, though only a few, seven quarters have been talked of. ARTIFICIAL V. FARM YARD MANURE.—" R." writes :—" I have been eurprieed at the small eoaount of diecession the publication of the Wobarn experiments has elicited, espé-. daily now that the Compensation Act will bring so mach interest to bear on the question involved. The experts are evidently all surprised, and, I may add, disappointed, at the result. For myself, I have always had the feeling that cake-fed manure was appraised too highly. I believe the view expressed that It has left a lot of fertility in the soil at Woburn is erroneous, for the results of that experiment go to prove the direct contrary. The first year or two the cake-fed manure, from its greater richness and stimulating properties, gave better crops; bat, year by year, in place of advancing, it rather retrograded. On the other hand, the grain-fed manure, liberally supplied, being a healthy diet, not only gave fair crops, but the action of the manure, not being evanescent as the former, continued to add fertility to the soil, and the crops grown with it year by year increased, until they overhauled those of the cake-fed plots. My im- pression is that if the land were now sown for a sequence of years without manure the grain-fed would produce the best crops, and would retain its fertility the longest." THE DAIRY SHOW SCHEDULE is issued. Including the handsome cups presented by the Lord Mayor and Corpora- tion, seven in number, there are special prizes of consider. able value for dairy cattle, milking trials, breeding pigs, collections of roots and buttermaking, in addition to medals for goats, butter, and cheese, and a valuable gold medal for cream separators. Classes have this year been added for Welsh, Guernsey, and Red Polled cattle, and for all the best known varieties of British pigs to be shown in breeding con- dition, this being quite a new feature in the dairy show. The prizes for cheeses are considerably augmented in num• her and value, classes being provided for many of the prin- cipal Continental makes. There are numeroJs classes for bacon and hams, and those for butter are very large in num- ber. This is the first time, it appears, that the last-named have been divided for butter made from sweet and sour cream in addition to that made from scalded cream. The model dairy, too, for which the medal is offered, is this year to be shown for efficiency and email cost, the elaborate and expensive contrivances of previous years thereby being ex- cluded. The butter-making contest is also open to farmers' wives and their female assistants, and is expected to be a very keen one. Prizes are offered for ensilage as well as for models of silos, which are to be accompanied with plans and specifications. Most valuable prizes, in addition to the Society's medal, are offered for designs for dairy homesteads of 180 acres, this class having been arranged by Mr. Gilbert Murray and Mr. Richard Waite. As no such schedule in connection with the dairy has ever been compiled in any country, there is no doubt that the exhibition will be the largest Of its kind. RATIONAL HORSE•SHOEING.—CoIoneI Gillon of Wall. house, again claims attention on behalf of the Charlier system of horse-shoeivg, with the experience of fourteen years as to its efficacy since he first addressed the public on the subject at a Highland and Agricultural Society's Show. The system was introduced at first under what proved an almost fatal disadvantage. The Charlier horse shoe is hardly a shoe in the ordinary sense of the word, but merely " a fertile or iron ring round the natural foot, to prevent ths breaking of the precious walls, as a fertile is placed round the bottom of a stick to prevent the splintering of the wood." The practical failure that attended the introduc- tion of the system was attributed to the insufficiency of iron as a material for so light a shoe as the Charlier. Bat Bes- semer steel has come to the rescue, and has rendered that possible which before was impossible. The Bessemer steel Charlier shoe gives an average wear of six to eight weeks, and, though made so much lighter than the ordinary shoe, it neither spreads at the heel nor breaks as the iron shoe did. The strong claim of the system to consideration is that under it, the foot of the horse never has to be pared, but is left practically in its natural state and brought in contact with the ground. Neither frog, bar, nor sole is rasped or interfered with. The lower edge only of the crust is pared away, and replaced by an artificial border, which gives more resistance than the natural horn, while it is as light and flexible. The process of shoeing on the Charlier system, as explained by Col. Gillon, is with a guided drawknife to form a groove on the lower edge of the crust," taking care not to cut so deep as the thickness of the sole, nor so broad as the depth of the crust, stopping on the white line that marks the separation of these two portions, just within the track of the old nails." This grove accommodates a shoe "not placed under the sole of the foot, but rather under the wall, as its continuation." It is kept level with the sole and frog of the foot; so that frog, sole, and bar are all left on the ground, to fulfil their natural functions. Col. Gillon contends that a strong and supple frog is the principle organ of elasticity in the foot of the horse, acting as a buffer to reduce shock on the tendons and joints. He argues that, when placed on the ground, in a natural way, the frog "ac- quires sufficient consistency to give play to the flexible branches of the crust," besides giving the animal a hold of the ground, greatly reducing the risk of slipping, and pre- venting the peculiar suction associated with the ordinary shoe on clayey or other heavy ground. Experience Colonel Gillon claims, has quite refuted the notion that the foot of the horse needs more protection than is afforded by the Charlier shoe from sharp stones and rough ground. The natural horn, if allowed to grow, becomes hard enough and thick enough to resist injury from any such cause; and, as the Charlier shoe is embedded in the hoof, no small stones can get embedded between it and the foot. The new shoe, moreover, is made "as elastic as the crust itself, which it follows in all its movements of expansion," and its light. nese leaves the horse freer in its action. The strong point in its favour is that it seems to involve a minimum of in- terference with nature. Provision is made for frozen roads by a couple of movable calkins, fixed towards the heel of the shoe. A correspondent writes to a contemporary :—At length the anxiously hoped for weather has come, and a few days of sun and light drying winds have once more put a fresh and cheerful aspect upon rural affairs. The farmers have not been slow to avail themselves of the opportunity to scrape into the barns and stacks all the hay which was be- coming weathered, and which with the warmth and mole. tore had begun to bleach the grass upon which the cocks have rested. The quantity of hay which was down may be traced by the dappled appearance of the meadows. Monday evening saw nearly all the arrears cleared-off, and mewing was begun again with spirit. The hay which has been lying out has lost in quality from exposure, but there will be no really bad hay like we had say three years sgo. There will, on the other hand, be loss and depreciated hay from over-sweating, and the amount of mischief from this source will be even greater than I was aware of when I wrote last week. The over-anxiety to get the earlier crops of old mea- dow grass as well as the first crops of clovers has shown itself in many cases by stacks firing or approaching that danger. The number of turnings or re-making of clover stacks is greater and covers a larger extent of country than I was at first led to suppose. The brittleness due to the great heat of the sun ought not to mislead a practical farmer, and the labour required to turn' a stack would be much better turned in another direction. One of the largest and most successful cropping farmers in Lancashire, a map WhO worked himself up from a day labourer to Oecupying from 400 tQ NO Of arable laud, alaii whose wife used to lead the hafvest field with her sickles, always gave his clover a day extra before hous- ing it, and he always commanded the top price in the market. This is a useful hint if kindly followed, and ills attending to such points which enriches the farmer and im- proves the quality of the people's food. The quantity of hay grass which is standing is far greater than is warranted Iby the weather that we have had. Although the bottom grass has gained weight the top grass has lost both in weight and nutriment, and there will be a great amount of very tough fibrous fodder. The effect of the better weather upon the grain crops is invaluable; every day removes traces of the late rains and improves the grain perceptibly. The ears of wheat are in many cases short of the average size, and if these should be underfed or unevenly ripened, as was threatened, it will seriously affect both bulk and quality, but the last three or four days have very much relieved the anxiety felt on that score. Other signs, too, are improved. Where the crops are not too far gone the stems have par- tially regained their uprisht position, and considering the generally excellent crops of wheat there is so little down as not to appreciably affect the sample. Both the wheat and oat harvest have been thrown back by the rain, but if the weather will only continue fine from now the harvest will be earlier than it has been for half a dozen years past. Oats have improved in a very satisfactory manner, and are now in early places quite ready for cutting. In ten days cutting will become general on the dry early soils. The crop, on the whole, will scarcely, I fear, equal the promise of two months ago. Black oats, with few exceptions, have not done nearly so well as they did last year; indeed, they will hardly reach an average, Barley looks well. Beans, which wanted sun, promise a very good yield. Turnips, mangels, cabbages, and carrots are making rapid growth. Natures are full of grass, much improved in quality owing to the dryness of May and June. I visited the splendid cropping district which lies north of the Wyre. In the Irwell Valley to Halshaw Moor there is scarcely any hay to be got in, and the grain and root crops are promising a full average. In the Croal Valley, north of Lostock, there is more than half of the hay crop to get, but as soon as one reaches the water- shed of the Douglas the hay harvest is more advanced, and all the way to Chorley there will be scarcely a third of the crop to get. The yield will be just a bare average. Oats from Lostock to quitting the Douglas at Adlington are looking very fair, bats little short in the straw, and there are several very lair fields of wheat for the district. On leaving Chorley very little hay has been got, and there is a large quantity to cut. Near Salwick there is the worst crop of oats and the worst potatoes that I have seen daring the year. The former is evidently due to the grub, hut since I was here some five weeks ago there is a wonder- ful improvement in the face of the country—grass, pota- toes, cattle, and sheep now looking so very well. On Weeton Moss and Singleton Carre, where there is excellent cropping land, oats in many instances have done very '

badly, and some bave done but the whOle will not amount to a fair average. Second crops of clover are growing very satisfactorily, and there is muca heavy hay grass .to house which will require ten days or a fort- night to clear. Potatoes are looking very well, so are beans, and oats are better on the Poulton side, where there are some excellent fields. On the north side of the Wyre, about Hambleton and Rawaliffe, the country looks remarkably well, both for roots, grass, and grain. Along Union Lane, and thence to the Head Dike Lane, there is a large tract of the old moss land, part of the great swamp known as Pilling Moss, which is some of the beat cropping land in this country, and is admirably farmed by a class of men who have been bred in the loca- lity and know their business thoroughly. I walked over a great area of this land, and taken as a whole, I never any- where saw better crops area for area. Wheat is a splendid crop, the straw being as high as the breast of a fali-eizsd man field after field in succession. The ears are large, feeding very nicely. Oats are a splendid crop, havi plenty of straw and large heads. Beans are very heavy. Seve r ga7l finer beans anvwbaleiThls it a grand potato , well as grain-growing district) and the imagination coul( not conjure up a finer spectacle than they now present. There is no trace of the disease, and many of the fields are in flower, which in the bright sun are the very piAure of luxuriance. This growth was not limited to a few rank spots, but appeared to fairly represent field after field. Magnum bonums and champions constitute the main crop, but there are some Reading heroes planted, chiefly experi- mentally and for the first time. There are some turnips and mange's grown, and, taken as a whole, they are doing very well. In Thornton the crops are disappointing, the drought having been too severe for the peculiar nature of the ground, but there are a few good fields of grain and potatoes, be- tween Bourne Hall and Poulton. In a walk of a dozen or fourteen miles through an excellent farming district both for dairy and cropping, the crops of all kinds are looking as well as could be desired. By permission of the farmers, I entered the grain and potato fields, and was the better able to examine the crops closely. The eight is a most .gratify- ing one.

THE SUSSEX FOWL. We recently described the Dorking in this column, and, as is well known, this breed is a native of the Sussex and Surrey hills. Aroued the town which gives that fowl its name it is to be found in great abundance; but there is another variety, or, as some of its upholders believe' the real variety of Dorking, known as the Sussex Fowl. This is rearei by the cottagers and small farmers of Surrey and Sussex for the London market, and vast numbers are sent there every week. To the casual observer there would not appear much differeuce between the Dorking and this Sus- sex Fowl. Both have the large, square body and the white legs and feet, but on closer examination there are found to be decided differences. The exhibition Dorking is bred timer in respect to its feather, and appears much finer in that direction, whilst the Sussex has a coarser, rougher look, though this is external only, for the flesh is, if anything, the finer and whiter of the two. The truth im there has been an infusion of other blood into the exhibition Dorking, or into some of the straks of it, and as this has been an Asiatic cross it has not added to the good quality of the flesh, the pure whiteness of the legs, or the shapeliness of the fowl. This crossing is a very great evil, and we protest against it. We mean crossing into a pure breed, and then palming off the progeny as pare stock. As our readers are aware, we have no objection whatever to crossing between two pure- bred races when the cross is acknowledged, and no attempt is made to engraft one breed upon another. This Sussex fowl is not known out of its special district, and some facts respecting it will be welcome. We quote from a letter, which appeared some time ago, written by Mr. Harrison Weir, upon this breed of fowls. He says "One feels rather inclined to wonder and ask how it is that one of our oldest and best breeds has been totally ignored, by not only one or two, but by all show committees. I allude to the old Surrey or Sussex fowls. I cannot call to mind at any time seeing a prize or prizes offered for this fine breed of table fowls—a breed that always used to be quoted in the market prices of the day as being, next to the Dorking, of superior excellence to all others. No doubt there are many who on reading the foregoing will well re- member the old stout and sturdy breed, not big by the mixture of Asiatic crosses, like the present so-called Dork- ing, but large by selection, and hardy by long, I may say, rough usage for at most of the farms they roosted in the apple or other fruit trees, and sought their living at the farm yard about the ricks, stacks, and the barn-door. Now let it not be inferred from this that the breed was no more nor less than that which was called the ' bam-door' fowl. There was much pain and trouble taken to put up the stock as to quality, and many of the farmers' wives were cele- brated in the neighbourhood in which they resided for the largeness and plumpness of their poultry; and an alliance with those of a neighbour, and sometimes from stock at a long distance off, was as seriously considered—ay, and more so—than the selection of a cross at the present time. The Surrey or Sussex fowl was generally of a gray colour, often a sandy-brown, and brown, like a black. red Game hen. I have put the colours in the order in which they were moat admired, and in which size was generally to be found. They were large, strong-made, sprightly, good flyers, and excellent foragers, fair layers, with large white eggs; their legs and feet were of a clear soft-looking pinky white, breast more broad than very deep, with much flesh, and also good on the thighs, dm. They were very close in feather' thereby not looking nearly the size they actually were. Some of the breeds were bearded, but these were somewhat smaller. I never remember seeing any with topknots. The combs were single, and the earlobe a pinky white, like the time Dorking. In this latter particu- lar note was often taken, the red earlobe proving a cross with the Game not unfrequently ; as to this day in the Dorking it proves, or rather helps to prove, the coarse Asiatic cross. By the way, I may mentton here that in breeding Dorkings, I would never select a bird with a red earlobe to breed from. unless I wanted sooty feet. But to the Sussex and Surrey fowls; I should mention they were rather longer in the leg than the Dorking; but, as I have said before, equally white, and had but four toes. Any excrescence seen on the foot, and the bird was never bred from, this difference with the Dorking being well noted. Though they were large in size, I never saw any with a bumble foot.' Nor, indeed, for the matter of this, have I ever with the Dorking unless it was the modern 'exhibition' Docking; nor have ever had any in my own stock, except from the same cause. As regards the fifth toe being cause of bumble.foot, I do not—from very long experience—entertain the idea for one moment. However this may be, in the Surrey and Sussex fowl there is no such chance. The four-toed fowl is what many have 'cried out for' for many a long year—the four-toed with the white leg. Then why not have a class or classes for this breed—l feel sure they would fill—and if kept from the Asiatic cross the quality will be all that can be desired. But there is one drawback to the above suggestion. Where are they to be found ? I, for one, know not; but, let the classes be found, the prizes offered, and I have but little doubt the exhibitors will be equal to the occasion, and I predict that, in a few years, the collections at our shows will be as large, as good, as interesting, and as useful as any breed that the fancier has in hand at the present time." We take the liberty of making another quotation this time from a letter from Mr. Oliver, a very large breeder of fowls for the London market, and living in Sussex. He says :—" I am confident that if the Sussex fowls were better known, they would quickly become great favourites with a large number of fanciers. The young chickens are exceed- ingly hardy, they grow rapidly, and their feathers also grow very quickly. The chickens are Beady for market at a very early age, and, being of first-class quality, the highest market prices are obtained. The pullet° that are bred in April, and early in May, will commence laying in October, and will continue to produce a supply of eggs during the winter months. A small farmer in this neighbourhood, who keeps this lleed of fowls, reared a number of chickens early last spring. He sold ninety chickens at a fraction over 6s. 6d. per couple when the birds were about ten weeks old. They were Wren away from the house by the higgler, who purchased them in order to fatten them for the London markets, where they probably cost the consumer about 15e. per couple. The above-named farmer has now upwards of 100 strong young chickens that have been hatched (under hens) daring the past few weeks; and he has every reason to hope that he will be as successful in disposing of them this spring. I have for some time past been amused by the many suggestions which have appeared respecting the manu- facture of a fowl suitable for farmers. It has occurred to me that such fanciers are ralthough quite unaware of the fact) really endeavouring to produce a fowl that has been bred in East Sussex for many years previous to poultry shows being known. As the term hlggler, used above, will not be understood by many of your readers, I may explain that the chief districts in East Sussex where fowls are fat- tened for the London markets are the parishes of Warbleton and Heathfield. The men engaged in this industry are called higglers. The men drive strong, useful horses, and travel the country from twelve to twenty miles round with great regularity. They call upon the farmers and cottagers every week throughout the year, and purchase all the chickens that are ready for them—that is, when the chickens are about twelve weeks old. Some of the higglers who are unable to keep a horse work exceedingly hard. A man will leave his home early in the morning, with an empty crate strapped upon his back, and travel his usual journey on foot into the breeding districts. In the afternoon, having succeeded in filling his crate, he will stay at some wayside inn for an hour, to take some rest and refreshment. Having done this, the man again places the crate upon his back (which now contains from three to four dozen of fine plump chickens), and cheerfully starts on a long tramp towards his home, distant some twelve miles away. On his arrival home, the man takes the fowls to his employer, and is paid at the rate of about eighteenpence per dozen for his work in collecting them." SEASONABLE HINTS. It is not improbable that some of the earlier pullets will soon begin to lay. There may be some of the January and February hatched pullets laying already, but we do not care to force them on too early, as they never make such fine birds as when allowed to mature properly. It is to be preferred that pullets should commence laying about the end of September or beginning of October, if possible, as then eggs are getting scarce consequent of most of the old birds being in the moult, and they are then more likely to continue laying right through the winter. If the pullets are showing signs of laying, we should try to put them off by moving from one run to another, for, as a rule, this keeps them back and does no harm in any other way. Un- le.s this is done there is danger that the earlier hatched birds will moult in the autumn.

Roby, and our "Lancashire laureate," Edwin ugh. A correspondent of The Times sends particulars of a white starling, a white lark, and a sparrow with white head and body, but having a few dark feathers in its wings and tail. Mr. G. F. Batt, F Z.S., mentions the birth of a cuckoo in his garden near Regent's Park. The young bird soon fell a prey to that observant naturalist, the domestic cat. Sir Edward Watkin and the directors of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company are sparing no pains to turn the sad lesson of the Penistone disaster to advantage, and are engaged in considering whether elec- trici cannot btk employed 40 as to detect the minutest fault in fee. Professor Hughes, the clement electrician, , have been consulted on the subject and c and experi- ments shortly be made. How TO TARE A PILL.—Dr. Samuel E. Willis, of the United States, asserts that if the head be kept in the posi- tion usual when eating at table, "it will surprise the patient and gratify the doctor to witness the facility with which a pill will be swallowed." It is a common custom to throw the head back, as in laughing; but if we consider that to attempt to swallow food in such an attitude would almost inevitably lead to choking, the difficulty experienced in swallowing a pill under similar conditions is not remarkable. Dr. Willis finds that the head is in the proper position when the patient keeps his eyes on his toes. Wo think a trial will prove the wisdom of this, THERMO-CAUTERY A CURE FOR CAROER.—Professor von Nussbaum ( lVein. Med. Zeit.) declares that he has dis- covered a positive cure for cancer in the use of the thermo- cautery, with which instrument a deep channel is made quite around the cancerous growth, thus cutting off en- tirely the supply of blood and other nutritive fluids from the surrounding tissues. He considers that this method of starving malignant growths by cutting off every channel of peripheral nutrition has a brilliant future, the results he has obtained by its use being astonishing; and he strongly recommends it to the attention and practice of at those who have occasion to treat the more desperate cases of cancer in which death is imminent from bfemorrhage. THE PRESSURE OF Tan SaA.—lt is often asked, when an ocean-going vessel has been lost at sea, and it is supposed she has foundered, why none of her timbers rise to the sur- face again and float, as submerged wood will nearer shore. The explanation is that if the vessel has been sunk in deep water, the pressure to which it is subjected will be so great that a certain quantity of water will be forced into the pores of the wood, and thus render it so heavy that, even when detached from the ship, a piece of the timber could not float. It is because of this constantly and rapidly in- creasing pressure, too, that a diver cannot descend to any very great distance below the surface. Fishes have, how- ever, been caught at a depth at which they must have borne a pressure of no less than eighty tons to each square foot of their bodies —Cassell's Magazine. Two more oil paintings by Lucas Cranach have been dia. covered walled up in the town church of Wittenberg. A similar find was made last year. There are four pictures by Lucas Cranach on the altar wall, a "Last Supper," the "Sermon," with a portrait of Luther in the foreground; the "Baptism," and "The Office of the Key," on the smaller side compartments. On further investigation of those first discovered oil paintings were found on the banks of the pictures one representing the "Raising of the Ser- pent by Moses," and the "Sacrifice of Abraham." Of the pictures last found the "Last Supper" has "Christ as Overcomer of Death and the Devil" on the back, and the "Sermon" has the "Resurrection on the Last Day." Three of the pictures are in very good preservation, and those first found are already well restored. The Gazzetta Musicale of Milan publishes the authentic text of an interesting document, which should definitively fix the date of Verdi's birth, so often erroneously stated in biographical accounts of the illustrious Italian. This is

his-ace de naissance, extracted from the r-gister of the commune of Basseto, in the ancient Duchy of Parma, for 12th October, 1813. The signatures are Italian, but the declaration itself is in French, the country being at that time under the domination of Napoleon, and it records the first public appearance of the future composer before the deputy mayor of Basset), who took the testimony of Charles Verdi, innkeeper, that his son was born on the 10th day of October, at eight o'clock in the evening, and would bear the name of Joseph-Forttmin-Francois. The presenta- tion of the boy in person when he was barely two days old was in compliance with that law which Mr. Herbert Spen- cer considers so hurtful to newly-born children in France, and which prevails in several other Continental countries.

NERVE STRETCHING AND NEURALGIA.— Mr. W. J. Weis- ham, of St. Bartholomew's Hospital, contributes to the Practitioner for July an interesting article on nerve-stretch- ing as a care for so-called incurable facial tic. This dread- ful affection was until quite recently regarded as incurable, the only treatment of it being the administration of drags (suoh as opium) calculated to deaden the acuteness of the pain. Nerve-stretching has been tried, but with varying success. Mr. Walsham, however, describes six ctses under his care within the last few years, in which he has per- formed the operation with (so far) complete success, and should the lapse of time prove the cures to be permanent, an important step will have been made in the treatment of a frightful malady. The first of Mr. Walsham's patients had had the neuralgia for ten years, the second for nine years, the third for eight years, the fourth for five years, the fifth for ten years, and the sixth for upwards of four- teen years. They have all enjoyed immunity from the time Of their respective operations. The details given in the paper are only of technical interest. We have referred to it because it marks an important advance in surgical practice, and removes one more disease—though happily a rare one —from the steadily diminishing list of Incurable ills.— Science Monthly.

" A PROPHET IS NOT WITHOUT HONOUR, SAVE IN HIS OWN COUNTRY."—The correspondent of the Lancet in Rome writes :—Professor Filippo Pacini, of Florence, the discoverer of the tactile corpuscles which bear his name, contributed in 1854 to the Gazetta Meelica Italiana a paner on the cholera visitation, in which occur the following words : " Examining minutely the different parts of the gastro- enteric tube of subjects dead from cholera when in the algid state, I was forced to the conviction that that epethelial lesion is covered by nothing but a very simple organism of extreme tenuity, which I shall call 'microbe,' a term generic and modern and with special reference to the dis- ease in question, cholerigenous microbe.'" As usual, this pregnant discovery was more quickly and thorougly appre- ciated by foreigners than by its author's own countrymen, and in 1865, on the next cholera visitation, Pacini wrote : " When my scientific labours, having made the tour of Europe, will have returned, arrayed in foreign garb to Florence, they will have permission to enter the schools, and then we shall be enjoying the tranquil repose of Tres- piano—in our grave, in short." This bitter forecast has been verified almost to the letter, Pacini's doctrine, reha- bilitated by the German Cholera Commission, being now adopted by his compatriots and taught in the Institut' Pathologici of Italy a year after his death. Mn. VANDERBILT'S S rRONG Box.—The construction of
Mr. Vanderbilt's treasure house in New York is described in

minute detail by one of the French papers, which begins by calling the exterior building itself a "formidable fortress of masonry and iron." This name is not, however, wholly in- appropriate, if it is true that no force, however numerous and well armed, would be at all likely to take it by storm without the aid of heavy artillery. The foundations of the house are laid, as it is said, on a solid rock, and the front wall is five feet thick, the side walls measuring three feet. All these are composed solely of brick and facing stone. There is no woodwork whatever about the place all the supports, sashes, and framings being of iron or steel, and the doors and windows of iron, marble, and plate glass. The sanctum of this abode is, of course, the strong room, 42ft. by 361 t. in dimensions, composed altogether of iron and steel, and having four doors, each of which weighs B,OOOTh. This chamber is built into the solid wall, which covers it on the top, and it Is, of course, fireproof, waterproof, and bur- glar proof. It is, moreover, guarded day and night by fully-armed men, subjected to the strictest discipline, under- standing the word in a truly American sense. That is to say, their movements as they are on guard are reported to the upper part of the house by electric clocks, and this upper part of the house communicates again with all the other telegraph stations of the system, as well as with the central public office. It is calculated that 100 men posted in the inside of the building, and armed with mitrailleuses, could easily defend it against 10,000 assailants, which is more than even the enemies of Mr. Vanderbilt are likely to be able to bring together for the siege. THE LARGEST CHINA VASE IN THg WORLD.—It has been left to a well-known firm of English potters to pro- duce a china vase that is not only the largest in the world, but is also a beautiful work of art. The chief feature of the vase is a globe representing the earth, which is sup- ported on a pedestal rising from a square plinth and sur- mounted by a figure of Ceres, who, aided by a number of Cupids, is occupied in showering her gifts of fruitfulness and plenty upon the earth. Round the centre of the globe runs a frieze divided into four panels, on which more Cupids are seen busied in the pursuits typical of the four seasons. The subjects are separated by brackets, on which are other figures emblematic of the seasons. :The pedestal contains a splendid frieze, on which are represented as many as sixty cupids occupied in rural work. The plinth supporting the whole is ornamented in keeping with the general design. The colour of the globe is a subdued green called celadon, the figures are china bisque, and the other decorations white glazed china. From the pedestal to the top of the figure of Ceres, the vase is eleven feet high, and the diameter, including the ornamental figures, is six feet four inches. Notwithstanding its massive proportions, it is elegant and chaste, the design, which is by Mr. L. H. Jahn, being in the Renaissance style and thoroughly artistic. The figures have been modelled by the distinguished French sculptor, M. Carrier, and the whole has been constantly superintended by Messrs. Browfield and Sons. Before the vase left their works at Cobridge for the International Ex- hibition at the Crystal Palace, it was allowed to be inspec- ted on one day only by the workpeople of the Potteries district, and 25,000 persons availed themselves of the op- portunity of seeing it. The vase cost £3,soo.—Cassell's Magazine.

COTTAGE GARDENING

PARSLEY.—TheParsley bed frequently tarns out the most profitable piece of geound of its size in the whole garden, and it is almost incredible the number of pennyworths it will yield daring the winter. About this time we make a sowing so as to increase the chances of securing a good sup- ply six months hence. We select for the purpose a firm piece of ground or we make it so by treading, being con- vinced that the Parsley stands the winter and summer bet- ter under such conditions. A small bed sown last May without being made firm is and has been yellow for some weeks, and we have observed the same before if a period of hot dry weather sets in as it did this season. The seeds re- quire but very little covering, and we usually draw very shallow drills or sow broadcast, and in either case tread the seeds in. Plants from previous sowings may be transplanted, an operation whioh has frequently proved effectual in main- taining the plants in health during the winter. POTATOES.—If there are any symptoms of the disease in the early ones they should be taken up at once; for they will increase but little in size, and the disease will soon re- duce the number of sound tubers. The disease now is well known to be a fungus, and attacks the tops, and rapidly descends to the tubers. The spores are also scattered by the wind. For this reason scientific gentlemen attach much importance to the removal of the tops on the first appear- ance of the fungus or the Peronospora, and they maintain that if the first one or two were removed in time the entire crop in the garden may escape the disease. This operation applies at the present time to second early and late crops, the early as already stated being best out of the ground. All diseased tops should be burnt or buried, and some hot lime thrown over them before they are covered. From the nature of the disease we may conclude that if we exercise every precaution there is a probability of checking its course, if not entirely exterminating it. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Pansies and Violas may now be propagated by cuttings of such shoots as may be seen to emerge from the base, as the tops of those that have flowered are very uncertain; but it is frequently necessary to resort to these in a season when the others are scarce. A shady position should be selected, and with the view of shading further, as well as protecting them from slugs, we I would construct a frame of four 9-inch boards or there. abouts to place over them. The frame, which is really a box without a bottom, may be any dimensions, and one a foot square would contain about three dozen cuttings ; such a box, covered with a piece of glass, would be a perfect propagating box, if the upper surface is made to slope so that the glass may have a fall to throw off the water. Two or three small boxes are preferable to one large one, as in that case there may be enough cuttings to fill a small one, but not a large one, and the others could be filled when a sufficient number are ready. A good shading may be made by fastening pieces of calico on two pieces of wood, which may hang over each side of the frame, so that it may not be so readily moved by the wind. THE WINDOW.—SCHOOL BOARDS AND WINDOW PLANTS. —We learn from the Gardeners' Chronicle that "Messrs. Fisher, Son, and Sibray, of the Handsworth Nursery, Shef- field, are growing a large collection of the above for the Sheffield School Board. There are in all 10.000 plants, composed of Balsams, Petunias, Harrison's Musk, Fuchsias, and Zonal Pelargoniums. This large number of plants has to be delivered to the School Board on August the 9th. They will be distributed among the children attending the different schools in Sheffield under the control of the Board, and after being kept five or six weeks they will be exhibited for prizes in one central place. The plants are all in a uniform-sized pot, a kind of 48 (about 51n. diameter), and are all stamped with the letter "S." The weight of the 10,000 pots was 41 tons, and 12,000 gallons of soil were re- quired to pot them. The plants will be delivered in the , best condition, and their culture, under very diffetent and even difficult circumstances, will follow. It is paid that this novel experiment is the outcome of an effort on a smaller scale, but so interesting and valuable in its results that the Board have been induced to attempt it on a larger scale." Managers of schools and boards in other large towns should emulate the Sheffield School Board. Window boxes must be daily examined, for the soil will be by this full of roots, and if allowed to get dry the plants will suffer. If the space in the box will admit of it, an inch of decayed manure may be supplied to them as a top dressing. They would be alto , benefited by an occasional dose of liquid manure, and in order to preserve a fresh appearance the faded flowers and decayed leaves should be removed as they appear.
