MR. MUNDELLA. AND THE COTTON _ OPERATIVES.

Two notable presentations were made on Saturday in the Manchester Town Hall, in the presence of a large and re- presentative gathering. They consisted of a marble bust' of the Right Hon A J Mundella, M P. which was given to Mrs Mundella, and a candelabrum and four candlesticks in silver, which were presented to Mr Mandella. These gifts were the result of contributions by the workers in cotton factories in the Northern Counties, chiefly women and chil- dren, and were presented in grateful acknowledgment of Mr Mundella's services when he had charge of the bill whitt. I shortened the working hours of the cotton operatives. Mr J E Boehm was the sculptor of the bust, valued at 300 guineas, which was elevated on a pedestal on the right hand of the chairman's table. On the other side was displayed the plate, which is designed in the English style of the 18th century, and weighs 170 ounces. About a hundred little boys and girls, " half.timars," were seated on the front row of chairs, and made their shrill voices prominent in the cheering. Some delay took place in beginning the proceed- ings, owing to a block of trains, which prevented the ar- rival of the contingent of representatives from Burnley, Harwood, and Padiham. When it was announced that a telegram had been received to that effect the audience waited patiently for three-quarters of an hour. No music could be furnished to beg,ulle the time as tile organ was under repair.

The Mayor of Manchester (Mr P Goldsmidt), who presi- ded, was accompanied to the platform by the Right Hon A J Mandella, MP, Mrs Mundella, and Miss Mundella; Mr Talbot, Deputy Town Clerk; Alderman Hopkinson and Miss Hopkinson, Alderman Schofield and Mrs Schofield, Mr and Mrs Farlone, Mr Councillor Stewart, Mr D Bannerman, Mr. Birtwistle (4eneral t!:::lrgal";pf the OptraZiyeWeaverSe Association), M 7 James Maudsley (general secretary of th- Arnalgamated Operative Cotton Spinners), Mr Thomas Ash ton (secretary of the Operative Spinners of Oldham), &c. The Mayor expressed his complete ant hearty agreement and sympathy with the object for which the meeting had been called together. Mr Mundella bad thoroughly de- served the gratitude of the working classes. (Applause.) Mr Thomas Birtwistla said he had letters of apology to read. One was from the Venerable Lord Shaftesbury, who wrote :—" It would give me very sincere pleasure to attend any meeting held in honour of my old friend and fellow la- bourer' Mr Mundella, more especially as he ill be accom- panied by his excellent and admirable lady. I am delighted that yeu are about to present to him a tribute of your res- pect. He fully deserves it. for he has served you most heartily and effectually. I cannot, however, ba present, and join in the general acclamation, for I must start to-night for North Berwick, in search of repose and restoration to health"

Mr Birtwistle said he was extremely proud of being Se- lected, on behalf of such an important body as the factory workers of the Northern counties, to present to Mrs Mun- della an address and a bust of her esteemed hthhand. (Ap- plause.) In Lancashire alone there were 39 027,000 spindles and 499,000 looms, employing 423,000 parsons; of whom 253,800 were females above 13 years of age (60 per cent) ; 33,840 were males above 13 and under 18 (8 per cent); 29,610 were children below 13 (7 per cent); and 105,750 were adult males. The labour of cotton operatives was of a monotonous, tedious, and watchful nature, and somewhat unhealthy. An ordinary weaver had from B,OCO to 16,000 ends of threads to mind, which, supposing they averaged fifty "Counts," was one pound of cotton spun out into a length of more than 23 miles. When Mr Mundella, at the urgent request of the cotton operatives, came to their rescue in 1872 they were working 60 hours per week, and he asked Parliament to reduce them to 54 hours, the result being a compromise for 56 hours. When Mr Mundella commenced this agitation they bad few friends in the House of Com- mons. Mr Mundella spent much time in collecting factory statistics in England and on the Continent, and he was always careful not to overstate his case. One argument of their opponents was that reducing the bouts of labour would increase the cost of manufactured goods. That had not been the case. In the weaving department they - were producing 3 per cent more in WI hours than was produced in the 60 hours. (Hear, heir.) Mr Mandsley could speak to a similar increase of production in the spinning depart- ment. Another argument used was that the operatives wanted to raise their wages at the expense of their em- ployers. This fear had also proved fallacious, for they were working at 10 per cent less wages, which had never been greater since the Act was passed than at that time. Mr Birtwistle then read the achlress to Mrs Mundella, and un- covered, amidst cheering, the fine marble bust of Mr Mon- della, which bore this inscription :—" Presented to Mrs Mundella by 80,000 factory worke.s, chiefly women and children, in grateful acknowledgment of her husband's ser- vices." The address to Mrs Mary Mundella, wife of the Right Hon A J Mundella, Ml', was signed by Thomas" Ashton (chairman), Joshua Burrows. James Robinson, Geo Barker, and James Maudsley and Thomas Birtwistle (joint secretaries).
Mrs. Mundella, in a neat reply, said more especially did it appeal to her as a wife and mother that so many of the subscribers were women and children.

Mr. Thos. Ashton, of Oldh-am. , p—relnted the plate, which bore this incription :—"Presented to the Right Hon. A. J. Mundella, M.P., by cotton operatives of Lancashiae and ad- joining counties, in recognition of his great service to the factory workers generally." Mr. M undel la, in reply, remarked: I have to congratulate you to-day upon having arrived at the jubilee of factory legislation. (Loud cheers.) What a blessing this legisla- tion has been in the past. What a jubilee it is. It has saved us from what was a scandal to our country and from a system that was fast deteriorating tha whole race of factory operatives. If we had had no factory legistation we should have had an entirely different population, I believe, not only in your industries, but in all the industries of the united Kingdom. I shook hands before coming into this room with the last living member of the Committee of 1833, one who entered the factory at six years of age, not as a half-timer, but as a full-timer. He and Lord Shaftesbury are the last two representatives of that glorious and success- ful agitation. (Applause.) The victory was really wen when that small initiatory step was taken in 1833. It was limited, it is true, to cotton, woollen, and flax mills; but from that hour to this extension has been steadily going on, and in 1817, with the aid of that nobleman whose name I have mentioned to you, Lord Shaftesbury, and men like honest John Fielden and Joseph Bretherton, and many other men known in your district, you won the great victory of the Ten Hours Act, and from that time to this it has not been limited to your district, but these Acts have been steadily extended to every branch of the industries of the kingdom; so that it has now come to be re- , garded as a matter of necessity that wherever young persons and women are employed there shall be a Factory Act, or a Workshop Act, as the case may require, so that all prec iutions may be taken for health, for. ventilation, for comfortable conditions of working, and for the suitable education of the children before they are put to work. (Cheers.) If you will allow me, I will now say a few words on my part in this work. Von have come here to- day tb receenise the efforts that I made in the first and second Parliament in which I was a member. Now, my friends, the circumstances of my life were such as were favourable to my forming, I think, an accurate judgment upon this question. I was at work, earning my daily bread, before I wee ten years old, and I was not working " half- time "either. Before I was 201 was managing a mill, before I was 30 I owned mills, and at 42 I entered Parliament. The right hon. gentleman gave interesting reminiscences of his early days, and spoke of the time when children of 11 worked 60 hours a week. The right hon. gentleman pro- ceeded : I want to ask now what has been the effect of these Factory Acts upon the character of the factory operatives themselves ? There is a brief answer, my friends. There are no more self-reliant men on the face of the earth than the operatives of Lancashire. When I look at the manage- ment of your co-operative stores ; when I consider that within a ten or twenty miles radius of this places they manaee co-operative, distributive, and industrial concerns to the extent of ten millions of money, I say that is an illus- tration of independence of character, self-reliance, and in- telligence which has no comparison anywhere else in the world. Having expressed his thanks for the gifts, he added that while he had a place in Parliament nobody should ever touch the Factory Acts. (Applause.) Two defects detracted from the high character of the British workman, but they could be remedied, as he believed they were being remedied, by more education and mere temperance, (Cheers.) A vote of thanks to the Mayor concluded a memorable gathering.

WIFE MURDER AND SUICIDE.—News from Pressburg on Saturday says that Captain Hofer, of the infantry, an officer who has distinguished himself in several campaigns, has shot his wife dead and afterwards committed suicide. DEPRESSION IN TRADE.—In consequence of the depres- sion in trade, the rivet makers of South Staffordshire and East Worcestershire have been called upon to submit to a reduction of from 10 to 15 per cent., taking effect from Mon- day last. THE MiSTERIOVS MURDER OF AN IRISH POLICEMAN.— The Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland has refused compensation to the relatives of Sergt. Brown of the Royal Irish Constabu- lary, who was mysteriously murdered some time since at Parstonstown, his assassin escaping and remaining unde- tected. The conclusion arrived at is that the murder had no political significance, but was an act of private vengeance for the seduction of a young girl by the murdered officer.

BOATING AND BATIIING ACCIDENTS. Thomas Samuel Maddock, aged four, son of a farmer residing at Whitchurcb. fell in the canal while attempting to catch flies. His sister gallantly jumped in and tried to rescue him. Help ar- rived, but the boy was drowned, although his sister was rescued in an exhausted state.— Whilst bathing in the river Ouse at King's Lynn, a hawker, named Alexander McLeod, was drowned.—During six days there have been five fatalities in North Lancashire through bathing, inclu- ding one near Garstang. William Dyson, labourer, has been drowned at Southport.—Four young men (three bro- thers and a cousin), named Durham, have been drowned in the Ouse, near Selby. They rowed out to meet the tidal wave, and their boat upset. —The dead body of Samuel Whit- field, a Batman, 38 years of age, has been found in the Old Dock, Widnes Marsh. Deceased was lame, and no doubt stumbled in trying to reach a flat.— On the Cornish coast near St. Austell, on Saturday, a young lady named Agnes Guy, daughter of the postmaster of St. Austell, got beyond her depth whilst bathing. Another young lady named Edith Giles went to her assistance, and both were drowned —On Saturday, as three young men belonging to Ulverston were bathing on the sands of Morecamhe Bay, near Leven Viaduct, one of them, James Hodgson Thompson, plumber, aged 20, was washed out by the tide and drowned.—Drown- ing cases at Blackpool, and in the Ribble, and elsewhere, i are reported.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—SATunDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 12.20. Mr. GLADSTONE moved that the House resolve itself into Committee on the Bishopric of Bristol Bill, which had come down from the Lords. The Premier, touching on objections raised by members not friendly to the connection between Church and State, suggested that "so long as two parties have to live together they bad better live together on decent and civil terms.' I hat, he said, was the maxim upon which he had always acted with regard to Church matters.—After protests from Sir W. Lawson and Mr. Caine, the motion, which was supported by Lord John Manners and Mr. Monk, was agreed to, and the Bill passed through Committee with- out amendment—The Post Office Protection Bill having passed through Committee, Mr COURTNEY moved the second reading of the Appropriation Bill.—Sir George Campbell, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, Mr. Lowther, and Mr. Labou- chere having reiterated their views on the Egyptian ques- tion, Lord 13.rjIZMAUEICE replied, incidentally likening Sir George Campbell to the Ancient Mariner, who stopped the Wedding Guest ;Mr Courtney) as he was proceeding with the ordinary business of the Appropriation Bill.--Mr. LABOUCHERE illustrated the prevailing feeling of the coun- try by a little anecdote. A friend of his, addressing a meeting in the country, and proposing to discuss Egyptian affairs, was interrupted by a man in the crowd, who called out, "We don't care about the Mah-di or the Sou-dan, or any o' those gentlemen. What we want to know is, Whit are you going to do with the House of Lords? " He ex- pressed his regret that the Conference bad failed, because he approved entirely of one of the proposals laid before it, that the bondholders should only get what was left after the ex- penses of administration had been paid. He approved also of Lord Northbreok's mission.—After some remarks from Sir E Wihnot, Mr F Buxton, and Mr Newdegate, who at length found an opportunity of discoursing on " the letter from the Adm;ral of the Fleet," the second reading of the Appropriation Bill was agreed to.—The Matrimonial Causes Bill was passed through Committee and read a third time, and several other kills were passed through their remaining

stages. The House rose at 4-20. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his Beat at 445. THE FRANCHISE AND REDISTRIBUTION.—Lord RICHES- DALE asked her Majesty's Government whether, as they had admitted that redistribution ought to accompany the extension of the franchise, they were prepared to inform the House before the session closed how far they had per- fected any scheme for redistribution; and whether the neces- sary provisions on that subject would be submitted to Par- liament at the commencement of the autumnal session, or when.-. Lord KIMBERLEY replied that her Majesty's Go- vernment had already indicated in both Houses the general principle on which they proposed to proceed in their meas- ure for redistribution. At the time which they should con- sider fitting for the introduction of the measure, they would explain its provisions. That was the usual course. As already stated by Lord Granville, the Franchise Bill would be re-introduced in the autumn session, and when it was passed by Parliament the Government would bring in a Re- distribution Bill.—Lord REDESDALE again expressed his disappointment at the course pursued by the Government, and Lord COLCHESTER joined him in maintaining that the franchise and redistribution ought not to be separated; while Lord WAVENY expressed his opinion that in these days no Minister could manage redistribution so as to give his own party an undue advantage. The Cholera, drc., Protection Bill nassed through Commit- tee ; the Disused Burial Grounds Bill was read a second time ; and the Revenue, Sm., Bill and the Public Health (Ireland) (Districts) Bill were read a third time and passed. Their lordships rose at 5-55. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 2-50. OBSTRUCTING COLONIAL CONFEDERATION.—Mr. GLAD- ram, in answer to Mr. Parnell and Sir S. Northcote, said it had not been found possible to introduce the Australian Confederation Bill, as the Opposition did not see its way to passing it without any discnssloo, and it would be prema- ture at present tn say whether this or any other business besides the Franchiee Bill could be introduced in the au- tumnal session. GENERAL GORDON.—Lord HARLINGTON stated that ac- tive preparations were now being made for doing whatever might be neceesary for General Gordon's safety. The Go- vernment were dome all they could to inform him of the preparations which were being made. EGYPT.—LORD NORTHBROOK'S MISSION.—After the Post Office Protection Bill had been passed through its final stages, and on the order for committing the Appropriatioa Bill, Sir S. NouvacoTE moved for papers relating to the mission of Lord Northbrook, and celled attention to the present con- dition of the Egyptian question. His chief desire, he said, was to dwell on the conditions of the Anglo-French agree- ment, of which, though it was said to be in abeyance. he was afraid the country had not heard the last. He had three Objections to tins Anglo-French treatment—first, the posi- tion in which the Commission of the Caisse was to be placed; secondly, the fixing of a date for the evacuation ; and, thirdly, the proposed neutralisation of Egypt. Justice to the people of Egypt called upon U 9 to adopt a more vig- orous policy, and England would be disgraced if she refrained from using her powers is redress their condition for fear of being misrepresented.—Mr GLADSTONE remarked that the argument to be deduced from Sir S Northcete's description of the condition of the fellaheen was our permanent reten- tion of power in Egypt, and complained that he had sup- pressed all mention of the reforms accomplished by our agents, because thy had- been appointed by his political opponents.—This rsinark provoked a loud protest, and Sir S NORTHCOTE called for its withdrawal as a statement which he had no right to mike—Mr GLADSTONE then passed to Lord Northbrook's mission, about which. he said, it would be impossible for the Government to give further informa- tion at preeent. Finally, he said that though the difficulties of the Eevptian question hid been greatly increased by in- cessant diecussiea, he admitted the right of Parliament to the fullest information, and assured the House that the Government never would be parties to com- mitting the country to any policy without the assent and behind the bac:: of Parliament.—'•ir H WOLFF remark, d that the Prime Minister had been more nebulous than ever. He accused the Govern- ment of having falsified the pipers, especially to establish the charge that they had inherited the situation from the late Government, and denied that the Government had im- proved the condition of the fellaheen.-Mrneroan A dissented from this, and regretted the failure of the Conference.—Sir G Eatacer thought that the weak point in the Ministerial policy had been its deference to France —Mr FORSTER re- joiced to hear that the Anglo-French ;agreement was dead, and that Lord Northbrook would be free to act as well as to advise.—Mr CHAPLIN maintained that Lord Northbrook's mission could only be intended to give the Government another opportunity of shirking their responsibilities.—Sir J Lubbock said to hand over Egypt to all the troubles of civil war would be the height of cruelty, and we ought to remain there as long as was necessary to secure order and tran- quilty.—Sir BARTLELOL hoped that now its hands were untied the Government would not sacrifice the interests of the Egyptian people and the safety of our route to India to any sentimental tenderness for the susceptibilitiee of the French people.—Mr VILLIERS-STUART maintained that our best policy wou'd be to gain the affections of the Egyptian people.—Sir R PEEL diecussed the Egyptian policy of the Government and the proceedings in the Conference at con- siderable length, reproaching the Government with evading discussion and undue subservience to France.—The CHAN- CELLOR of the Ex-Dew:ran replied to the objections raised to proceedings in the Cenference, and to the charges of mis- leading Parliament and keeping it,in the dark. As to the general question, he asserted that in the serious responsi- bility thrown on them by the failure of the Conference, the Government were acting wisly in sending one of their num- ber to investigate the new condition of the problem, and, if so, they were justified in maintaining silence at the present moment.—Sir M Hicas BEAM complained of the obstinate silence of the Goecrnment in resent to General Gordon. He hoped that Lord literthbrook's mission would be the turning over of a new leaf, and though lie was anxious for the ter- mination of our occupation, he thought that the fixing of the date ought to rest with us alone.--Mr Ashmead-Bartlett and Mr Finch-Hatton also spoke, and the subject then dropped. frame GRIEVANCES.—After this there was a further con- versation on the Tubbercurry arrests and the Maamtrasna murders, in which Mr O'Brien, Mr Herrington, and other Irish members took part, and the Appropriation Bill passed through Committee and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15 The Commons' e.mendments to the Intestates' Estates Bill was agreed to. The Public Health Members and Officers Bill was read a second time, and, the standing orders having been suspended, the hill passed through the remaining stages. The Disused Burial Grounds Bill and the ChOlera, arcs Protection Bill were read a third time and passed. The House then adjourned during pleasure. Their lordships re- assembled at seven o'clock, and the Appropriation Bill haying been brought from the Commons and read a first time, adjourned till three o'clock next day. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 3-10. ITALY, TURKEY, AND THE CONFERENCE. In reply to Sir R. Peel's question (put by Sir H. Holland), Lord E. FILZSIALMICE said the British Ministers at Rome and Con- stantinople had been iestructed to express to the Italian and Turkish Governments the thanks of Her Majesty's Government for the cordial support given to the British proposals in the Conference. The precedent of 1873 did not apply, and there was no intertion to act as suggested in the question, and present a piece of plate to the Italian delegate. ZULUS AND Bonus.—Tn reply to Mr. A. Bartlett's ques- tion (asked by Lord It. Churchill), Mr. ASHLEY said the account in The Times regarding the Boer attack on Uelbspu was founded on the statement of Mr. Dart, one of the white men who, for weal or not, had thrown in their lot with Usibepn. Mr. Ashley had nothing to add to former answers. Her Majesty's Government recognised their obligation to preserve order in the Zulu reserve, but they recognised no obligation to interfere between the Zulus and the Beers in- vited into their country. Lust; QUESLIONS.—TIIO SOLICITOR-GENERAL for IRE- LAND promised to make inquiries as to the alleged issue of a Public circular in Ireland directing the movements of Mr. J. R. Cox, the secretary to the Lord Mayor of Dublin, to he carefully watched.—ln answer to Mr. T. P. O'Connor, Sir W. HARCOURT also promised to inquire into the alleged arrest of Mr. Ennis, president of the Land League at KU- more.
APPROPRIATION BILL. On the motion of the thiid reading of the Appropriation

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: Bill, Lord R. CHURCHILL desired to call attention to the i enormous growth of the expenditure of the country. There was an increase in the total amount appropriated this year I as compared with last year of something like five millions, and he was persuaded that there would be no salutary check on the expenditure of the country until the accounts of each of the great spending departments underwent a rigid investigation from a select committee of the House. He could not congratulate the Chancellor of the Exchequer on the circumstances that had marked his tenure of office, and characterised as a piece of Ministerial indecency the fact that the proposal he had made for debasing the half-sovereign had been allowed to drop without any explanation either of tbe reasons for which it was brought forward or those for which it was withdrawn. He forebore from detailed com- ment on the manner in which the principal measures brought forward by the Government had been abandoned, because it was apparent to everyone both as to the London Government Bill and the Merchant Shipping Bill, that the Government had never had any serious idea of carrying these •• :r •Irtn etete. measures, although in the Case of me taw., ments of the Governmnnt were true as to the loss of life the bill was intended to remedy, their conduct in its with- drawal had been flagitious. The result of the action of the Government had been the total waste of a whole session. The noble lord went on to speak of the appointment of Lord Northbrook as High Commissioner to Egypt, and the send- ing out of Sir Evelyn Baring in company with him, remark- ing that both those individuals were members of the great house of Baring, and that the Government might as well have sent out two members of the house of Rothschild, and entrusted to them the entire control of England's political and financial interests in the East. The CHANCELLOR of the Excanet JER, replying to the criticisms just indulged in said the noble lord seemed to think that the mantles cf Lord Lyndhurst and I.ord Bea- consfield, who were in the habit of summing up the doings of a session, had fallen upon him ; but there was this mar- ked difference, that the weapons of Lords Lyndhurst and Beaconsfield in attacking the policy of their opponents did not consist, as did those of the noble lord himself, of abu- sive language and the calling of names. These were the things which principally distinguished the oratory of the noble lord, whose vulgar abuse, howeeer, did no harm. As to the accounts of the different public departments, be remin- ded the House that the Prime Minister had expressed the readiness of the Government to accept the appointment of a Select Committee of the souse to consider the expenditure of the different departments, bat the House had not taken any step in that direction. With regard to the noble lord's insinuations with reference to Lord Northbrook's connection with the house of Baring, the fact was that Lord Northbrook had no commercial connection with that holm at all, and the attack made upon him would have been- considered un- worthy of the noble lord (Churchill) were it not that he made these attacks so frequently and so frivelously that no one took any serious notice of them. In reply to Sir H. Holland, Mt.E. ASHLEY elated that he was unable to give any information as to the recall of Mr. Mackenzie, the British resident In Bechuanalad:-111r-W E. FORnTER urged the necessity of insisting on, the preeer- ration of order. Mr.Rrrenne, entered upon a general condemnation of the Government's conduct in abandoning useful meascres be- cause they had been checked in regard to an incomplete pro- posal in the direction of Parliamentery reform. Mr. O'BRIEN called attention to the refusal of tho Solici- tor-General for Ireland to grant him a-return in the shape of Lord Justice Fry's report to the Lord Chancellor of Ireland % as to the frauds of Mr. George Bolton upon his wife.'—The SOLICITOR•GENERAL for IRELAND replied that the docu- ments asked for were confidential.--After remaras from Mr. Callan and Mr. Harrington on the same subject, Mr. Atel•• MEAD Beetenna-r condemned the conduct of the Foreign Office as having strained the relations 04 England with -the French Republic. Mr. Broome recalled attention to the Bolton case.—Mr. O'Coetwon asked for protection to a family in Queen's - County who were harassed by night viaite under the Crimes Act from a sergeant of constabulary.—Mr. COURTNEY pro- mised inquiry into the complaint of 'Mr. O'Connor. Tha bill was then read a thi-d time, and the House ad,- journed at 1i55, until Thursday. HOUSE OF LORDS.—WEDN2SIAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsatk, shortly after three o'clock. THE APPROPRIATION BILL, &c.—Lord Motesoet moved the- second reading of the Consolidated Fund (Appropriation) Bill.—Lord DENMAN, in the cours of a long speech, wee understood to complain that the barren result of the session was owing to the making of excessively berg speeches, and, to defend his right and that of every other lay Peer to deliver jedgment on appeal cases,-The Bill was read a second time. The Committee stage was negatived, and the Standing Orders having been suspended the measure was read a third. time and passed—The Corrupt Practices (Suspension of. Elections) Bill was read a third time and paned. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty-five minutes after three o'clock. The Peers present in addition to the Lord Chancellor were- Lord Monson, Lord Stratheden and Campbell, Lord Ash- hurnham, and Lord Denman. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tnunmetev. THE PROROGATION. The fifth session of the tenth Parliament of the Queen. was prorogued on Thursday afterno.n by Royal Commission. The Lord Chancellor entered the House shortly after two o'clock, attended by the Mace and Purse Bearers, and hav- ing taken his place in front of the WOOiSiCiI, prayers were said by the Bishop of London. The Peers present were Lord Barrington, the Earl of Ashburnham, Lord Keane, Lord Car- rington, and Lord Monson. The benches on the opposite side of the House were occupied by ladies, who had obtained tickets of admission, as had also the ladies and gentlemen in the strangers' gallery, from the Lord Chamberlain's office. The Speaker of the House of Commons, attended by the Ser- geant at Arms, carrying the mace, and a number of the members of the Lower House, appeared at the bar in the course of a few minutes. THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. The Lord Chancellor then read the Qemen's speech as follows :

MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN,— The satisfaction with which I ordinarily release you from discharging the duties of the Session is, on the present oc- casion, qualified by a sincere regret that an important part of your labours should have failed to result in a legislative enactment. The most friendly intercourse continues to subsist between myself and all foreign powers. Diplomatic relations have been resumed with Mexico, and a preliminary agreement has been signed providing for the negotiation of a new treaty of commerce and navi- gation. I have to lament the failure of the effoits which were made by the European Powers assembled in the recent con- ference to devise means for restoring the equilibrium in the finances of Egypt, which is so important an element in its well-being and good order. I shall continue to fulfil with fidelity the duties which grow out of the presence of my troops in the Valley of the Nile, and I trust that the special mission which I have de- termined upon sending to the country may materially aid ma I: considering what counsels to tender to the Egyptian Goverummt, and what steps to adopt in connection there- with. Imperial authority has been resumed in Basutoland, and as much progress made in the settlement of its affairs as I could reasonably have anticipated. The Convention concluded with the delegates from the Transvaal has been ratified by the Volksraad. I regret that the condition of Zululand outside the Reserve continues to be disturbed. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,— I thank you for the liberal provision which you have made to sustain the Establishment of the country.

MY LORDS AND GENTLCURN,— I continue to view with unabated satisfaction the mitiga- tion and diminution of agrarian crime in Ireland, and the substantial improvement in the condition of its people. I acknowledge with thankfulness the favourable season, and the prospect it affords ef an alleviation of the pressure which has no long and so severely affected the agricultural industry of the country. I have had pleasure in giving my assent to the Act for. lightening the burden of the National Debt, by the conver- sion of stock, the Act for the Repression of the Corrupt Practices at Municipal Elections, the Act relating to the Contagious Diseases of Animals imported from abroad, and the Act for the Extension of the hours of polling in Boroughs. It is my design again at an early period to draw your at- tention, as I have done during the session now expiring, to the great subject of the representation of the people. I rsjoice to observe amidst the numerous indications of the interest generally felt in this subject constant proofs of loyalty to the Throne and respect for the law. These indi- cations inspire me with a full belief that a great national aim will on this, as on many other occasions, be pursued with order and moderation, the best securities for such a settlement as may, under the blessing of Divine Providence, conduce to the happiness and liberties of the people, and the strength of the Empire. The Speaker and the House of Commons then retired, and the session came to an end at half-past two o'clock.

div.p: HOUSE OF CONDIONS.-THIIRSDAY.,

_ The Speaker entered the House shortly after half-past one, but did not take the Chair, there not being a quorum pre- sent. Sir Charles Dilke, Lord Edmund Fitzmaurice, and Mr. G. Russell were the only members of the Government on the Treasury Bench. The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod (Admiral Sr J. R. Drummond) made his appearance at eight minutes past two, and summoned the members to at- tend in the other House to hear the Royal Assent read by commission to maasures agreed upoa by bath Houses. On their return at half-past two the Speaker, there being still no quorum, took his seat in the place where Sir Erskine May usually sits at the table. Addressinz the members present the Speaker said : For the convenience of the House I will read Her Majeaty's Most Gracious Speech to both Houses, of which I have obtained a copy. He then read the speech, all the members uncovering. At the close the members present filed p Ist the Speaker, who shook bands and bade good-bye to each member, the hand-shaking being repeated as the members passed Sir Erskine May and Cap- tain Gossett. The proceedings were closed at 20 minutes to three.

ATTEMPTED TRIPLE MURDER —Early on Thursday mor- ning a man named Fisher, residing in Lambeth, attacked his wife, her sister, and her mother, the last named being aged eighty-one, with a stone-mason's mallet, breiakin, the last named's arm and injuring her head, besides inflicting severe injuries upon the others. Scarcely any hope is en- tertained of the r,.coyery of Fisher's mother-in law and sister-in-law, who are in hospital.

FOREIGN NEWS.

_ EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. CAIRO, SUNDAY NIGHT.—MaSOII Bey telegraphs from Massowah that Gallabut has fallen into the hands of the rebels, and that the people of Gedarif have teen ordered to retire upon Kassala. The preparations for the Gordon relief expedition are progressing rapidly. Four hundred camels are being purchased for the ueo of the mounted infantry, which will be under the command of Major Gough, in the absence of Major Hutton. Sir E. Wood starts up the Nile on a tour of inspection on Wednesday, and will probably push on to Dongola, accompanied by Major Malloy, RE, Zahrah Bey, Major Sandwitb, and Major Wingate. The South Staffordshire Regiment will be sent on to the frent in the course of the week: Rue Alula is inciting the 13oghos tribes to insurrection, and the state of Abyssinia is emi- nently unsatisfactory. In accordance with the advice given by Major Kitchener to the Sheiks the meeting of the Birba-1 reen tribes has been postponed. Saleh Aglia holds the road Routh of Debbih with a large force. The weather here is exceedingly hot. WADY Hama, SIINDAY.—The Nile has now reached its highest point, after fifteen days' rise, and is passable for dahabeeyahs. An extensive system of fortification is being I carried out here. The works can already shelter 600 men against all attacks unaided by artillery, and when finished will hold 1,200 men. Jo hostile force has been near this place for a month past, and it is quite impossible, with the present system of vedettes and Bedouin scouts, for any rebe'e to approach us unawares. ASIOUAN, MONDAY, 7 P M.—Major Stuart Wortley is leaving here for Esneh, and will take the remainder of the Bedouins to Wady Haifa. The 2ad Battalion of the Essex Regiment has arrived at Esneh. The engines of the steamer conveying them have broken down, and another steamer has gone to render assistance. CAIRO, MONDAX.—The 10th Battalion of the Egyptian Ar ny, with a camel company. will start up the Nile from Assouan to•morrow. Major Kitchener has been most enthu- siastically renived in Debbeh and on his waythither. Major Kitchener left Debbch yesterday. Major Stuart Wortley reports that the recapture of Berber by General Gordon is generally credited above Wady Haifa, and that Hussein Pasha Khania, former Governor of Barber, has been taken to El Obeid. THE VICTORY OF THE muma OF DONGOLA. Cern°, TV/MAY.— Major Kitchener is still at Debbeh. He confirms toe statement tSat the Mudir of Donsola has gained a victory over the rebel there, in which many of the latter were killed. THE NILE EXPEDITION.—BRITISH TROOPS

NOTES BY TEIE WAY.

At St. Helens, on Saturday, the Victoria Rangers defeated the Albert Institute, the scores being—Rangers, 46; Insti- tute, 34. The Peasley Cross Rangers and the Garn--- Amateurs (2nd elevens) met at Pee. 1.2,-; Cross, the result being—Amateurs, 32 • -P-e-ogers, 29. The Albion Amateurs tcccteston) defeated the Albiod Star by 106 runs to 65; and the York-street schools 2ad eleven defeated the Groves Rangers by 61 rens to 29. Rain largely interfered with the match Gloucestershire v. Australians at Clifton, on Saturday, and eventually caused it to be abandoned as a draw, but there was sufficient play for the county to obtain a great batting triumph. Making allowance for the ground being in favour of the batting side, the performance was a fine one, and should go a great way towards improving the reputation of Gloucestershire as a cricketing county. The main credit rests with Messrs. Brain and Pullen. These two young Gloucester amateurs got together when the score was 22 for one wicket, and put on 159 runs before they were pirted. Brain, who went in first, scored 108 out of 181, and though missed before he had mode a run, and again at 45, his innings could scarcely have been surpassed for a display ef dashing cricket. Pal en. who went in when the score was 22, was not out for 68 when the game had to be abandoned. He was missed by the wicket-keeper when he had made 29, and again at 33. Some idea of the rapid nature of the run-getting may be gathered from the fact that 230 runs were obtained in two hours and twenty minutes' play. Mr. Brain's 108 is the tenth innings of three figures hit against the present team.—Middleeex beat Kent on Saturday, at Canterbury. by five wickets. When play was resumed in the morning Kent, who had lost nine wickets in their second atttempt for 190 over night, finished off their innings for 209, leaving Middlesex 173 to get to win. Score: Kent, 169 and 209: Middlesex, 206, and 173 for five wickets.—Lancashire secured an easy vic- tory over Leicestershire on Saturday, winning by an innings and 62 runs. Score : Leicestershire, 115 and 118; Lanca- shire, 293.—Hampshire on Saturday beat Somerset at South- ampton by an billings and 169 runs. The Somersetshire eleven made good use of the excellent wicket at Taunton, on Tuesday, bat they were so handi- capped by their failure on Monday tbat the better cricket only mitigated in a slight degree theserarity of their defeat,l and late in the afternoon Lancashire had gained a decisive ' victory by eight wickets. Mr. C. Newton played a fine innings of 62, and, together with Mr. Terry, raised the score from 39 to 85, the Somersetshire captain making 62 out of the 90 totalled while he was batting. Lancashire had 68 runs to win, and Mr. Hornby and Whittaker made a good start, the score being 44 before they were separated: Mt. Hornby was ~ut at 55 to a good catch at long off. The Northern county owed their victory in a large measure to Mr. Hornby and Watson. The former made 102 runs in the match, and Watson took eleven wickets for an average of ander 11 runs each. Score : Lancashire, 215 and 88; Somersetshire, 86 and 196. After three days' hard cricket, the laet of the three repre- sentative matches ended on Wednesday, at Kennington Oval, in a draw. England at the finish being 120 runs be- hind, with eight wickets to fall. The result will be received with great pleasure by all lovers of English cricket, as, after the tremendous score of the Australians, the Englishmen , had only to play for a draw, and in this endeavour they proved immensely suacessful.—ln match Sussex v. Derby- shire, at Brightln, on Tuesday, Derbyshire, in the follow on, had lost three wickets for 73 runs. On resuming play, on Wednesday, Sugg and Woodsims raised the figures to 107, when Humphreys was deputed with slows. The change was effectual, botk batsmen being stumped after batting well for their respective scores. The innings closed for 236. Sussex, requiring 75 to obtain a:victory., lost three wickets in obtain- ing the required number. At ten minutes to five Sussex had won the match by seven wickets. At the Trent Bridge ground, Nottingham, on Thursday, Mr I D Walker, in the return match between Middlesex and Nottinghamshire, payed a remarkably fine innings of 80. He went in first for Middlesex and was out seventh, the tot al when he left being 170 —Mackinnon played a brilliant innings of 102 for Kent, against Yorkshire, at Gravesend, on Thursday. He wed tin first and was out sixth, with the total at 185. Mackinnon, Lord Harris, and Kemp made between them more than three-fourths of the runs for their county.

SIMLA, WEDITMAY.—In pursnance of directions from the Home Government the let Battalion of the 18th Regi- ment and the 70th Regiment, now onde orders for England On ordinary reliefs, will proceed to Egypt. The former will start on the 81st inct, and the latter on September 8. The Indian Government b understood to be opposed to the deple- tion of the British forte in India. Canso, WEDNESDAV3.—Sir Evelyn Wood, accompanied by his staff, Red Major Sandwith, started this morning up the Nile to inspect the fortifications and the Enslish and Egyptian camps. The chartered transport liankow sailed to-day tor Bom- bay. Porantount, WEDNEMOY. The troopship Otontes sailed hence this afternoon. for Queenstown to take in•mili- tary drafts for Gibraltar, thence going on with a regiment to Alexandria. Assouakss, TRIIRSDLY, 2P.ll.—CAptain Roardman, has arrived here, and will take command of tho-flotilla of war steamers in place of Captain Bedford. The 58th Regiment, numbering 670 men. arrived hem at daybreak. The troops were enthusiastically cheered. Official intelligence has boen received that the expeaion for the relief of General Gordon will go by, way of thisl place up the Nile to Khartoum. Calttoi TITCTRSDAY.-Sit Redvers Buller is shortly expected to leave England for Egypt ar.thief of staff to Major-Geneval, Earle.

THE CEOLERA. TOULON, SATURDAY, 9-40 A zu—There were riree death from cholera here last night. One death from cholera has• occurred in the suburbs, and Caere has been another at La, Sevne to-day. TOULON, SCNDAY, 6 A.ll.—There were four dastbs from- cholera here last night. There has not been a siagle death. here from cholera since ten o'clock this morning. One death

has occurred at Le Beausset. MARSRILLES, SUNDAY, 8-49 "2:w.—The officiat• bulletin issue, this evening gives the number of deaths i.trting the- last 24 hours at 49, of which 14 were from cholera. MAREDILLES, MONDAY, 8-30 -.,:ist.—The official bulletin issued this morning gives the number of deaths during the- last 24 hours as 42, of which 15 were from cholera, Tout.ors, MONDAY.—Since ten o'clock this morning there have been no deaths from cholera here, though there were three deaths last night and two more at Montroft-sur- Argens. It is estimated that sinus the outbreak of the epi- demic 8,000 persons have been attacked, of whom SOO have

died. Rome, MONDAY. Te-day's official sanitary bulletin. states that a death from cholera, has occurred at Valderno, near Cairo Montennotte. At Siermezzana, near Minuciano, province Massa Carrarra, there have been two cases, one followed by death; at Castelnovo, near Garfagnana, three fatal cases; and at Pancaliere four fresh cases, two of which were fatal. One death also occurred among patients already under treatment. Another case has been reported from Osasio. MARSEILLES, TUESDAY MORDINO.—There have been four deaths from cholera since eight o'clock last evening. TOULON, TUESDAY MORNING—NO deaths from cholera here last night. ROME, TUESDAY.—Three deaths from cholera are officially reported from the provinces to-day. FRANCE AND CHINA. EH/an:MAI, SUNDAY—The French squadron under the command of Admiral Lessens, consisting of Eye vessels, has bombarded the town of in the island of For- mosa. There was no loss on the French side. The Chinese losses are unknown. The amount of the French indem- nity is reduced to 8000,030 ft%, payable in tea annual in- stalments. FOOCHOW, MONDAY —Ks-lung has not yet been actually taken. The French destroyed the forts and then retired. Their losses are unknown. The Chinese are daily becoming more and more emboldened by the inaction of the French. PAILIS, TUESDAY —To-day's Voltaire publishes an account of the taking of Kin-lung by the French, which says opera- tions were effected with a French loss of one killed and two wounded. The Voltaire adds that a squadron under Admiral Lespes remains before Ke-lung preventing Chinese vessels from coaling. The naval division under Admiral Courbet, with the exception of four vessels which have taken up a position before Woosung, at the entrance to the river, re- mains before Foochow, in order, if necessary, to support M. Patenotre's demands. A further despatch from Admiral Lespes states that the French losses were two killed and four wounded. FRENCH WAR PREPARATIONS. SHANGHAI, WEDNESDAY.—The Tsung-li-Yainen has pro- tested to the treaty Powers against the bombardment of Kr-lung without a declaration of war, and has announced its determination to resist the French demands. The port of Tam Sui, in Formosa, is being defended by torpedoes. Li Hung Chang has been impeached for transferring the China Merchants' fleet to an American firm. THE FRENCH REVISION CONGRESS. PARIS, SATURDAY.—:Up to the present Congress has ire- jected five amendments directed against the Revision Bill, but 20 more still remain to he discussed. There were no disturbances ai the sitting to-day. VERSAILLES, MONDAY.—The Congress to-day rejected by a large majority two further amendments to the Revision Bill, and subsequently, by 523 votes against 139, adopted Article lof the measure. The Assembly then commenced the discussion of Article 2, which prohibits any proposal for the revision of the Republican form of Gav<rnment„ and declares that Princes belonging to former reigning families in France are ineligible for the post of President of the Re. public. Monsignor Freppel declared that the Article was useless. If the French people should at any time become tired of the Republic and desire to return to the hour& of France, which had made the glory and unity of I!, ance, the article would not prevent tt doing. SO, (Members of the Left uttered tries of 4. Which Houfie of Frilled; I") Mgr. Freppel replied, " There is only one House of Franca—that represented by the Comte do Paris." This remark occa- sioned considerable disturbance among members of the Left, and M. Fioquet exclaimed, "You have just pro- nounced the condemnation of the Comte de Paris, and we will carry it out.—A proposal to discuss the Tonquin ques- tion was deferred till the close of the Congress on Wednes- day or Thursday. VERSAILLES, "TUESDAY.—The Congress this afternoon re- jected two amendments to the the Revision Bill—one for the abolition of the presidency of the Republic, and the other providing that the President should be directly elected by universal suffrage. VERSAILLES, TUESDAY —The Congress rejected without I discussion an amendment prohibiting the princes of former French reigning families from residing in French territory, and proposing to confiscate their property.—The Congress will probably conclude tomorrow. VERSAILLES, Wm:no:sr:ay.—The Congress after speeches delivered by Senator Daugbin and M. Clemenceau, to-day rejected by 418 votes against 327 votes, the amendment proposed by M. Lavergne for the election of the members of the Senate by universal suffrage. The Congress subse- quently adopted all the articles of the Revision Bill after having thrown out all the amendments proposed. The bill in its entirety was then adopted by 509 votes against 172. The Extreme Left abstained from voting, declaring that the principles of democracy had been violated. Count de Muni (Clerical) declared that the debates in Congress had demon- stri.ted the powerlessness of the Republicans, and declared that France would judge the result. The President then declared the session of Congress clos id The Cham'Ar of Deputies will discuss the Tonquin credits to-morrow. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR. PARTS, THLIRSDAY.—The•Sente to-day adopted by 179 votes against one the vote of credit of five million francs esked for by the Government on account of operations in Madagascar. FATAL FLOODS IN AUSTRIA. VIENNA, SONDAY.—The town of Jaslo, in Galicia, a place of some extent, has been almost entirely destroyed by fire. div.head: TERRIBLE THUNDERSTORMS.
div.p: TERRIBLE THUNDERSTORMS.
SEVERAL PERSONS KILLED AND GREAT DAMAGE TO PROPERTY-.

- - A terrible thunderstorm, resulting in the destruction of an enormous amount of property, broke over the Rossendale Valley OR Saturday afternoon. It extended from the source of the river Irwell on the one hand to Haslingden and Ac- criagtoh Moors on the other. The heavy rains powing upon the hillsides formed innumerable rills, which, rushing into the Irwell, raised its depth several feet in 20 minutes. The storm raged with great fury over Newchurch, Waterfoot, and Cowpe. For a quarter of an hour there was a shower of ice, in fragments globular, conical, and square, varying from three inches long to an inch in thickness. These large pieces of ice were not exceptional, but general, and their destructive effects are he be seen in the damage they have caused to property over an area ef two miles. Rows of houses, schools, churches, and mills appear as if they had suffele4.l from a riot, wherein the rioters bad wreaked their fury on the windows, manv of which had every square broken. There were 180 squares of glass broken in the Catholic School at Newchurch; at St.. Nicholas's Church the windows faclng the south are all riddled as if with shot, and only the stained glass windows, which are protected with wire fencing, remain intact. Nearly all the houses in the district have their windows broken, in one there being no fewer than 76 broken panes. Nearly all the hothouses have suffered, and the skylights of the mills and fruit works are all demolished. The gardens have been spoiled, the roadways are washed up—in a great many places farrows being ploughed several feet deep—and mills and cellars were flooded. The damage sustained by shop- keepers and cottage property owners for broken windows alone will amount to several hundred pounds. By far the most serious damage has been sustained in the Cowpe Valley, which is about a mile and'a half in extent. A terrific thunderstorm occurred at Stratford-on-Avon on Saturday afternoon, shortly before two o'clock. Rain and hailstones descended in torrents. The latter were about three quarters of an inch in diameter, and lay upon the roads from two to three inches deep. The thunder has been heavier than has been known for many years. Women screamed and fainted. An immense ball of fire was seen to fall close to Shakespeare's birthplace, fortunately without

doing any damage. A severe thunderstorm has burst over Blackpool, Preston, and the greater part of North Lancashire, and lasted till about two o'clock on Monday morning. The storm was exceedingly heavy, and at times rain fell in torrents. Some damage is reported, but no fatalities. The storm Came at the close of a day said to be the hottest during the present year. A terrific thunderstorm burst over Ramsey at one o'clock on Monday morning, prevailing over an hour. The house of Mr Kellow Lucas was struck, the roof smashed In, and some furniture and a looking glass destroyed. A nurse and two children sleeping in one room had a marvellous escape. 'The marble mantel piece ornaments and furniture in a room below were also destroyed. Mr. Lucas is absent yachting in Scotland. Another house was struck, and a young man lodger was stunned temporarily. The lightning entered his bedroom, twisted the iron bedstead, smashing the furniture and wall. A heary thunderstorm visited the Dumfriesshire district on I • Tuesci -ix morning, followed by drenching rain. During the height of the storm in London, on Tuesday morning, a house in Mile End-road was struck by lightning, and its chimney fell into the street, some men, proceeding to work, having a narrow escape. The telegraph wires in the same road were struck, and one of the wires fell across the carriage way. During a violent thunderstorm which passed over Leith on Tuesday morning, a four-storeyed house was struck by lightning and very seriously 'damaged, but none of- the inmates were injured. The storm WAS followed by heavy darkness, which enveloped the town until about 12 o'clock at noon. The new parish church of Glenrinnes, Banffshire, has been struck by lightning, and set on fire. The belfry was completely consumed and the roof much injured, before the flames could be extinguished. The bell fell into the edifice

and smashed some seats and woodwork. At Little Langton. near Northallerton, a mmn was struck by lightning and killed. A child in his arms escaped un- injured. A severe thunderstorm visited Middlesborough on Tues- day. A woman at North Ormesby was rendered insensible by the lightning. Michael NGuellin, a farm labourer. aged nineteen, whilst engaged in sprinkling lime on a field at Old Ormesby, was struck by lightning and killed instan- taneously. A telegram reached Edinburgh on Tuesday evening re- porting that during a terrible thunderstorm in the Lauder district Lord Lauderdale was struck on the moors by light- ning. His lordship, who was mounted on a pony, was pro- ceeding across the Braidshaw Rigg on the Lauderdale estate when the storm was at its height. His lordship and the pony were both struck by lightning. A later account states that his lordship has died from the injury he re- ceived. A church was struck and damaged by lightning, as was also a large chimneystack, at Johnstone, the latter indeed being completely wrecked. At Johnstone also hayricks were set on fire, and factories, ttc, damaged by the rain and floods. At Irvine a cottaue was fired and burnt to the ground, and a number of hayricks were destroyed. At Castle Douglas the gable of a house was knocked down. and a photographer's studio shattered into fragments. At Annan the lightning entered a house, injuring two girls therein, killiag a dog, and wrecking the building. Haystacks were burnt at Tar- bolton, and the tower of Birkwood House sustained consi- derable damage.

During the whole of Tuesday thare were throughout the entire North of Ireland terrific thunderstorms, accompanied by lightning. Much damage has been done in various dis- tricts. The storm in Belfast was in the morning. During the day a great deal of injury was done in the counties of Antrim, Down, Derry, ami Armagh. Two men are reported killed by lightning at Ballyward, seven miles from Castle. wellan county Down. Three valuable cows and a horse were killed at Waterask, between Newcastle and Dundrum ; and a horse was killed near Castlewellan. Four cows were killed between Newcastle and Annalong. From many dis- tricts similar reports are being received. On Tuesday afternoon a violent thunderstorm visited For- far and district, and continuad about four hours. The dark- ness at one o'clock was so great that gas had to be lighted. The thunder and lightning were almost incessant, and rain fell in torrents, Two houses were struck by lightning, but no persons were injured. Reports from the country around Glasgow allow that the lightning hes caused much havoc. Sunnyside Railway Station was struck, and the chimneys and roof were abet- tered, but no one area injured. At Irvine the house of a ploughman was burned, and stacks of by were destroyed in several places. In many districts the crops were laid flat and fields flooded by the overflow of rivers. At Leith the storm continued till about four o'clock. The ro3f of Bennington Sugar Refinery was struck by lightning, which also entered the police station at Newhaven, ignited the gas, and destroyed the wire communication with the head office. The lightning also set fire to North Trinity House, and caused considerable damage. Grecian Cottage, Trinity, was also struck, and the gas ignited. The darkness at noon was intense, and heavy rain and hail fell. At Cimbusdoon several sheep were killed under a tree. . .
In Mayhole the chimney stack of a shoe factory was shattered, and the spire of the parish church was greatly

_ damaged. A Middlesborough telegram states that a severe thunder- storm visited that place on Tuesday. A woman at North Ormesby was rendered insensible by lightning. Mic'ael M`Guellin, farm labourer, aged 19, while engaged in sprink ling lime on a field at Old Ormesby, was struck by light- ning and killed instantaneously. A telegram from Cardiff states that shortly after ten a.m. a terrific thunderstorm burst over the place, accompanied by lightning and thunder. Rain fell in perfect torrents, and the thunder was so heavy as to cause buildings to shake to the foundations. A large tower on a block of buildings in the town was struck by the lightning and much damaged. Two !muses at Stockton were struck, one being completely wrecked.
At Lewisham, near Whitby, the storm caused a fall of earth from an embankment, blocking the railway.

A P Eccles was easily bowled, and Dobell and Aldrich were together, the score standing at 68. Both played carefully, and change after change of bowling was tried, but without success. div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
MEETING if LIVERPOOL. •

A meeting of gentlemen interested in the construction of a canal between Liverpool and Manchester was held on Wednesday at the office of Mr Marshall Stephens, Fenwick- street, Liverpoel. In addition to Mr Stephens, who was almost the sole Liverpool representative upon the commit- tee for the promotion of the Ship Canal, there were present —Mr Adamson, the chairman of the committee; Mr J'acob Bright, M.P. and other gentlemen from Manchester, to meet whom Lieutenant-Colonel Paris, Mr Edward Paul, and MrJohn Paterson, Liverpool, had been invited. An informal conversation took place as to the nature of a new water cam- munication between Liverpool and'ildanchester, in regard to which there should be the minimum of opposition ; and the Manchester representatives were led to understand that the great anxiety of Liverpool being to preserve intact the estuary of the Mersey, any scheme which did not imperil that condition would not be likely to meet with opposition but rather with co-operation. The dimensions of the canal e., whether it should be adapted for ships or merely for large barges—and the route which it should pursue, were matters left over for further consideration. After the meet- ing the Manchester visitors, with Mr Stephens, took a steamer and visited the points upon tha Lancashire side of the Mersey at Hale, and on the Cheshire side nearly oppo- site, where, in the modified canal schemes which have been suggested since the rejection of the maier project, it is pro- posed the canal should debouch.

div.p: WORKMEN'S CLUB SPORTS.

An amateur athletic festival under the auspices of the Warrington Workmen's Club was held in a field adjoining St James's Church, Latchford, on Saturday afternoon, in brilliant weather. The attendance wia4rot as good as might have been expected, as the programme, which was a lengthy one, included some very good events. Counter attractions in the neighbourhood no doubt influeneed the attendance in a considerable measure. The ground was in excellent con- dition, and the general arrangements gave satisfaction. div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

A DISPENSARY AND COTTAGE HOSPITAL FOR HUTTON.-- A correspondent writes urging upon the inhabitants of the Huyton district, from a sanitary point of view, the import- ance of establishing an institution of this sort similar to those existing in various parishes throughout the country, to their manifest and great advantage in many ways. The writer states the have helped to secure tke co-operation of their medical talent, so as to be available in cases of accidents, the early treatment of sickness and disease, and the prevention and spread of fever epidemics, dtc. They are very popular, and the provident dispensary found to be self-supporting or nearly so. Every facility is at hand for establishing the same here with equal benefit. We have the members of the Local Board, the Vicars of Huyton and of Roby, the committee of the schools, several popular clergymen, many able and efficient medical Men, wealthy eentry, merchants, builders, and others. The prin- cipal landowners are Lord Derby, Lord Salisbury, the Earl of Sefton, Captain Willis, the trustees of Mr Case and of Major Seel. A suitable plot of land could easily he selected between the railway ststions Of Roby, Huvton, Huyton Quarry, Whiston, or Tarbuck, which on the applicatioh of the local authorities would likely be given, and perhaps some benefactions might be found to endow it. Every in- formation needful, with suitable plans, rules, &c., may readily be obtained from the secretary ot the National Health Exhibition in London. If those who are favourable to the project were to address Canon Penrbyn, Vicar of Huyton, and enlist his services, ,tbis eminently useful and philanthropic institution would Won be established to the decided benefit of the neighbourhood.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT —On Thursday nitht, as a Windsor special train in connection with the races was approaching Staines it came into collision with a train of "empties" which Was being shunted into a siding. Several passengers land the guard of the express were injured, some of the car- riages were much damaged, and the permanent way was torn up for a considerable distance.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

1 The Queen, with the Princess Beatrice and the Duchess of Albany and children (the younger of whom is said to be very weakly), will probably leave for Scotland in the second week in September. A Cleator Moor Orangeman, named Denizen, was on Thursday committed for trial for h wing attempted to murder Police-constable Forbes, at whom he fired with a re- volver on Saturday last. A verdict of manslaughter has been found by a coroner's Jury at Derby against the man Payne, who threw at his wife a paraffin lamp, which, setting fire to her clothes, burnt her so dreadfully that she died. The outbreak of English cholera at Rishton is now almost a thing of the past. The cas,2s which remain are convales- cent, and by the end of the week the to 4nship is expt cted to be entirely free from the disease. It is now reported that duriug the severe thunderstorm in tne eastern and northern counties of e-corland on Tuesday four persons were killed by lightning, in addifioa to num- bers of horses, cattle, and sheep. THE DUEE OF EDINBURGH, Whe is cruising cff the west coast of Ireland, eras presented with an address of welcome, on Wednesday, at Galway. The Duke seems to have been delighted with the cordiality of his reception. Michael Spence, arrested on Monday at Stalybridge on suspicion of murdering his wife, was on Wednesday released from custody, a post mortem examination haring proved that the women died from apoplexy after a drinking bout. An artilleryman named Bader, stationed at the Curragb, made a 'confession " on Wednesday that three years ago he shot a Kerry farmer, for whose murder two men were afterwards executed. Boder's mental condition is being inquired into. An Under Sheriff's jury at Preston. on Thursday, awarded the sum of £7O to Margaret Ross, a factory operative, re• siddng at Newton Heath, who sued a young man named Jas. Holt for breach of promise of marriage. Thrace was no defence to the action. At a meeting of silk weavers' delegates, hrld at Macclem- field, it has been decided to suspend for a month the trade union formed nine months ago, with a view of testing whether trade will improve by allowing men to make their own terms with employers. The nomination for South Devon took place on Wednes- day, and Mr John Tremayne was returned unopposed. The new member, like his predecessor, is a Conservative, bat he is not in favour of the course which the Lords have taken with regard to the Franchise Bill. The Oldham magistrates on Thursday committed for trial on the capital charge Harry Swindell., who was accused of shooting his brother-iwlaw, James Wild, in July last year. 'lre prisoner had been in America, for twelve months, but voluntarily returned and surrendered a fortnight ago. THE CONDEMNED MAN AT LIFTBPOOL.—There has been so far no reprieve received for the men Peter Cassidy-, now lying in Kirldale Gaol under sentence of death for the murder of his wife at Bootle. Next'Tuesday week has been. fixed for the execution, and Berry, of Bradford, eii be the hangman. A RAILWAY MYSTERY.—On the arrival of the 10-30 p.m. train from Paddington at Slough,. on Monday, a gen- tleman—apparently a foreigner—was diecovered in a dying condition, having shot himself with a revolver. He died in the workhouse infirmary on Tw sday morning, and re- mains unknown. DitownEn IN A MILL LODGE —On 'Aursday morning, James Rooftop, aged six, of Newbold-street, Heywood, Was found drcwned in a warm water lodge belonging to Har- greave's mill. The deceased had to scale- a six feet wall to get to the water. He was last seen alive yesterday by his sister, who found him drowned. Lord Spencer has spared us the shocking spectacle of the execution of a woman by reprieving Catherine Dooley, who was to have been hanged on Saturday at Tellarnore. The woman deliberately murdered her cousin for the sake of his I money, and afterwards had the hardihood to bury the corpse in her own farmyard. EXPRESS TRAINS.—The fastest as well as the longest ran , in the world is that on the Great Northern line from Gran- -1 tbam to Loudon (depart 4-17, arrive at 6 15). 104 miles in , 1 hour 53 minutes, at the rate of .53 2 3 miles as hour, as against the Great Western speed of 53 1-5. and this over a much longer and more difficult route. * WIFE Meatuser.—Thomas Harris, a market gardener, of Harrowroad, Hammersmith, is in custody charged with murdering his wife by catting her threat. Prisoner ad- mitted having committed the murder, adding that he had I been driven to do it by his wife's bad conduct. It is under- stood that the parties have squandered a fortune. "Tan TweL=."—The grouse season opened under varying conditions in different parts of the kinedom. On Tuesday the weather was fine on most of the-Eaglish moan's, and in Yorkshire, Lancashire, Derbyshire, and North Wales excellent sport was obtained, the grouse being strong and disease was quite absent. Rabbits and hares, too, were i plentiful.

PLAYING WITH A REVOLVER.—A Bacup mill manager named Greenwood has accidentally shot a young woman with a revolver, the ball from which entered her shoulder. Greenwood got the revolver the same night from the chim- ney of a house be once occupied, and se he was going along the road he commenced playing with it, not knowing it to be loaded, and he accidentally discharged it. SHEEP Sxxszlign.—At the Wrexham County Police Court, on Wednesday, John Lee, master butcher, having a , shop in Wrexham marker, and Philip Jones, shepherd, employed by Mr William Lee, of Borras and Wrexham, a large farmer and butcher, and father of the prisoner Lee, were committed for tritl noon a charge of stealing two sheep, the property of Mr Robert Thomas Parry, farmer, Borras Hall.

SHOCKING BintrrarrrY.—Richard Dunces, fireman on one of the Wallasey ferry steamers, was on Wednesday, at the Wallasey Police Court, committed to take his trial at the sessions on a charge of unlawfully wounding I- dward Tur- ner. a bricksetter. The evidence for the prosecution was that on Saturday night Turner was set upon by two men, and that while he was on the ground the prisoner bit off a piece of his under lip. EARLY CLosisa.—A series of public meetings in favour of the objects of the Shop Hours' Labour League, and in support of the measure introduced by Sir John Lubbock, Bart., into the House of Commons, is at present being con- ducted by some of the provincial towns. These over, it is Intended to carry on the agitation in the metropolis during the autumn and winter in the same manner as larit year and the twelvemonths previous. SIR EEASIIUS WILSON, late President of the Royal Col- lege of Surgeons, died on Friday; at his residence, The Bungalow, Westgate-on-Sea. He was horn in 1809 s Having amassed great wealth by his practice and his medical works, he gave his money away for charitable objects with great liberality. Her Majesty conferred the honour of knighthood on Mr Wilson in 1881, by which time Sir Rramus had earned national fame of a new sort by bringing the so-called " Cleopatra's Needle" to England. THE Duns OF WELLINGTON died suddenly of heart disease, on Wednesday, at Brighton railway station. He was in his 77th year. The life of the late Duke was , strikingly uneventful and insignificant by comparison with that of hie illustrious father. He is succeeded by his nephew, Henry Wellesley, son of the late Lord Chines Wellesley. The new Duke was formerly a colonel in the I Grenadier Guards, and member of Parliament for Andover. THE BRADFORD CHIMNEY ACCIDENT.—The Leeds jury to which was submitted tbe question of liability in connec- tion with the Bradford mill chimney disaster reassembled on Wednesday and had the evidence again reviewed by the judge. After consultation the jurors agreed in stating that shortly befora the ohimney fell it was in a dangerous con- dition, but they could not agree upon the main question as to who was responsible. They were accordingly dis- charged. FIRE IN LONDON AND Loss or Foul LtvEs.—A destruc- tive and fatal fire broke.out shortly befoie 8 a.m, on Tues- day, at Mr Abraham's, a hatter's shop in Wilton-street. Pimlico. Despite the strenuous efforts of the firemen, at least four persons Perished in the flames. Several members of Mr Abraham's family, who were aroused from their sleep, hesitated to escape until it became neceesary to jump from I the second floor window. Mrs Abrahams and one daughter, Jeannette, saved themselves in this way. but Mark Abra- hams, proprietor of the shop; Mrs Marks, his motner-in- law ; Lily Abrahams, a daughter, and another were burnt to death. The aged lady was found in a chair in her bedroom, having been rendered imientible by smoke before the fire I reached her. DEATH OF A CHESTER MISEIL—A well-known character named Abraham Price, better known by the sebriquet of Abraham Hodge, was buried on Saturday, in Chester Ceme- tery. He kept a bookstall on a vacant space in the Eaetgate-row. He was a clever and assiduous book collec- tor, dirty in appearance and miserable in his habits. He was originally a member of the Chester police force. Recently he had been confined to his home from Maim. He had no relatives, and nothing is known of his early life. He was repeatedly presaed to make his will, but he kept repeat- ing the formula, "The Crown shall make my will." When he died the Chester police took possession on behalf of the Crown of Hodge's property and cash, and it was found that the old miser was possessed in goods and money of 15,000. TERRIBLE BOILER EXPLOSION. FOUR PER3ONS KIL- LED:At Tinsley Iron, Steel, and Wire Works of William Cooke and Co, near Sheffield, on Monday afternoon, a boiler exp`oded, killing four men and injuring several others. A I urnaceman named Hammond, aged 40, was feeding the fur- nace at the time, and be was blown to pieces. Joseph Nunn, 45, carter, and Thomas Applewhite, labourer, aged 40, were passing at the time, whec a portion of the boiler struck them with fatal effect. Three of tbe injured men were taken to the infirmary, where one died shortly after admit- /don, making the fourth death. Two horses were killed. Theugh the works were seriously damaged, the machinery has sus'ained comparatively little injury. The cause of the explosion is uektiown. The boiler is stated to have been new eight years ago, and at the time of the explosion the men were getting up steam, there being only a pressure of 33Ibs, while the boiler iec-nstructed to withstand 501bs pres- sure. Ail the injured men at the infirmary are progressing favourably with the exception of James Hughes, who has sustained internal injuries, the precise nature of which hies not been ascertained. e. SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1884.

- LORD SALISBURY has at last "descended into the streets,' after sneering from his loftY 1 pedestal in the House of Lords at tiler Liberals who preceded him in this mode c° appealing to the people. But he is nothing 1 if not inconsistent ; and, after having, as Mr' BRIGHT once said, prostituted his talents t° obtain the reversion of a place which.he maY never secure, there seems to be no limit tn, the depth of the degradation he is prepare° to undergo. His audacity and mendacit,Y, are alike measureless, and in this respect ° may indeed be said that he is following jue the footsteps of Lord BEACONSFIELD, WIIP 1 the difference that the adroit Jew had mot! flexibility and grace of movement. Granten, 1 , that he was "the villain " of the politiCa' drama, he wasn't quite so " heavy" a villain as Lord SALISBURY. But looked at from attY point of view, it is appalling to witness the disregard of principle which is being show" by the leaders of the Tory party, excepting; let us add, Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE. Lo" RANDOLPH CHURCHILL in December last denounced, in the old-fashioned Tory stYlef the proposal to extend the franchise ; but he , found that it was "not agreeable" to the party managers, and, as he coolly admits, he took a fresh tack In the House of Cony mons, not many weeks ago, he gave the, House of Lords to understand that it wouln be dangerous and foolish to reject the Frall' chise Bill. At Manchester, on Saturday, her stood on a platform to support the House 0,; Lords in doing what, in anticipation, he bal: himself condemned. It is not suggested tha' he has honestly changed his mind; he bas simply found that his views were " not agree' able to the Tory party," and he baS' therefore, turned about and "jumped PI Crow." He may think this very clever, ao , that he does it with easy grace. "It is Os easy as lying," as HAMLET says, and, let e 5 add, as disreputable and demoralising. It I the same with Lord SALISBURY. He 114 I displayed a life-lono• contempt for II:, masses ; he left the Tory Cabinet in 187 , because Mr. DISRAELI, yielding to the pre/t- -sure of the Liberals, was disposed to assend to a large extension of the Franchise; it l't not twelve months since he argued tb,,3e nobody wanted a further extension of tPe_ Suffrage; it is not twelve weeks sin,..co i he quailed before Lord GRANVILLE. vit,',r challenged him to say that he was in favn"to of the Franchise Bill ; and yet he comes , Nlanchester, and would have the public be lieve that he is more anxious than Mr. GL,4.90; STONE for a complete Reform Bill ! Wles regard to Redistribution, he says the ToLl 0 are fighting for it and the Liberals aga'':,s it—a perversion of the truth so monstrolt, that one scarcely knows how to deal wit') Ile But his lordship refutes himself when pc quotes Mr. CHAMBERLAIN as saying se e later than last year that—.. FORTHCOMING BALL AT WIDNES.—From an advert isement elsewhere it will be seen that a grand ball, organised by Mr Mellon, of the Theatre Royal, will take place in the Vol- unteer Hall on Monday evening. HALTON PAROCHIAL TRIY.—The Bth annual excursion in connection with Halton Pariah Church took place on Monday, when about 80 persons j mrneyed by train to Blackpool.and sant an enjoyable day. NELSON-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. Mr J Blackburst, of Tunstall on Sunday preached the anniversary sermons in connection with this school, Mr John Simpson in the afternoon addressing a good congregation of teachers, scholars, and friends in Camden Chapel. The collections amounted to £2l 3s. rENKETH —SALVATION ARMY TEA MEETING.—OT S UT. day afternoon the members of the Salvation Army held their iirst annual tea party at their place of meeting in Bold lane, Penketh. There wee a considerable number present. The cateting wee entrusted to Miss Holding, Mrs Williams, Mrs Holding, Stc. After tea a public meeting was held, when addresses were delivered by various membees of the Army

from Widnes. RUNCORN BURIAL ROARD.—The monthly meeting Was held at the Cemetery Offices on Wednesday, Mr J Handley presiding. There were present Mes,rs Whi,taker, Norman, Moss, Col burn, Littler, and W F Salkeld (the secretary).— The secret try reported that the interments for four months ending July 25th were 107 ; corresponding period last year 108. The fees received during the same period amounted to £ll9 2s 5d • last year £lO7 13s 81, increase £ll The Finance Committee recommended, and the Hoard con- firmed, the payment of accoun!s amounting to £42 Ils. REscuE FROH DROWNING AT WESTON POINT —Several boys mete bathing in the river at Weeton Point on Monday evening, when one of their number, named Hughes, got beyond his depth. He was being rapidly carried away by the tide, when he reached a shallow part of the river and managed to " bottom " with his feet. In this perilous posi- tion he remained for some time until a man who was known to be a good swimmer arrived on the spot, and divesting himself of his clothing plunged into the water and succeeded ' in safely bringing the terrified boy to the bank.
