Private T Pierpoint . 23 12 9 41 Private G Littfemme Private G Tomllnson PRESENTATION TO PROFESSOR FLETCHER AT RUNCORN. —OD Wednesday evening, a meeting was held in Bethesda Schoolroom, Runcorn, for the purpase of presenting Pro- fessor Fletcher, the herbalist, with a token of the esteem and respect in which he is held by his grateful patients. There was a good attendance, the members of the local Blue Ribbon Army mustering in strong force The Rev W Valise presided, and in opening the' proceedings observed that he was glad to be there to j3in in the expression of gratitude to Mr Fletcher, because that gentleman was a respected member of the church with which he was con- nected, and one respecting whom he had never heard a really adverse word, and ono whose moral and religious character, so far as he had seen, stood high. He was glad that a number of people living in Runcorn found cause in their hearts to present some kind of testimonial to a member of his church. (Applause.) He (the chairman) was well known as a warm advocate on the temperance quastion, and he thought that Mr Fletcher was doing as much for the temperance cause as any other man in Run- corn.—Mr J Woods described how Mr Fletcher had cured the apparently incurable illness of his dauehter, and stated that be had collected the subscriptions for the present from persons who had been benefited by Mr Fletcher's treatment. He hoped that Mr Fletcber would have health to enjoy the present—(applause)—and thet he would prosper in every- thing he undertook.-Mrs Rushton, Mr Jones, and Mr.." Fair- less (the leader of the local Blue Ribbon Army), also bore testimony to Mr Fletcher's skill.—The presentation was then made by Mr F Parker, accompanied with a few euloeistic remarks. The watch, which was a beautiful gold hunter, bore the following inscription : "Presented to Professor Fletcher tag merle, of his patients as a token of their great esteem. May he live long to do good. Run- corn."—Professor Fletcher, who was cordially received, thanked them for the handsome present he had received, and observed that he had tried to do good and not evil all the days of his life. Ile had received a present from Her Majesty's own fingers he had had medals d other pre- sents given to him, ban but he had never received a present which he should prize so highly as the one the people of Runcorn had honoured him with. He should never forget the kindness he had received in Runcorn, and with God's blessing he would continue to do good amongst the people. —The meeting then terminated. During the evening Mr and Mrs Rushton gave recitations, and Mr and Mrs Bate Bang several temperance melodies. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR THOMAS JORNSON.—Oar readers will regret to hear of the death of a member of an old Runcorn family in the person of Mr Thomas Johnson, who died at Bryn-Aber-Abergele on Sunday at the advanced ago of 80 years. The deceased gentleman and his brothw were the proprietors of a large soap works, and were indeed the founders of the soap industry in Runcorn. About 18 years ago the firm was converted into a limited liability company, and although its real title is Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, it is still popularly known as Johnson's eoapery amongst the inhabitants. Daring his residence in the town Mr Johnson was a member of the old Highway Board, and on the passing of the Improvement Act in 1852 he was elected one of the first members of the Board of Im- proVement Commissioners. He was also an active member of the Burial Board. In these various capacities be faith- fully guarded the interests of the ratepayers. He was also a justice of the peace for the county of Chester. Iu con- junction with his brother he took an active part in many religious and philanthropic works. They were very large subscribers towards the cost of erecting Holy Trinity Church, and when it was completed, endowed the living in a very generous spirit. At their own expense they built the ragged school at Mill-brow and maintained it until sold to the School Board, and they bore almost the entire coat of providing a new school. Other local movements also received their sympathy and aid. and the name of Johnson will always find on honoured place in the annals of Runcorn. The de- ceased gentleman gave his hearty support towards the for- mation of a local volunteer corps, and alwaysmenifested the keenest interest in its welfare. The funeral took place at the Runcorn Parish church on Thursday morning, the Rev W Preston, MA, vicar of Holy Trinity Church, officiating. The body arrived by train from Abergele, at half-past ten, and was met at the railway etation by the Reoe ve l'reston, 51 A, Messrs J W Lightburn, E Aaron, R Norman, R Lea, T Kerkham, Edward Buckley, T Hogan, and J J Speakman. The body was placed in a hearse supplied by Mr Peck; end the relatives, Mr T E Reethe Johnson (eon), Mr John Al- cock Johnson (nephew), and Mr Walter Wynne entered a mourning coach. The cortege then wound its way to the churchyard, where a considerable number of people had as' sembled to view the solemn ceremony. The laparers were Messrs S Partington, J Sherlock, P Brazendale, and Edward Brazendale, and the body was lowered into the family vault. The coffin bore the fol- lowing inscription:—" Born 4th Septonber, 1801, died 10th August, 1884." It was not generally' known that the de- ceased was to be interred at Runcorn, otherwise the funeral would have partaken of a public cli r.actor, .n any gentlemen iq the town having expressed a wish to show respect to a honoured house by following the body to the grave.

With an 'extract from a speech by Mr. GLAD- I' STONE to the effect that Redistribution was a question " only second in importance to that of the Franchise itself." He did not seem to see that he was giving the best pos- sible reason. for taking second that which was "second in importance." But, as we have all along pointed out in these columns, bewildering as the Tory leaders are in the false reasons they gave for the false position they have taken up, there is one thing that they have clearly in mind, and that is to force a dissolution, if they can, upon the present register. Speaking of the Government, Lord SALISBURY says—'lf they think we are wrong let them go to those from whom they hold their power, dna are wrong." A pretty doctrine truly, that every time a wrong-headed body of peers thinks fit to say the Government is in the wrong there must be a dissolution ! Lord SALishuitx has been frequently taken to task of late for hi sun- constitutional doctrine, but so far from showing Sign of withdrawal he brings it again to the fore front. Once upon a time there were people outside lunatic asylums who pro- claimed that "the King can do no wrong." One king had to be shortened by a head be- fore this nonsense could be got rid of; and now it is cropping up in another form. The lord of HATFIELD preaches to-day from the house tops that "the House of Lords can do no wrong," and if he will be stupid enough to push his doctrine hard enough there can be no doubt of such an answer being given as will wipe the House of Lords altogether off the scene. We are also told that—" The dis- tinction between the position of the House of Lords and the House of Commons at this moment is this, that the House of Lords is willing and anxious to submit its decisions to the arbitrament of the people, and there is nothing that the House of Commons so much dreads as that." This is ingenious in its way —an ingenious lie. The real difference is that the present House of Commons was elected by the people on the distinct under- standing that there must be an assimilation of the borough and county franchise and a redistribution of seats ; and now, when the work is half done, the Lords have blocked the way, and they have the impertinence to talk of an appeal to the people whom they have insulted and outraged. Appeal to the People! Ay, and the response is coming. It is coming from the men of the loom, the forge, and the plough, who have seen the lordly disdain with which they have been trampled on in the past ; who have seen how a literal and therefore blasphemous rendering has been given of the passage—" The earth is the lords' and the fulness thereof;" who have seen "the drones of the community" live on the fat of the land, while to them was thrown the-husks which the swine do eat; who have seen every good and perfect gift „which a beneficent Government would have conferred upon them jeered at and finally destroyed or mutilated; who have listened till they are heart sick to those "juggling fiends"

That crilter with un in a double sense, That keep the wo!d of promise to our ear, And break it to our hope_ The response is indeed coming from every hamlet, and town, and city in the kingdom, and the cry which day by day grows clearer and stronger is—`. Up with the Reform Bill, and down with th-t House of Lords I"

The Conservatives of Warrington seem to have a " screw loose somewhere," or shall we say "there's a slate off? " They Ir-ve got Sir GILBERT GREENALL for a candidate, and yet they are not happy. The baronet retired defeated and disheartened after the last F.'arliamentary election; he shook off the dust of his shoes upon the town; but a pub- lic meeting of the party was held in his favour; he was induced to withdraw his withdrawal ; and since the present year came in there has been meeting on meeting at all which Conservative voters have pledged themselves to support his candidature at the next General Election. All seems to have gone as merry as a marriage bell with what Lord It. Crum CHILL politely calls "the tag-rag and bobtail," but meanwhile the heads of the party have been ominously shaking. Now as a rule when you go on shaking a thing something comes of it, and so it has been in this instance. This came of it; there as a meeting last week of the "heads "—the most influential heads, it is said at a certain hotel in the town, and after, we un- derstand, taking iced drinks to assist them in a preliminary discussion of the hot weather,the question of the Conservative candidature was broached—just as they might have broached a barrel of Wilderspool ale. The conclusion come to—soberly come to—as to the ap.. proaching race for Parliamentary honours was that Sir GILBERT "wasn't in it." They wanted a man of energy, force of character, and ability—one who was something under seventy-six years of age, and who was not handicapped with dead-weight votes in favour of Flogging in the Army and against the Enfranchisement of Working-men. They wanted someone who would shoot ahead of all corners, and alas! with sorrow be it said, they were in something of a fix until, happy thought! one of the heads suggested Mr. DANIEL ADAMSON, of Manchester Ship Canal fame. "A Daniel come to judgment" verily, and he was carried, so to speak, shoulder- height. There was again a shaking of heads, ' this time joyfully, and the company parted happy in the consciousness that they could ' now see their way to laying Sire GILBERT on the shelf, jerrymandering his supoorters, and giving the Liberals of Warrington their ever- lasting quietus. It was done admirably, charmingly; and they saw the idea expand like an air balloon under inflation growing bigger and bigger and more beautiful to the eye—until pop lit suddenly burst—the wise men of Warrinß ton discovered, spare us ye gods and little Walton fishes, that dear de- lightful DANIEL, the man upon whom these Tories had set their hearts was—a Liberal! Was there ever such a collapse! Beats cock- fighting ? Cock-fighting is nowhere to it. It was a funny thing when the man who had been absent from home for forty years re• turned full of sentiment and was found cry- ing on the wrong doorstep. It was funny when an indignant shareholder made a slashing speech at the wrong railway meeting. It was funny when the late Sir Jonx HOLKER, strolling late into the House. one night, got up and commenced arg-aing against the side taken by the Government of which he was a member. But the funniest of funny things is this conference of the heads of the Tory party in Warrington—this solemn selection of an out-and-out Liberal to fight the battle of Toryism. Oh, the humour of the situation— but we must stop; our sides ache.

- SOUTH-WP,St LANCASHIRE will make its voice 'heard to day at Earlestown on the con- duct of the House of Lords in rejecting the Franclii-ie Bill, awl we winture to predict that there will be no uncertain sound. If the re- sidents of towns who already exercise the

right of voting are enthusiastic in the matter of Reform, what should be the feeling or' those who are being treated as political serfs? They know whether they want the Franchise or not, and they know. too, whilst the door was being opened to them, when and how it has been slammed in their faces. But they mean to keep knocking until they are let in, and will give a knock on Newton Common which will, we trust be heard at St. Stephen's Excellent arrangements are being made to ensure the success of the Demonstration. There is sure to be a large assembly, and, in order that there may be no dumb show, there will be three platforms. at each of which there will be speakers who are hosts in then-1- .01.9 Amongst those annouticed to be present are Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P., Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., Mr. S. Williamson, M.P., Mr. S Smith, M.P., and last, but by no means least, Mr. Joseph Arch. For other details, we have pleasure in directing our readers to our advertising and news columns.

WIDNRB Perm —Amongst the certificates gained at the exemination held in connection with 'Dimity College, London, on July 11th to 23rd. at Liverpool, the name of Miss Edith Pemberton, Simin's Cross Seminary, stands third on the list of the primary division. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN —Patrick Whelan, an old man who had been ailing for some time, died suddenly on Thursday night. He was seen leaning against the R cyst Hotel railines as though in great pain, and he was assisted to his house on Trinity-brow. Dr MacDougall was sent for, but Whelan died in a few moments after that gentleman's arrival. GARDEN PARTY AT HALE HALL —Cohireland Blaeltbnrne, M.P., entertained a large number of the 4lite of the neigh• blurhaad at a garden party at Hale Id all on Tuts lay after- noon last. The weather was everything that could be el.:- sired; and the picturesque park and grounds were looking ' their best. The company begin to arrive at four o'clock, at which hour the hand of the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment commenced playing. BRISTOL JOINT STOCK BANK.—In another column will be found details of this new cempana- which are worthy the attention of investors. The proposed capital is £l,OOO 000 with an issue of 20,000 shares of £lO each. one-half of the subscribed capital, or £5 per share, to remain uncalled as a reserved liability. Banking has in many cases proved very profitable in the past, and from statistics that are published there seems to be an unusually good opening for the Bristol Joint Stock Bank. PENKETII LSBERtL ASSOCIATION.—The Liberals of Pen- keth on Saturday afternoon had their first picnic, the place selected being Frodsham. The mmeners assembled at the clubroom at one p.m., where conveyances were provided by Mr F Massey, Warrington. They arriveePat Frodsharn about four p.m., and after a ramble on the hills and refreshing the inner men, they re-assembled at 7-30 to proceed home, ar- riving at Penketh at 10 o'clock, all having thoroughly en- joyed themselves. THEFT or ROPE AT Runconer.—At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, before Mr W Bankes and Mr James Handley, Edward Johnson, a man of Ho fixed occupation, was charged with stealing 10Ins. of rope, the property of the Bridgewater Navigation Company. It appeared that Adam Peacock missed the rope from "float" numher 24 on Thursday evening, and it was subsequently discavered that the prisoner lead sold it for 51 to Mr Sproston, marine store dealer, Top Locks. Dock Constable Jones appre- hended the prisoner, who was sentenced to a month's hard labour, GALLANT RESCUE FROM DROWNING AT RUNCORN.—A Boy named John Price, about 12 years of age, was bathing on the river side off" No man's laud" on Sunday afternoon, when be got beyond his depth and screamed for help. He was sinking for the third time when a young fellow named Patrick or William Collins, who lives in Vicar-street, came upon the spot and without pausing to divest himself of his clothes, jumped into the water and brought the drowning boy to the bank. The usual remedies were applied with success and the rescuer went home to change his damaged clothing. BOWLING MATCH AT Bratoonet.—The return match be- tween Crewe and Runcorn Bowling Clubs took place on the green attached to Mr George Hayes's, Bridge Hotel, Run- corn, on Thursday. With one exception the -Runcorn players beat their opponents, the scores being—Runcorn 1112, Crewe 74. On the former occasion Runcorn were the victors by 36 points, Crewe having thus lost on both games by 154 points. At the cenclusion of the play, on Thurs- day, the teams adjourned to the Souffi Berth Hotel, where they sat down to a good spread, afterwards spending the evening in a convivial manner. ELECTION OF ASSISTANT OVERSEER.--On Saturday after- noon the poll for the election of an assistant overseer for Frodsham Lordship, in the place of Mr Samuel Astonae• bizned, was held in the Boys' school at Overton. Mr Robert Ashton presided and announced the result of the poll as follows :—Mr John Challoner, 110; Mr Henry Tiley, 62 ; Mr George Jones, 9. Mr John Challoner was thereupon declared daily elected. A vote of thanks HAS unaniinously accorded to Mr Robert Ashten for the impartial in-inner in which he had conducted the poll, the motion being proposed by Mr W H Linaker, seconded by Mr John elle:loner, and supported by Mr Henr.y AriDn; E T.S.—The weekly meeting was held on inureday evening. The Rev A P Ilaininon Wilson, who presided, advised those present to endeavour at the next licensing sessions to get up a numerously signed petition against the granting of licenses, and instanced the success which sach an effort might meet by the fact that in Barrow- in-Furness the petition of a 1 -age number of residents ex- ercised so great an influence that licenses were ouly granted to one public-house and one refreshment room.—The Rev C Rumfitt also delivered an address.—Songs were c intritauted by Messrs hjunt.Taylor,J Heeketh, Cook, and Holmes, and Mr J Stride gave a recitation. Sr. LUKE'S SUNDAY Scnooa, Rmecortre.—The anniversary sermons in connection with this sclool were preached in Bethesda Congregational Chapel on Sunday morning and evening by the Rev Thomas Cole, of Gerstein. The choir and children rendered music specially selected for the occa- sion. In the afternoon a children's service was held at St. Luke's School, addresses being delivered by the Rev T Cole and Mr Slade. The collections at the three services amounted to £4 12s. On Monday the children attending the school had their annual treat. To the number of about 240, accompanied by the Rev J D Thomas and Mr G Lacey, the superintendent, they journeyed to Keckwick along the canal, proceeding to a field on Mr Done's farm. Tea and other refreshments were provided and as the weather was very fine an enjoyable day was spent. THE ELECTRIC LIGHT IN RAILWAY CARRIAGES.—An im- portant new departure in railway lighting is being made by the London and North-Western Company. This is the utilization of electricity for lighting the carriages on the line between Liverpool and 'Manchester by the help of Swan's incandescent 20 candle power lamps, and Brother- hood's patent engine, stationed on the tender, and fed with steam from the locomotive boiler, locomotives being speci- ally fitted for this service. The electric current passes from the engine, through the train, and back to the locomo- motive, where, fixed to the footplate, is a regulator fitted with an electric burner showing the driver the power of light in the trail]. Each compartment of the train is fitted with a duplicate lamp, the arrangement securing the instant lighting of one lamp if the other should become extin- guished. ItErNCORN AND DISTRICT (406TH) STARE-BOWNETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—The directors yesterday issued their third annual report, in which they state that, as was confi- dently anticipated, the society has filled daring the year, the 500th certificate being issued on May 12th, since which date several of the early lapsed register numbers have also been re-issued. The amount received in subscriptions during the year was £1,095 Be 6d, being an increase on last year's sub- scription receipts of £315 Os 6d which is a very satisfac- tory result. The income from re-payments (including re- demption of a mortgage) amounted to £lB9 12s, being a substantial increase on last year's return. The total income for the year being £1,345 16s sd, and the beim-ice in favour of the society, after estimating the liabilities, being £5O 9s 61. During the year seven appropriations have been made, the total number balloted since the formation of the society being 15. Of these, 11. amounting to £1.,830, have been completed, another of £2OO has been completed during the past week, and three have been deferred for the present. LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE Itemway.—Toe half- yearly general meeting of the proprietors of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway was held in 'Manchester on Wednes- day. In moving the adoption of the report, Mr J Pearson (chairman) expressed the view that, taking all the circum- stances of the case into account, the fact that the Company had been able to maintain the dividend at the point which it reached a year ago and to carry forward £ll,OOO was not unsatisfactory. It was true, be said, that 4 per cent. Was not a high dividend, but he had warned the shareholders 12 months ago against expecting high dividends for several years to come. They might, however, be assured that whatever dividend was recommended would be honestly earned, and that the directors would not attempt to bolster it up by neglecting to make necessary repairs or additions to stock. The total increase in the receipts for the half-year was £18,857, and of passenger traffic £l4 $l5, although— for reasons which he explained—the Com; a, iy had booked 312,000 fewer passengers. The motion for ihe Adoption of the report, as well as the other resolutions which were sub- mitted, was tarried without opposition. After each game thri players and friends partook of an excellent tea, provided respectively by Mr Parkes, Central Hotel, Widnes, and Mr Johnson, Fiddler's Ferry Hotel. THE FRANCHISE DEMONSTRATION AT EARLESTOWN.— The Franchise demonstration at Eirlestown will be held to- day (Saturday), on the land at the top of Market-street, near the Common. There will be three platforms and three sets of speakers. The committee have decided to submit two resolutions. The Sims resolutions will be submitted at the several platforms. The chairman of No. 1 platform will be Mr Thomas Brocklebank, JP. chairman of the South-West Lancashire Committee; at No. 2, Mr R D Holt, .1 P. presi- dent of the Liverpool Liberal A sssciation ; and at No. 3, Mr Richard Pilkington, J P, of Rainford Hall, will preside. The platforms, which are only of a very limited area, will be reserved for speakers only. The speakers will ass,mble at the Earlestown Liberal Club, and those attending the meetiog will march through Market-street to the ground. The men in the district will march in procession from their villages, headed by their binds. The Ashton, Haydock, Colborne, and Lowron procession will start at 1.30 p us. From Ssuthport, Liverpool, Tyldes- ley, Leigh. Widnes. and other places sp cial trains will be run to Earlestown. Arrangements have been made by the local railway managers to place the return trains in the E trlestown goods yard, so that people can get in without difficulty and without interferinz with the through traffic. Amongst those who will be p-esent and speak at the itreting ire Mr Joseph Arch, Mr H Broadhurst. M.P, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P, Mr 8 Williamson, MY, and Mr 8 Smith, M.P. The local speakers will represent all shades of Liberal political opinion.

BRUTAL ASSAULT AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Wedneecley, Stephen Hoegh, flatman, 40 years of see, was brought up wader a warract charged with inde- cently assaulting Saran Jane Wnite.—lt appeared that the girl was left alone in her father's house in Cooper-street, when the prisoner entered, end acted in a moat indecent and brutal manner.—He Was committed to the eessions for trial. THEFT IN A RUNCORN PURLIC-HOUSE.— At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Captain Heelehurst, Mary Jane Jones was charged with frequenting the Rose and Crown beer-house with intent to commit a feiony.—Evidence was given to the effect that Alois Wycick, a sailor, and Robert Moores were in the Rose and Crown with the prisoner. Toe former lent her his ring to look at. She took it away, and refused to return it or say where it was until P.C. Morris was sent for, when she pointed out where she had hidden it in the yard.—She was sentenced to 14 days' bard labour. A PROFANE STREET SINGER AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Thuredey, Joseph Rebinson, a gray-halred old man, was charged with ben...flue: FeLeln-street—P.C.. ilasen said on the previous evening he sew the prisoner at- tempting to. sing in High-street, and hel ling his bat out for alms. When the constable asked him to move on he became very insulting, aud used language of an atom • inable character.. On a previous evening he had acted in a similar manner, and told Inspector Atherton that he would praise the Lard for him or anybody else.—The prisoner was sentenced to seven days' hard labour.. WEEN•END DRUNKENNESS AT WIDNES.—As usail a batch of persons were brought before the magistrates at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, charged wi.h behee drunk on Saturday and Sunday. Conductor, T Houghton, sen. STEALING BEER AT HALTON. Before Captain Ilazie- burst and Mr G L Davies, at Runcorn Police Court, on Sat- urday, Robert Hughes, George Nicholls, and Edward Hoff- land, young men, wer4 charged with stealing a quantity of beer, the property of William Phillips, of the Castle Hotel, Halton. On Monday the 4th inst, the defendants found three quarter casks of beer which had been left on the green and whilst the dancieg was going on, they pulled the cork from one of the barrels. Hughes filled his hat with liquor ' and invited several people to drink. :Because one young man declined he struck him. The other prisoner took some of the beer in glasses, one barrel being emptied. FURIOUS DRIVING AT RETNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday Henry Jones, boatman, Ellesnc:re-street,e Was summoned for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart on the s'h hist., and also for. furiously driving the same.—The defendant 'pleaded guilty.—lnspector Atherton said about nine o'clock on the evening in queetien he was on duty in Bridge-street, and saw the-defendant in charge of a horse and cart. BACON STEALING AT HALEWOOD.—At Widnes Police- Court, on Monday, before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., Edward Knowlee, Grenville-street, Widnes, and Thos. Brandwood, Oaklandmtreet, Widnes, were charged with stealing lib of bacon, the property of Richard Whitfield, keeper of the Beehive beerbouse, Halewood.—lt appeared that on Sunday evening the Prisonets entered a room in the Beehive where there were two hams and two flitches of bacon hanging up, and were served with beer. After they had departed the landlady missed some bacon, and followed , the prisoners. She threatened to fetch a police officer, when Knowles unbuttoned his vest and produced the bacon. They stated they had done the act through drink, and asked her to forgive them, as they were respectable men.—The pri- soners, who pleaded guilty, were sentenced to 14 days' hard Meer. A WAGES CASE: ALLEGED DESERTION OF A SHIP. —Before Mr JAMAS Handley and Mr G te Davies, at Run- corn Police Court, on Thursday. Thomas Adams, master of the schooner Mary Seymour. was summoned by Richard Monks, seamen on board the vessel, for 13s wages date to , him.—From the evidence it appeared that the cotnplainent shipped on board the vessel at Plymouth, his wages being fixed at £3 per month. The vessel c.me to Runcern with a cargo of china clay, and during the voyage the complainant had received certain advances on account, and now 13s was due to him.—The captain stated that the plaintiff had left the vessel witheutleave on Tbursday.and did notreturn until Friday afternoon. He had, he stated, therefore treated bin as a deserter, but when asked by the imagist ates to produce his log book where the official entry should be made, he said he had not got it with him.—The Bench were of opinion the captain was in fault, and ordered him to pay the amount claimed, with costs, total £1 63 fid:i DROWNED IN WIDNES DOCKS --On Tuesday afternoon, at the Commercial Ina, Widnes, Mr W T Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Samuel Whitfield, a waterman, 36 years of age, who was found drowned in the Old Dock, Widees, on Monday morning. From the evidence it appeared that Whitfield cohabited with a woman named Rebecca Mac Donough, at 34, Water-street, and on Thursday evening, abont seven o'clock, had his tea with her. About eight o'clock he left her to go on board the fiat Spider, on which he was employed. He was then quite sober. About eight o'clock on Monday morabag, Thomas Holland, a Bat- man living at 59, James-street, WAS waking along the quay side of the Old Dock, when he SAW tlge body of a men fl mt- ing between the flats Julia and Ellen. He with the aid of James Killalee pulled the body on board the Julia' end at once recognised it as that of Samuel Whitfield. The de- ceased, who was. lame, would have to cross two flats to get upon his own craft, and it is suptiosed that in doing so he fell into the water, and was unable to save himeelf. A ver- dict of found drowned was returned. A SCRIPTURE READER "ON THE SPRZE."—On Saturday a respectably-dressed blind man named John Morgan was brought before Alderman Burgess, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, charged with drunkenness.—P.C. Johnstone said that the prisoner was in Winwick street on the previous afternoon, in a drunken condition, and with a crowd collected round him. Prisoner had a" raised " copy of the Scriptures. The sum of 4s Id was found in his possession.—Prisone- said that be bad finished reading the Scriptures when the officer SAW him.—The magistrate said that it appeared prisoner put himself into a position to read that sacred book by getting drunk. He could not deal with him as he would With any ordinary person, owing to his in- firmity, but he would have the costs to pay. If he professed to read the Bible to the public he should see that he did it in a sober state. Morgan was brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday charged with being drunk in Water- loo-road on the previous day. The case was proved by P.C. Lamb, and Sup orintendent Barker said the prisoner was a nuisance to the neighbourhood. A fine of 55 and casts was

imposed. • A VIOLENT DRUNKARD AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, William Fielding, a respectable- looking labourer, Was brought up in custody charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also wi h assaulting P.C. Snowden whilst in the execution of Ilie duty.—P.C. Snowden sated that about 8 o'clock on the previous evening he was called into Chatham-street by the prisoner's son. When he got there he saw the prisoner was very drunk and acting lin a disorderly fashion. A large crowd of people bad gathered around him and he (witness) took him into custody. He became very violent, striking and kicking the officer several times. He had to get the assistance of another constable to bring him to the police station, and also to put the snaps on him. He continually threw himself to the ground and licked in a violent manner.—P.C. Almond and P.S. McGregor corroborated this statement, the latter officer remarking that the prisoner's son said the prisoner had acted I Ake a madman all night. —Superintendent . Barker said the prisoner had been several times convicted, and in June, 3881, he was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment for unlaw- fully wounding a constable. On the brevious evening the priaonet's son complained that his fetter had broken every- thing in the house.—Mr 11 Gasket! said V e prisoner was evidently a bed character, but the case did not seem to be a bad one, and the Bench thought jasticiwould be satisfied by fining him 10s and costs in each case. A RUNCORN WIFE BEATER SENT TO GAOL —Frederick Bushell, dock labourer, Surrev-s reet, WAS summoned to Riincorn Petty Sessions on Monday on a ch trge of assault- ing his wife, Margaret. —The complainant said on Wednes- day niebt, the 6h inst., the defendant, who was under the influence of drink, went home, taking with him his uncle. Ile asked her to get some tea ready for himself and his uncle. Her husband's tea was on the table, and she told him that that was all the food there Was in the house. He kicked the table over, and, rushing at her, knocked her violently against the cupboard and kicked her. Her father arrived on the scene to protect her, bet the defendant also kicked him, and treated a woman who came to her aid in a similar manner. He finished his violence by kicking the complainant violently about the body and legs, and throw- ing her on the sofa attempted to choke her. In reply to Mr Ashton, the complainant said she had not lived with the defendant since, and dare not do so. He constantly abused her when he was drunk, and also when be was sober. About two months ago he illtreafed her to such an extent that she consulted the police. On Wednesday nialit, when she was at her father's house, the defendant kicked the panels of the door in, and the police had to be sent for. She had been married two years next December.—anefeodant had nothing to say in answer to the charge —Mr IC 13 inlcE.s (chairman) said the defendant had been guilty of a most gross and un- warrantable assault, and the Bench would teach him that such brutal conduct would not t” tolerated by sending him to gaol for A month's bard labour.

An engine from Hale was • brought into play, but by ian etimit.itnt the hose got burned, and ae the fire was spread- ing assistance was summoned from Liverpool. The fire continutd smouldering on Sunday and Monday, and it is estimated that the damage amounts to about £5OO. AN INCIDENT IN THE SONS OF TEMPERANCE PROCES• SION. At Runcero Petty Sessions, on Monday, William Bate, a young man, employed as a dock labourer, was char- ged with assaulting kwaham Gondier, of B ntinct-street, on the 4th hist —Tee defendant pleaded that be had commit- ted the assanit in self defenca.—The complainant stated that on the day Darnel he was in the Sons of Temperance procession, and when he reached Savage's Bridge, the defen- dant reached out his hand and they shook baud lin the frieniiiest manner possible. Defendant, however, would not release his band, end Insisted in walking in the proces- sion. As he was drank the cemplarnant attempted to per. euadi him to leave the ranks but he refused, and being in his working clothes he mauled the complainant who was "tidied up," and made a mess of him. At last he pushed the defendant away, when the latter struck him on the neck and jaw.—Defendant: Well Abraham, I'm your uncle.— Cornpleinant : That's nothing to do with it..-Mr. G Marshall, chemist and druggist, Devonshire-squere, deposed to seeing the assault, and staled that the defendant ale) attempted to strike a woman near his shop.—Witness acknowledged that he was the complainant's brother-in-law, and the defendant said it was merely a family affair.—The defendant made a statement to the effect that in the morning be had a con- versation with the complainant about the corning procession, and he undertook to produce 10 men who took drink who should be equal to 10 teetotallers. He denied that he was drunk, as be had only had a pint of beer to his dinner. The defendant, against whom there were several previous convictions, was fined 20e, and costs lie ed.

lbs follewing minutes were recorded with respect to the Sankey Canal:—" Letter, 23rd July, from the Local Government Board, enclosing copy of correspondence be- tween that Board and Messrs G H Bolton, and J Johnson, of Penketh, respecting nuisance from this canal. The Clerk reported that he had sent a copy of the correspondence to the London and North-Western Railway Company, and asked them to give prompt attention. Instructions given to reply to the Local Government Board that attention is being given to the subject. Letter, 12th July, from Mr Worthington (London and North-Western Railway Company) saying that the state of the canal is caused by the water from the Sankey Brook, over which the Railway Company have no control. Letter, 24th July, from Mr Reay, (London and North- Western Railway Company) stating that their solicitor is in communication with the St. Helens Corporation with whom the matter rests, rather than with the company; also tele- gram, 4th August, from the Railway Company, stating they cannot do more than press the St. Helens Corporation. In- structions for reply given." Rainhill Sewage Farm;— Letter, 4th August, from the Local Government Board, respecting the Board's complaint about the pollution of water-course by Rainhill Sewage Farm, stating that they await a reply from the Rural Sanitary Authority. The Market Superintendent reported that the receipts for the month were £2O Is 41, being an increase of £3 14s 2d as compared with July, 1683. Eight shops wer9 now let.—Dr O'Keeffe moved the confirmation of the minutes, and, refer- ring to the Rainhill Sewage Farm, said the liquid from that place was running into an open ditch in the northern por- tion of Widnes township, and it was well known that cattle drank out of that ditch. 'The owner of the cows would send the milk into Widnes, may be to the paupers at Vi'histon, and perhaps even the Guardians themselves might possibly drink some of it. If they did, and got typhoid fever or English cholera or something else of a grave character which would imperil their valuable lives, then they might help I the Board in preventing this nuisance. The Local Govern- ment Board were not adopting any active measures to remedy this evil, but with their usael red tapeism Contented themselves with sending letters. If, however, the Local Boatd did anything which the august body in London thought was wrong they would be down noon Widnes even as "the Assyrian came down like a wolf on the fold.' (Laughter.) He hoped the next letter the clerk wrote would be of such a character as to cause the Local Government Board to send down an inspector at once.—Mr. Midwood seconded the motion. Referring to the Sankey canal he said it was not for the Board to go to St. Helens Oorporatiun or the Warring- ton Rural Sanitary Authority; it was for the Board to deal with the nuisance as they found it in their township for which the London and North-Western Railway Company were responsible.—Mr Johnston said samples of water in the ditch end the hainhill Sewage Farm had been obtained for analysis. What was the result ?—Dr O'Keefe replied that Dr C rmpbell Brown certified that the water was exceed- ingly injurious to health, and his report had been forwarded to the Local Government Board —The Chairman observed I that the Board had nothing to do with the origin of the I nuisance in the Sinkey canal ; and he suggested that the I clerk should write to the Railway Company and ask them to disinfect the natal by the liberal use of -chloride of lime as a temporary measure.—Mr Gaskell added that the company must be informed that the Board would not be satisfied unless a permanent remedy was found. 'The minutes were then passed and it was un- derstood that the Chairman's suggestion would be acted upon. A PUBLICAN'S LICENSE ENDORSED. Before Mr H Gaskell, senior' and Mr II Gaskell, junr, at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, William Ice, landlord of the Stonemasons' Arms beerbouse, John-street, was summoned to answer a charge of having on the 29th July permitted drunkenness on his premises, and also with selling intoxicating liquor to a drunken person. Mr J 0 Swi,t defended—is S Strickland deposed that at 8-2 o on the evening of the day in question be visited the defen- dant's house H 'Company with PC McMasters. He entered the t tproom, where be found five men and the landlady. A min named Dunn was present. He was very drunk. He I was sitting on a form leaning with his arms on the table in front of him. There was a half-pint glass full of beer, and there was a similar glass opposite another man. There was a man lying on the form asleep. The witness drew the land- lady's attention to Dunn, saying he was drunk, and he asked her if she had served him with beer. She replied "Yes I have served him • it is the first he has had here, I don't think he is drunk." He told her he should report her hus- band; Dunn was in such a state that any persan could see what was the matter with him.—Cross-exannined by Mr Swift: Witness said Dunn became disorderly when he got outside, and he was locked no Next morning he pleaded guilty to being drunk and was fined. PC Mc Masters cor- roborated —Mr Swift then addressed the Bench for the de- fence. He asked their worships to dismiss from their minds the fact that Dunn had been convicted ot drunkenness, and contended that be mi4ht have pleaded guilty as men often would do as the easiest way out of a difficulty. Dunn went into the defendant's house in com- pany with Charles Lavin, shortly after eight o'clock. They sat down quietly and ordered two glasses of beer, which Mrs Ince supplied, as she saw not the slightest signs of drunkenness —Mrs Inca corroborated this state- ment, and added that Dunn walked round the room steadily to show the officers that he was not drunk.—Thomas Dunn, Idynarer, 28, John-street, deposed that during the day he hat five gills of beer and a glass of whiskey, and then a glass of beer at Inca's. He could walk straight and talk, and was not drunk. When he got outside the officers knocked Lim to the ground, and Sergeant Strickland placed his knee on his chest, and said " fern, you are not as good a man as you used to be." The reason he pleaded guilty was because im thought he would get off with a light fine, and there would be an end of it.—Supt. Barker : But did you get off with a light file ? No, I didn't. It was heavier than I expected. Charles Lavin, labourer, Gerrard•street ; Michael Banner, Nelson street; and Jesse Grundy, joiner, Simms Cross, deposed that Dunn was not drunk.—James Fletcher, butcher, Widnes-road, was also called, and said Dunn walked steadily on his legs but moved big shoulders about—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s and costs 193 on the second charge, and dismissed the first charge.—Supt. Barker said the defendant had been previously fined 40e and costs for a breacn of the Licensing Act, and he asked that the license should be enclorsed.—Mr Swift obj ,cted, but the Chiirman said if this wel.e the fi-et offenbe the Bench would not endorse the license. His feeling was that every conviction should hi endorsed on the license. This being the second conviction against the defendant it must be en- dorsed.

Mr H M Stanley, the celebrated exolorer of the "Dirk Continent," is expectel shortly to vtsit Manchester. It Is stared that £10,750 has been subscribed towards the embellishment of Hyde Parke Corner. Mr. Boehm has nearly completed his model of the new memorial of the Duke ot I Wellington.

OUR LONDON LETIEII.
LONDON, THURSDAY. Parliament was prorogued to-day and the Erasion, neither useful to the public nor personally endearing, c;,mos to an

ead. The attendance of members did not reach a quorum, everybody being glad to getaway. There iemained, how. ever, a sufficient number to make some ehoat of procession as the Speaker wended his way across the hall with his trainbearer, the Sergeant at Arms carrying the mace, and the Chaplain depressed with a sense that his opportunities for usefulness in a distinguished field were temporarily ovcr. The congregation of members who wait to witness the pru- , rogation is thf oughout the life of a Parliament pretty mach the same, with the addition of one or two aew merubao wi.o have joined during the sessioa just closed. There Ara vari- OUR little ambitions among members of the Houso ot Corn. , mons that are pursued with as much eagerness and with as
steadfast .a pur'pose as if they .were subsCantial pr',x2s7. One
of these is to b's the first mail to enter the House at the ht.

div.head: ginning of a session. This is a competition in hiCh Mr. Monck has often honourably run, and has,./ think, on more . _
div.p: ginning of a session. This is a competition in hiCh Mr. Monck has often honourably run, and has,./ think, on more . _
than one ace talon won the [Atte ribbon.
it. Macfaylane, a
comparatively new corner, was "the first in last ECsSiOrt. Envious and defeated rivals put about the etoiy thrs be had
encamped in Palace-yard all .night, provisions:l- with an oat- me.il cake and a ()utile of whiskey, and so secartd the object
of desire.

Another of these minor distinctions much prized is that of being the last to shake hands with the Speaker. It is pretty to watch m.?.rnbers on the last day of the sessim hinging about near the bar or peeping in at. the door to coo bow far

„ the queue is shortening, and when will be the precise motnect accidentally to walk in and come up last. Mr. Callan is the most successful strategist in this direction, and as he has not that dello icy of feeling which induces tiller members to attempt to conceal the manoeuvre, and in,..kc the thing seem accidental, he occupies a position of advar,tarre. It is nothing to him to stand by the table openly permitting members to pass him, and then dAib,rately fail in as the last roan.
Yet another distinction, the strife for wh!ch shows how much the House of Commons has in cammon with a achool
of boys, is to be the first through the lobby in a division. In
this ;aCe Sir Charles Dilke is Eclipse, the rest being no- where. I don't know how he daes it ; but tho fact remains

- that in every bitt division, for since he has become a Cabi- net Minister Sir Charles has given up the centest on &Lail divisions, the President of the Lee tl Government Beard will be seen entesing the House with that rapid striae, whits is caricatured in Punch's lobby sketchea of the House. Be is not only the fleet of his own side, but is in advanco of the Opposition, beiug in fact for a measurable space of time the only member in the House save the Speaker. A fourth duty , which members impose noon themselves is to be present at ,I the opening and the closing ceremony of the session. How- ever laie the House may sit, however wearisome may have been the eeision, and however tempting the country may . seem, these gentlemen are not to be drawn away from the narrow path of duty. This is a habit in which bit' Charles again distinguishes himself. I qoestion whether there is any opening of Parliament or prorogation from which the right hon. gentleman has been absent since he first sat for Chelsea. These were the gentlemen who tiled in behind the Speaker this afternoon, and gave some appearance of life to the mummery of the prorogation by Royal Cenamiesion. Amongst members who have shaken bands with the Speaker for the last time is Mr Blake, the member or Waterford. Mr Blake is not a particularly bright man, as :v.s shown' the other day by his indignant letter to a newspaper which. 1 announcing hie forthcoming retirement, said that step was undertaken because not being always eble to agree with the policy of Mr Parnell, he felt he could I not honourably bold his seat. To Mr Blake's mildly muddled mind this harmless and kindly meant state- ment appeared to convey the imputation that no honourable man could work with Mr Parnell, and lee rushed into print to disclaim the supposed imputation. But if be is nut as bright as some of his colleagues ha is a good deal more resp ,cted in the House of Commons. His Parliamentary fame will chiefly rest upon the charming story he told daring an all night sitting on the Irish Sunday Closing Bill. Mr Blake confided to the House that he had an uncle who used to drink eight tumblers of punch a day. Concerned for his uncle's health, he wrote lo hira in kindly remonstrance, beseeching bins to at least reduce the quantity, promising him if he would do so he would find his days considerably lengthened. " Try four tumblers tO begin with," he pleaded. A short time afterwards be re. eeiyed the following letter from his uncle:—" Pear nephew, —I have taken your advice, and yesterday drank only four tumblers of whisky punch. You are quite right about its lengthening my days, for, bedad, it was the longeet 'lay I ever spent in my life." There is no man in politics whose future career is more frequently talked of than is Lerd Randolph Chute:lll's. It is generally conceded that, if he lives, he will become the Leader of the Conservative Opposition, and will leave his mark upon the history of the ceuntry. In calculating his chances, however, it would be exceedingly usefal to have at hand a trustworthy forecast of the average temperature of the summer during the next five or six years. If we wcre to have a frequent recurrence of such weather as has dur- ing the past tortnight burnt up London, Lord Randolph's chances of distinction would be considerably curtailed. Hot weather has a melancholy effect upon Lien, making him hopelessly limp, and as he himself says, perfectly useless. He was to have spoken on Monday night but it was toe hot, and it was only in desperation, and with evident diffi- culty that on Tuesday he nerved himself up to the pitch of oratory. Evidently a man who cannot staad a hot day, which, as likely as not, would .cone at some critical epoch, is heavily handicapped in political races. The demand, which a short time ago rose to passionate heights, for the re instalmsnt of Valentine Baker in bisstatus in the British army has died away. It boat up against the rock of royal will that insisted upon Baker's degradation, and is not to be moved by any expressions of generous de- sire on the pert of the public or arguments toatle about anmement on the field of battle. I met Geneeal Biker at dinner the other night, in company which showed that though he is officially ostracised in deference to the expresa alone of the Queen's personal wish he is in private wel- comed and made much of by the highest persenagcs and authorities in the State. He has grown considerably stouter since I last saw him on the eve of his departure for Egypt. 'rhe only trace he bars of the terrihle wound he received in the advance on Osman Dignatit force is a blue-black fear about an inch long just under his right eye. Half an inch higher and the /shot must have entered his brain. The wound has healed up wonderfully to external appearances, but from Hine to time, in certain aspems of the weather or in varying health, Baker still feels its effects. It will b 3 remembered that when some time ago the Prince of Wales went down to review the 10th Hussars OM their return from Egypt, it was stated in the papers that he was met at the railway station by General Valentine Baker. There the record ended, and I confess I have always felt curiosity to know how the Prince met an old friend, who, in former years was one of the joyous "set " that gathered round His Royal Highness. I was glad to learn that though the Court Cireu? ar, and, as it appears, 1,0 oCeer journal might take notice of the fact, the Prince warmly greeted the gallant soldier, remaiaing in conversation with him or several minutes. Undeterred by the experience of Lord Cfr ries Beresford, Mrs. Langtry has treated herself to the luxary of a Chinese boy. Lord Charles, it will be remembered, p6ened up his boy at Hong Kong, and after a few weeka training dia. covered in him an indispensable servant, ef whose many virtues be was never tired of talking. He dl all a valet's work, did not disdain upon occasion to wait at table, and was always willing to do anything to conduce to his noble master's comfort. So anxious was he to save his lordship trouble that he sat up late at night practising his signature, and when he had perfected the imitation, appended it to a series of cheques, drawn over a period of twelve months, and reaching solicitous to save his master trouble he did not even hand the in the aggregate the earn or £l,OOO. still money over to him, but spent it himself, how remains a mystery to this day, though it is generally believed that he gambled it. Mrs. Langtrk's boy will probably not have such oppor- tunities of voluntarily extending his persenal service. She picked him up in San Francisco, and claims for bine that he is of poor but honest parent lee. " Mo," as be is Celled, is dressed in his national costume and is a very pretty bit of ornament whether in the house or on the litex seat eta Vic- toria. Except in respect of a ditvinct hainees as na the difference between mourn and /rum, the Chineee, taken young, make the best, servants in, tee wet Id, a fact which they ere already beginning to find out in California, where the Irish helps hive one teeded in bringing about the pronibi- bon of further importation of these dang,ea,as tiVais in household work, ehopkeeping.and handicraft.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
• WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATIIRDAY—The business is reported elsewhe:e. MONDAY—Before the Mlyor, Councillor Monks, and Mr - . .

J Fairclough. DRUNKENNESS.—The following were dealt with for drun- kenness, viz :—John Carrington, Patrick Finn, and John Finn, fined 53 and coats each or 7 days; Amy Gregg, sent to prison for 14 days; John B dley and Mark McGann, fined 103 and costs or 14 days; James Sauce, fined 5s and costs or 7 days; Edward Griffin and Mary Ann Warburton, fined 58 including costs; Jane Riley, fined 103 and coats or 14 days. ALLEGED ASSAULT BY A FEMALE.—AIIII 110(1.4S011 was charged with assaulting a man named John Hickey, but as that person did not appear and she said she had received great provocation, the Bench dismissed the case.. DRUNK IN THE PARK —Edwin Gaund, a respectabledook- ing, man, was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly in Bask Park on Saturday.—Mr A Browne defended. NEGLECT OF FAMlLY.—Plumpton Siddle was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and family.—Mr. Shearer, relieving officer, pressed the case on behalf of the Guardians, stating that the prisoner deserted his wife and I had been living with another woman at Macclesfield.—The Mayor said that the prisoner had acted in a cruel and heart- less manner towards his wife. He would be sent to prison for 14 days. STRAYING ANIMALS —Edward Brown, for allowing an ass to stray in Buttermarket-street on the 6th inst, was fined 2361 including costs; and Peter Clare, for allowing a pony to stray, was similarly dealt with. INnxcstqcv.—Thomas Eg,m, e youth, was fined 23 61 including costs, for bathing in the river near Mersey-st., on the 31st ult. SUPPRESSION OF NUISANCES.—Thomas Gibson was sum- moned at the instance of Inspector Norman, for allowing a nuisance to exist on his premises at Latchford.—lnspector Norman explained that the nuisance was caused by the state of a ditch, and the magistrates made an order for it to be remedied within seven days', the defendant to be liable to the forfeiture of 20s a day after that period if the nuisance was not abated.—Mary Goofier, for allowing a nuisance at a slaughter house, was fined 5s including costs. THE OVERCROWDING NUISANCE —Thomas Bridge, Back- ley-street, was fined 103 and costs for allowing a greater number of persons to sleep in his house thin it was regis- tered for.—Joseph Mulletts, Stamford-street, John Tynan, lierwood-street. and Edward Delooz., Buckley-street, were summoned for keeping lodgers without having their houses registered. Mullets, who had eight persons in a house adapted for four, was lined 53, including costs ; Tynan was dismiese I, and Delooze, who had nine per- sons in a house adapted for four, was fined 20s and costs ASSAULTS. —• Darby Rowan, charged with assaulting an ex-policeman named Johnstone, was bound over in his own recogaisances fn.' six months. DESERTERS.—dames Howard and James Duff, last from Gibraltar, who admitted being deserters from Her Majesty's 2nd Batallion Dublin Fusiliers, were remanded to await escort. TUESDAY.—Before Councillors 13roalbent and Mont.

DRUNKENNESS.— Patrick Gilgannon, for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart in Bridge-st., on the pre- vious afternoon, was fined 5s and costs.--Mary Smith, an elderly womaa, was charged with being drunk whilst at the police station. She was discharged. THREATENING A WIFE.—ThOGIAS Edmonds was charged with using threats towards his wife.—Complainant said that her husbind came home drunk, with a bottle of rum, which be insisted upon drinking. Afterwards, because she decli- ned to fetch him some beer, he threatened to take her life. —lie was bound over to keep the peace for six months. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Fairclough. DRUNKENNESS—Mary Cowen and Mary Dolan were each fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-street on the previous evening.—John Ryan, charged with being drunk and dtserderly, in Church-street, was allowed t) go free en paying the lock-np fee. DESERTION—Henry Johnstone, who pleaded guilty to being a deserter from Her Majesty's 3rd Bittalion, Manches- ter Regiment, s'ationed at Ashton-under-Lyne, was re- manded to Walton to await an escort.

div.head: THURSDAY—Before Captain. Litton.
div.p: THURSDAY—Before Captain. Litton.
DRUNK AND DisormEaLy.—Edward Kelly, a stranger, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Sankey- street on the previous evening. He was discharged on promising to leave the town. _
FRlDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Captain Reynolds.

A REFRACTORY PAUPER —Walter Kay Sykes was charged with refusing to perform his task of work whilst a casual inmate of the vagrant ward of the Warrington Union. Prisoner would not work and resused to give any reason for his refusal. He had now nothing to say and was committed for seven days._ . .

DRUNK AND INLECENT.—Mary Ellen Belligan, for beiag drunk an disorderly and indecent in Academy-street, was fined 53 and costs 0r 7 days. SLEEPING Our—Rebecca Holt and Esther Ann Harrison, young girls, were sent to prison for 14 days for being found sleeping in an unoccupied house in Rose-yard, without any visible means of subsistence. PROVOKING LANGUAGE —Ann Lawton was charged with using provoking language to Mary Roscoe on the 11th Aug., and was dismissed on payment of costs.—Rowland Roscoe, wife of the previous complainant, was then charged with using threatening language to Ann LAWNE. He was dis- missed on payment of costs.—LydiaUnsworth was sum- moned for using provoking language to Francis Agnes Green. Bound over to keep the peace for six months. MAINTENANCE.—Peter Naylor was summoned by Mr Shearer, relieving officer, to show cause why he should not ba committed for disobeying an order for the maintenance of his mother in the Union. The Bench made an order of is per week, being 81 on the original order and 4d on the arrears.—John Maloney was summoned for £1 15s 6d for the maintenance of his mother. He agreed to pay 2s 6d a week for the arrearo, which was accepted.—Patrick Murphy was similarly summoned for £1 12s 6d, in respect to the maintenance of his father at 2s a week. Original order re- duced to is 61 a week, and 61 a week to be paid towards the arrears. REFUSING TO QUlT.—Daniel Hyam and John Smith were summoned for refusing to quit Cie Ship Inn, Bank Quay, on the 9th August.—Dismissed for want of sufficient evidence. Grtass.—Toro little boys named Charles Rush- ton an 4 William Kaly, were summoned for doing damage to growing grass in a field belonging to Messrs Fairclough and Sons.—Ordered to pay coon. ASSAULTS.—Catherine Kelly was charged with assaulting Ada Smith.—Mr P Davies defended. A quarrel arose in consequence of the defendant invitig thrown some water on a little girl, and complainant alleged that defendant struck her with a broom after using filthy language to her.—Bound over in her own security of £5 to keep the peace for six months.--Thomas Graham was summoned for assaulting Ann Dempsy on the 11th August. Complainant said that Graham u,erl disgusting language and struck her severely. —The affair appeared to have been a general quarrel, and the Bench dismissed the defendant.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. Before Mr W B.nkes and Mr G L Davies. MiscELLANoors.—Efizabeth Sankey, for making use of obscene and profane longings in Bridge-street on the 4th lost, was fined 103 and costs.--For wandering about with- out any visible means of subsistence, Mary Kirkham, a had character, was sent to gaol for 21 days.—P.C. Morris proved the ease.--Margaret Kilgress was convicted of assaulting Sarah Inglefield-at Weston on the 7th inst and she was fined 101 atd costs.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. U. Gaskell, sen., and Mr. H. Gaskell, jun. DRUNICENNESS.—The following persons were fined for drunkenness :—Ann O'Neil, Richard Williams' Catherine David Murray, Catherine Mattben 8, Martin, John Davitt, William Wallace, and Bernard Feeney. A "COURTING" INCIDENT.—James Rawlinson and Elizabeth Jollaker were charged with cnnmitting a breach of the peace in Warrington-road.—P.C. Pitt proved the case.—Mrs Jollaker explained that Rawlinson was courting her daughter, and on the night in question he was standing with her in the road after her father had gone to bed. Mrs Jollaker called to her to come in, and she replied that she was coming, but continued to stand there, Shortly after- wards Rawlinson struck her daughter, and she went to him and called him a scamp.—Rawlinson was bound over to keep the wane for three months, and the summons against Mrs Jollaker was dismissed. A STRXY HonsE.—Edward Newman, of Milton-road, was charged with allowing his horse to stray in Victoria-road on the 31st ult., but the Bench dismissed the case after bearing the evidence. A. SSAIILTS.—Mary Donegan summoned Bridget Carlan for using defamatory language to her.—Complainant stated that she was a widow with four children, and endeavoured to obtain a living by keeping lodgers, but in consequence of the vile accusations of the defendant her life was becoming a burden to her.—Thomas Murphy, one of her lodgers, was then charged with assaulting Bridget Carlin. It was
GOLBORN E.

IPUGILISTIC FEMALES-..Jit the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Ellen Morris and Catherine Cunningham pleaded t guilty to committing a breach of the peace at Golborne, en the 2nd instant.—P.C. Whiting stated that the defendants were fighting together and otherwise creating a great dis- turbance. He went to them, and after a lot of trouble I separated them, and they went inside the house.—They were each bound over to keep the peace. TOWNSHIP OFFICES.—It is not unlikely the ratepayers ' of Golborne may soon have to take into consideration the advisibility of erecting public offices for the use of the township officers, Parochial Committee, die. For a number of years the last mentioned body have had the free use of Mr Brewis's private office, but as the family have lately re- moved to the house situated on the mill premises it is likely, we learn, that the room will be required for other pur- poses. FIRE AT GOLBORNE MILL. On Friday morning an alarming fire broke out in the second storey of Golborne Old Mill, belonging to Messrs John Brewis and Company. For- tunately the building is fireproof and the flames were conse- quently confined to the room in which the fire originated, at oae of the " mules." The mill brigade soon got to work, and ;to evinguish the fire a large quantity of hose piping was ' utilised. The fire was put out In about an hour; the dam- age, which is pretty considerable, being covered by insur- ance. Before the fumes were extinguished a large volume of black smoke issued from the building, which from the ou,side appeared doomed to destruction. I PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE—AU ordinary meeting of this committee was to have been held in Mr Brewis's offices, 1 Golborne, on Wednesday afternoon, but owing to there not being et quorum present it was adjourned till next month. The only members present were Messrs Gardiner and Mit- chell, and the Surveyor (..111 Bennie.) If the business had been transacted in the ordinary Connie the Sarveyor would have reported that all the work in connection with this year's length of the High-street improvement was now com- pleted, except the paving of the roadway between the chan- nels —Mr James Taylor refused to pay his water rent on account of the charge being based on the rateable value of his house and farm buildidgs, on the grounds that only the dwellinghouse is supplied, and that the water is used for purely do- mestic purposes. Ile (the surveyor) had since made in- quiries as to the charges made for water supplied to farms in other districts, and found that they were made on the same basis as their own, but he had no doubt tbat in many instances the water was used for all purposes about the farms, whereas in this particular instance it was used for domestic purposes only. He should therefore be glad if they would consider the question, and he might remark that they had the power to make a reduction if they thought it justifiable. ,f, however, an alteration was made in this instance he moot ask them to consider other charges on firms in the township, particu- larly Mr Pierpoint's whose water rate was based on an assessment which included the isolated farm buildings iii Pierpoint-street and Carn-laue, and as a matter of course, his water rent was a very high one, considering the quantity of water used. The inspector of nuisances had served Mr. J. E. Pardey with notice to fill up a pond at Golborne Smithies into which the water from the flushing station at that end of tho township ran. Mr. Legh's sur- veyor had called upon him and said that if they thought it desirable they might run the water into another pond, which was fifty yards further, by paying a slight acknowledgment, and this might be done by laying earthen-vare pipes at a cost of £2. If they were not willing to adopt this plan they might reverse the fluehing val 73 so that the water might be conveyed away by the Lowton-road sewer, nnd be recom- mended this plan. The consumption of water for the fosr weeks ending lot August equallel 99900 gallons, which was much above the average, but it was accounted for by two heavy leakages which had occurred, one in Worsley- street, and the other in the Wigan-road. These leakages were of course attended to as soon as discovered.—The con- sideration of this report Was Of Callri9 left over to the next meeting.

alleged that the defendant struck the plaintiff on the head 1 with a brick, inflicting a severe wound.—Defendant stated the complainant had aggravated him by her language. and her husband had sant the brick at him. He sent the brick back at the husband, but it struck the woman.—Carlan was bound over to keep the peace for three months, in two sureties of £5 each, and Murphy was fined 10s and costs.— Mary Ann Culbert was charged with assaulting Catherine McHugh on tho 7th inst.—Complainant alleged that the de- fendant threw a bucket of water over her, and struck her on the head with a brick. Since then she had frequently had fits.—Defendant denied the assault and called a witness who stated the complainant had had fits for the last ten years A fine of 103 and costs was imposed.--Mary Mularkey was charged with assaulting Mary Lawler on the 28th July. An altercation took place between the parties about the de- fendant beating the complainant's children, when the for- mer, using language of a most disgusting character, ran at the complainant with her head and damaged her lips and teeth.—The defendant was fined 103 and costs.

div.head: ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

FRIDAY:BefOre Mr. C. J. Bishop and Mr. A. Sinclair. MISCELLANEOUS CASES.—Sarah Priestly was charged with using obscene and profane language in Bridge-street, %Incite, and was fined 2s 61 and costs.—John Lowe was charged with allowing the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire at Sutton, on the 2nd inst. He was fined 6d and costs.—Michael Nolan was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the support of his son, who is in an Industrial School. Supt. Johnston said defendant was earning 3s a day. The Bench ordered him to pay is 6d per week. ASSAULTS —John Hoogan, Windle, was charged with assaulting James Mcßrvde, at Sutton, on the 30th of last month. Complainant is employed at the Sutton Lodge Chemical Works as a weighman. The defendant is a salt- cake worker in the name works. It was stated that the de- fendant and complainant had a scuffle, and it was alleged defendant put his leg round that of complainant and en- deavoured to throw him' but complainant being a tall man , ha failed.. About two hours after the scuffle complainant I felt severe pain in his ankle and could hardly walk. He I believed it was owing to defendant having kicked him while Ihe was trying to throw him. In consequence of the assault defendant had been dismissed the works. Mr. Hains I (Massey and Hahn), who appeared on behalf of the manager of the works, said he had been instructed to press for a heavy penalty. The defend Int was fined 5s and costs. —A man named Lowton was charged with assaulting Peter Sephton. It appears that defendant lodges with complain- ant, and has three children. He came home about half-past twelve, and committed the offence without any provocation. , Fined 103 and costs. I MONDAY.-13:fore Councillorit Pilkingtcn and Alderman
J. Cook.
BEGOING.—Mary Saosüeld,amiddle.agod woman, was charged with begging fram door to door in Doulton-street, Eccleston, on Saturday night, and was committed to priaon for seven days.

div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

ASHTON LOCXL BO 11113.—0 n Wednesday week, the monthly meeting of this board was held at the offices of the board, Mr Moubert presiding. There were also present Messrs Gaskell, Lowe, C Latham, Painter, Roberts, W La- tham, Boardman, Stone, Wright, Goldsworth (surveyor) Bill (clerk), and Chambers (nuisance inspector.)—Highway and Sanitary and Gas and Water Committees: A meet- ing of these committees was held on Wednesday, July 16th. The plans of the proposed new sewer along the brook from the Congregational Chapel to the gas works, together with an estimate of the cost, were laid before the meeting. The board was recommended to instruct the surveyor to proceed with the work at once. The surveyor was instructed to do what was necessary for the purpese of putting subsidences in Wigan-road, Robinson's-lane, and Liverpool-road, in a safe condition. The minutes were passed.—Special Meet- ing: A special meeting of the board was held on Wednes- day, July 16th. Tenders for the buildings in connection with the proposed extensions and improvements at the gas- works were laid before the meeting, and that of Mr Joseph Mitchell was accepted. The clerk was instructed to prepare the necessary contract. The minutes were confirmed.— Highway and Sanitary Committee: This committee met on Wednesday, July 30th. Tendtrs for the pipes required for the proposed new sewer from the Congregational Church to the gasworks were laid before the • meeting. The tender of the Staveley Iron Compzny was accepted. The surveyor stated that the medical officer's assistant had informed him that po fresh cases of scarlet fever had eome to his know- ledge, with the exception of two, both of which had been sent to the board's temporary hospital, and were making satisfactory progress. The proceedings of the committee were adopted.—Fmance and General Purposes Committee: A special meeting of this committee was held on July 2nd. The collector was allowed to use the room under the board- room for an office, and the surveyor was instructed to procure the necessary furniture. The ordinary meeting of the Finance and General Purposes. Committee was held afterwards. On general district rate account the balance in the bank was £360 13s 4d; gasworks account, due to bank, £371 193 ld ; waterworks account, due to bank, £2,560 1.7 s 64. The minutes were pissed.— The Gas and Water Committee met on Wednesday, July 30th. The surveyor was instructed to see Mr. Paterson and arrange with him for taking in tenders for the iron work. The Surveyor submitted the following statement showing the probable cost of carrying water to those parts of the district not yet supplied, and the probable return, viz: 3in main from Ashten Cross to Blackhrook, along the Liverpool- road, 3,480 yards, £435 105, probable return, £35 78; 3in main front Rye Croft farm to Coroner's Brook, 1,080 yards, £133, probable return, £8 Os 84 ; 3in main from Heath-road to the top of Ashton Heath, 450 yards, £67 103, probable return, £4 ls 81; lin main from Tithbarmhillock to tho end of Garswood-lane, 666 yards,£s9 .13s 31, probable return, £2 123. The matter was deferred to the next meeting of the committee. The surveyor and the clerk were instructed to prepare a return of the farms using the Board's water, and to make inquiries to what extent the water is used for trade purposes, and report to the next meeting of the committee. ATTEMPT TO STRANGLE AN PARLESTOWN CONSTABLE. —Michael Coomer, of Newton, was charged at the Newton Town Hall on Monday, before Mr T J Gillespie, with being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on Saturday night.— From the evidence of P.C. Lloyd, it seemed that about half- past eight'on Saturday night the prisoner was drunk and smashing the windows of a house where he had been lodg- ing, and out of which he had been turned. The constable asked him to desist and go away, but the prisoner immedi- ately rushed at him, pushed him against the wall, and made an attempt to strangle him. Two shopkeepers in Bridge- street went to the rescue of the constable, who ultimately secured Coomer and locked him up—Mr Gilleepie said the prisoner was lucky in not being charged with assaulting the constable in addition to the charge of drunkenness. He I would be fined 5s and costs for the latter offence.
