div.head: REFORM AGITATION. CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION IN MAN-
div.p: THE REFORM AGITATION. CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION IN MAN-
CHESTER.

Favoured until the commencement with brilliant weather, the advantage of two weeks of special "drumming up," and the inducement of very cheap excursion tickets, the Con- servative forces were marshalled at the Pomona Palace, Manchester, on Saturday, as a counter demonstration to the great and enthusiastic Liberal meetings so readily gathered together in the same place, amid the rain, a fortnight before. Inside the Palace, the rain actually assisted the success of the Liberal meeting, whilst the Tories, not long braving the , heat, largely preferred to be addressed outside, so that which was supposed to be their chief gathering lost much of its possible effect, and Lord Salisbury's first speech could not be heard over a very large area owing to the noise around the refreshment counter. It was noticeable that Lord Salts. bury and Lord Churchill had virtually each his own meet- ing, and apparently avoided coming in each other's presence. The numbers inside the Palace were extravagantly stated, and the correspondent of a contemporary, who hart a turn for figures, says he was so astounded by the estimates given by Lord Salisbury and Mr Chaplin of the numbers present in the Palace that he put the following figures together to satisfy himself that they had been grossly exaggerated : There were in the reserved seats about 1.200; unreserved seats, about 1.300; gallery and platform, 500; standing on Chairman's right, 150; standing on Chairman's left, 3,000; standing at back of hall, 450; total, 6,600. This is a toler- ably accurate statement of the numbers present in the Palace whilst Lord Salisbury was speaking. It must not be , forgotten, however, that the above figures have nothing to do with the overflow meetings, of which at one time three ' were being held. The most reliable estimates place the total numbers present at less than 25000, though Tory ex- travagance has amusingly talked about 120,000. Sir Richard Cross took the chair at the Palace shortly before 4 p.m., having Lord Salisbury on his right hand, and Mr Chaplin, M I", on his left. Amongst other gentlemen present at this or the meetings elsewhere were Lord It Churchill, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, M P, Lord C J Hamil- ton, M P, Lord Cranbourne, the Hon A P Egerton, M P. Mr W H Houldsworth, M P, Mr A J Balfour, M P, Mr W T Marriott, M P, Mr W W B Hulton, Mr T Gibson-Bowles, the Hon A Be Tatten Egerton, M P, Mr E Hardcestle, Mr F S Powell, Mr H H Howarth, Mr T H Birley, Mr J Maclure, and Mr J Grant-Lawson. The CHAIRMAN formally opened the proceeeings by an- nouncing that a number of addresses would first be pre- sented. Mr W TOUCHSTONE presented 176 addresses to the Mar- quis of Salisbury, and read that sent by the South-East Lan- cashire Conservative Association as expressing the senti- ments of the rest. Lettl SeLteneatv, whose rising was the signal for an en- thusiastic demonstration, said; I am heartily glad to receive this kind welcome from so large and enormreue an assembly, because the cause which I am representing here is the cause of freedom and constitutional order. I wish that it were possible that some of Her Majesty's Government could be here to witness this great assembly. I believe that the numbers which have assembled fir the present demonstra- tion exceed anything of which we have had experience before—(hear, hear,)—and that as many as 120,000 tickets have been taken for this demonstration. (Cheers.) That number gives me great consolation, because tlr Chamberlain —(hieses and hooting)-has been threatening at Birmingham that be is going to march an army of 100,000 men upon London. (Cheers.) lam very glad to think that we shall be able to hang upon his rear with a Lancashire army quite as large as that, for Lancashire has a special interest in this battle for redistribution which we are fighting. (Cheers ) The present representation of Lancashire is 33 members. If Lancashire had the members which, according to a merely arithmetical computation, would fall to her, she would have 03 members, Therefore Mr. Charn• berlain may be sure If he goes to London at the head of 100,000 men to prevent the passing of a good redistribution scheme, Lancashire will be prepared to see that justice Is done. (Cheers.) Middlesex has even a greater interest than Lancashire in the paseing of a fair redistribution scheme. It has now 16 members. It would have is right under a strict computation to 54 members. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Chamberlain is very fond of calling your memories back to 1832, aed he thinks you know so little of hietory that you will imagine that the conflict at present is the same as the conflict was then. There are one or two important distinctions. In the first place the Reform Bill of 1832 was sent, up to the House of Lords after a disselution in which the mind of the people was taken, and most unequivocally expressed. In the second place, after the House of Lords had put aside that bill, which I think they did most unwisely— what did the Government do ? Why, the Government re- signed, and it was not until they had resigned, and the Op- position had declared that they were unable to take their places, it was not until then that all these terrible measures which Mr. Chamberlain recalls were put into force. If Mr. Chamberlain is so fond of the precedent of 1832, I want him to follow it to the letter. (Cheers.) I venture to say that if the Government did follow the precedent of 1832, and did resign, that there would be no difficulty in filling up their places, and that the result of that step would be that the passing both of a Franchise Bill and a Redistribu- tion Bill would not be delayed, but would be acceleeated. (Cheers.) There is one other difference .between 1832 and the present time. Then the Liberals were fighting for re- distribution ; now they are fighting against it And that is the vital difference between the two epochs. Redistribution then, as now, as Mr. Bright had told us, is the soul of the question of reform Then it was the Liberals who were pushing redistribution, and the Tories most unwisely re- sisting it. Now it is the Tories that are pushing redistribu- tion, and the Liberals that are most unwisely resisting it. Mr. Brieht spoke on the importance of redistribution in 1859. But Mr. Chamberlain told us last year what he thought of the importance of redistribution and enfran- chisement. It was only last year at Birmingham. Bid he then tell you that the two could be held separately F Not a bit. What be said woe, "There is a more important matter before us " (mind' you, a more important matter than the franchise.) We have to see that an ecral value is given to the vote. It is no use," says Mr. Chamberlain, "increasing the number of voters if yom water them and minimise tha political influence which the rote confers. (Cheers.) It is no use putting a million in the place of a hundred thousand if the million has no greater power than the hundred thousand has." That was the Liberal doctrine till, for party purposes, the Liberal party thought they could do better without it. (Cheers and in- terruption.) They were very fond of imputing to us opinions we do not hold and have never eerpeessed, and among them they are fond of stating that redistribution is a thing they especially care about, and which, is no interest of ours to press forward. One of your townemen has put in ray hands a computation, of the accuracy or which I have no doubt, that there are 266 members of the House of Commans re- presenting constituencies of less than 5,000 electors, and out of these 83 are Conservative and 1.33 Liberal. (Cheers and laughter.) /am justified, therefore, in saving that no Re- distribution Bill which is tolerably fair and sufficiently ex- tensive can do otherwise than add to the force of the Con- servative party. (Cheers.) The arraignment against us is that we have stopped the bill for enfranchising these two million voters. Have we stopped it ? ' (Cries of "No.") It is even now in the power of the Government, if they choose to do it, to pass that bill. We have attached a condition to its passing, namely, that it shall be complete, and if it made complete we shall pass it with pleasure. (Cheem.) The bill is still alive. If the Government choose, they misht, instead of prorog.uing, adjourn the Houses, bring up, a ft'distribution Bill in the autumn, and when that bill had Passed the House of Commons it would eefin this bill, which is remaining in the House of Lords, and both would pass• into law—(cheers)—and though undoubtedly ills not usual' to substitute an adjournment for a prorogation, yet it hap. been done, and it was done only the other day in order to pass those new rules that are called the closure, which has done so little for the House of Commons, (Hear, hear.) Or, If the Government wished, instead of wasting next session as they propose, repeating exactly the mitstakes of the ses- sion that has passed by, they might introduce a Redistribu- tion Bill first, and then when the Redistribution Bill had passed, I venture to assure you, and to be quite certain, that the enfranchising bill would have no difficulty in pas- sing through both Houses. (Cheers.) But they have a more summary, and a more complete method than that; they have simply to dissolve. (Loud cheers.) If they think we are wrong, let them go to those froln whom they hold their power and ask whether we are wrong. (Cheers.)

Mr. CHAPLIN. M.P., congratulated the meeting upon its colossal proportions. He held that the agitation against the Lords was a sham one and quite artificial, and therefore bound to fail.—Mr. W. W. B. HIILTCN movcd "That this meeting heartily supports the House of Lords in insisting upon a complete Reform Bill, combining redistribution with the extension of the franchise."—Me. W. H. Houldsworth, M.P., in seconding the resolution, said he had no hesitation in declaring that the voice of the great majority of Lanca- shire men was in favour of supporting the House of Lords in the reasonable and patriotic course which they had adop- ted. (Hear, hear). Sir M. fircirs-BEAca rose, amid loud cheers, to support the resolution. It seemed to him presumptuous for anyone to suppose, in a county like Lancaster, where there is hardly a difference in large parts of that county between the borough and the county populations, that the question a reform could ho properly dealt with unless it included the redistribution of seats. He considered the present agi- tation more serious for the Liberal party than for the House of Lords.

Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, who also supported the re- solution, received a most enthusiastic greeting. He said : The Radical party, with Mr. Gladstone at its head—(hiss- ing)—is outraged and indignant with the Tories because we have adopted as our party cry an appeal to the peoole. (Loud cheers.) The Radicals say that anything more monstrous, more unconstitutional, cannot be imagined. Mr. John Morley, like Felix, the Roman governor, on being preached to on judgment to come, gives a feeble and stam- mering explanation, "Yes, perhaps, very likely, but at a more convenient season. (Laughter and cheers) Lard Rartington, who was here the other day,—(hooting)— asked the men of Lanca.hire to remember 1832, and to re- member 1866. But I declare theta is no analogy between those times and the present. What is the great feature of the changed times which have cline over us since 1832, and the changed parties which have accompanied these times? Why, it is the growth of the Tory party in our great nor- thern cities. Every liberal meeting is followed by a Tory meeting, at which the Liberal sophistries. Liberal misrepre- sentation, and Liberal impostures are confuted, corrected, and exposed. And last, but not least, thank Ged, we have

div.p: COUNTER RigICAL. DEMONSTRATION.

On Saturday an open-air demonstration, promoted by the. Manchester Radical Association to advocate the abolition of the House of Lords, was held in Stevenson-square, Man- chester. Several thousands of people attended, and speak- ing took place from two platforms. At the first platform the chair was taken by Mr Percy Glass, who argued that an hereditary House of Lords was an incompatibility in a free country.—Mr E El PARKINSON. a working man, proposed a resolutiontiffirrning that the House of Lords ought to be abolished, and legislative power entrusted solely to the representative chamber.—Mr GEORGE MASON seconded the resolution.—Dr R M PANKIIIIRST, barrister-at-law, in sup- porting it, asked them to enter iota a solemn league and covenant against the House of Lords.—The resolution was carried with loud cheers.—A similar resolution was submit- ted from the other platform and passed.

Saturday was a notable day in the political history of Todinorden, when a great Liberal demonstration took place, attended by some 4,000 persons. When the gentlemen ap- peared on the platform who were to conduct the meeting there was a loud burst of applause, and the chair was taken by Mr J H Wilson, of Coruholme, who gave a short, vigorous address. The members of Parliament who were present afterwards addressed the meeting. Mr Isaac Holden spoke first, and Me John O'Connor Power and Mr Daniel Grant followed.

A meeting in support of the action taken by the House of Lords with reference to the Franchise Bill took place on Monday evening in the Ashton Town Hall, when, despite the oppressive condition of the weather, there was a crow- ded and enthusiastic attendance. Mr. Thomas Heginbottom presided, and he was supported by Earl Cardogan' Mr. T. Gibson Bowles, the second Conservative candidate for Sal- ford, and others —lt was resolved " That this meeting, while desirous that household suffrage should be extended to the counties, cordially agrees with the House of Lords in repudiating without mercy' any measure unless accom- panied by a just redistributien of political power, and fur- ther desires that the opinion of the country should be taken on the complete scheme." A Conservative demonstration was held at Bangor on Sat- Urday. Colosel the Hon. W. E. Sackville West presiding.— The Earl of Carnarvon proposed a resolution which was oar, red, condemnatory of the conduct of public aff4irs hpagg and abroad by her Majesty's Governm,ni. . .

On S)ttirday aftcrB9o4 4 iteform demonstration took Place ai Loughborough, Noah Leicestershire and proved a great success. Mr. ARNOLD MORLEY, said that the ohject of those demonstrations was to convince Lord Sails- bury and those who followed him that the people were really in earnest upon that question, and that they were deter- mined that the Franchise Bill should speedily pass into an Act of Parliament.

Speaking on Saturday at a great open-air demonstration of the Liberals at Cleckheaton, Mr. E. L. STANLEY, M.P., said the present Reform Bill erred on the eide of moderation, and in his opinion ought to have been drawn on the lines of residential suffrage, whereby a man should vote only oneel, as be strongly objected to voters travelling all over the country nd voting.down the real opinion of the neighbour- hood in which toe election was contested. An open-air demonstration, attended by several thousand persons, was held at Rochester on Saturday evening to pro. test against the rejection by the House of Lords of the Fran- chise Bill.—Mr Campbell-Bannerman, M P., smuted the idea that the Lords were to dictate to the Government of the csuntry when an election should take place.—The reso• lotion was carried by an overwhelming majority. A precession of the Liberals of Castleford and district was held tert Monday, headed by five bands, after which a meet- ing was held on the Rectory Estate to consider the franchise questirth It is calculated 3,000 people were present. Mr H 1) McClokie,Castleford, presided, and the meeting was very enthusiastic.

Ate largely-attenthd meeting at Grantham en Monday night, resolutions were unanimously passed assuring the Government of their hearty support in any measure they might adopt t,) put an end to the power of veto of the House of Lords.

A crowded meeting of Liberals, convened by the Mid- Somerset Liberal Association, was held on Monday at Wells. Resolutions were passed condemning the action of the Peers, and urging the Government to take the nicessary steps to put an end to the power of veto in the Tipper House. An open-air demonstration in support of the Franchise Bill was held on Saturday at Bingley, Bradford. Resolu- tions in support of the House of Commons and condemna- tory of the House of Lords were carried unanimously. A great demonstration to protest against the refusal of the Lords to pass the Franchise Bill took place at Scarborough on Saturday. Resolutions in accordance with the objects of the meeting were unanimously passed. MR PETER HYLANDS, M.P., AT STALTERIDGE.--OTI Satur- day afternoon a great Liberal demonstration in support of the Franchisa Bill was held at Stalybridge, amongst those present being Mr Illingworth, Mr Summers, Mr Lee, and Mr Rylands, M P.'s.—Mr Peter Rylanda, M.P., in moving the second resolution, which demanded a revision of the constitution and powers of the HOU9O of Lords so ae to bring its action into harmony with the exegessed judg- ment ef the nation, said he did not know whether they ever beard el a number of -publicans and beerselters com,bining and calling themselves the sons of temperance—(laughter) —but if they ever did it would be about as surprising a thing as the Tories calling themselves reformers. (Laugh- ter, and hear, hear.) The reformers of 183 T, bad to fight the House of Lords, as the reformers of to-day had to tight them. Recently the Tories had been holding a" pic-nia."- t Hughenden Park, the residence of the late Lord Beacons- held. Sir Stafford Northcote, who spoke at that meeting, said he could imagine the shade of Lord BeaconsilelCo leaking down—(laughter)—at what was going on in this sublun lry sphere and saying What has become of the Conserrative party that they are supposed to be op- 1 posing Reforne? (Laughter.) Sir Siafford litirthcote then went on to say that his party gave household suffrage to the boroughs. He (Mr Rylands) had great respect for Sir Staf- ford Northcote, but it tweeted to him that on this occasion— speaking in the preseuce as he supposed of the spirit of his former leader—(laughter)—he had been rather influenced by the spirit, and used language of a very misleading character. The House of Commons was now determined to support Mr Gladstone. The Lords would probably reject the Bill again, but the th'ad time it must be sent up, as Lord Riahard Grosvenor hod add, with a sting in its tail., (Cheers.) For hiaown part, he hoped Mr Gladstone would compel the Lords to accept the Bill by getting the Queen's authority to create a number of new peers. (Hear, hear.) They would get the-Bill in the end, and a good measure of redistribution would, be passe3, no doubt, by the present Government.

The motion was carried unpimously. A large open-air gathering, attended by about 4,000 per- sons, was held on Saturday, in West Hartlepool. Mr. W. Gray, J P.,.preeided.. Sir Josenh W. Pesse, , 8 tid that , the Lords might turn out the Franchise Bill in October and even in the spring again, but it would come forward con- lineally till pissed, and action like that cf the Home of Lords would never be forgotten. Liberals had nothing to fear from redistribution, but the Franchise Dill must le drat carried.—Resoluiions of confidence in the Government and condemning the Try Peers were passed. Lord Randolph Churchill will, it is said, take part in the, Conservative demonstration to be held in Midlothian shortly after Mr. Oladstone's departure. Lord Salisbury and Sizi Stafford Plortlrcote hove- undertaken to spsak on the same occasion. _ _ _

ALiblral demonstration was held at I,l:•gan, on Tuesdkx night, Mr T Lea, Mr Summers, and Mr Villiam on, mnm, hers of Parliament, being present. Resol•ations were passed approving of the home and foreign policy of the Govern- ment, and urging the necessity for such measures as woniri prevent the linase of Lards from continuing to thwart v.ial defeat the will of the people.

HOT WEATHER! The intense heat of our New England cities had the effect of driving me into the country, where I might expect to find cool airs and quiet rest. Incessant travelling in a broiling sun and in railroad cars that refresh with ice water, and clouds of grit from the eagine, had made we feel as tioigh a dip in the Atlantic, with a shark in sight, would be prefe-rable to any further experience on land. The oppor- tunity for a change came upoil me like a message from .home. I and a friend, a brother " ink-slinger," were invited by another to spend a day or two with him. it, teas simply to be a neighbourly visit, and not more than 146 Miles away. Our only chance being at the end of the week, we set out at five o'clock On Saturday morning, the 28th June, the Bret break of our journey being Boston, Mass. A stroll through the classic city in the early morning, ere the sun had got fairly to work, we took as an augury of how delightful the rest of our "out" would be. At train time we took the "steam care" on the Eastern Railroad to "Great Falls," in New Hampshire. Our reception at Great Falls was warm in more senses than one. The cordial shake of the hand was right and welcome. But that part of the reception the sun had to do with was blistering. Its face had been newly burnished, and arrayed in a mantle of brightest blue, it sent its shafts of heat down upon us with blades red from its scorching fire. It was greatly assisted in its effect by a mirror of sand that was ankle deep, and the absence of as much as a bean pole to cast upon us its meagre shadow. But at a distance from the station the road was overhung with umbrageous trees beneath which we weeld have stayed awhile had we not been urged on to our home for the 'day. 9ut' host Was a thoroughly representative Scotchman, but preferred lager to whisky,—well, such of the latter as could be had in a pro- hibited State. The welcome we received, and the cosy quar- ters placed at our service, did not provide us with that which we wanted most,—just a breath from the North Pole nicely distributed. If windows were opened wide, and the rooms darkened until we could hardly Sce each Other- it Was only the Oven with its door opened; the heat was all the same. How were we to pass our time under the circumstances ? It was unfit to be out of doors, and quite as unfit to be indoors. " Thiseway," said a friend, and we submitted ourselves to be led through the burning streets until we reached the river' where we crossed out of New Hampshire into the State of Maine. Some mysterious movements were here observable at we stood at the corner of a low building, over the door of which a rude !signboard informed us that the building was the " Post-office." This was in the town of Berwick, not on Tweed, but on the "Newitchiwannah." A kind of freemasonary was going on to which I had not been initiated, but was about to be, I could gather. "Open, Sesame!" and the next moment I found myself in a crowd where drinking was going on with a briskness that we some- times see at a flower-show, when the day is hot, and the band has ceased to play, and everybody wants to be served at once, and this in the model State of Maine, where no in- toxicating liquor is allowed to be distilled, and it is unlawful for railway companies to carry it. This latter statement must be taken with a grain of salt, as it nets upon about as much authority as the history of "Tom Thumb," or "Jack the Giant-Killer." From what I saw here on Saturday, June 28, I had no hope that I could spend the "fourth of July" of glorious memory, as far from the "madding crowd" I might desire. But pray never let me again hear Maine held up as an example to drunken England. I have seen in half-an-hour more tippling within the shadow of the police-station than can be witnessed in any similar sized room in Manchester. I could not have believed it had I not seen it. I was asked to look round on Sunday, but I had not the courage to face so much hypocrisy. I had seen enough. The same thing prevails in New Hampshire; and there is an evil attending this sly drinking which can only be guarded against in places where the consumption of ardent spirits is not accounted to be unlawful. Much of the villainous stuff that no one else will drink is sent here, as competition is shut out, and drinkers have to take any- thing they can get, wh.ch is so much the sweeter because, like stealing apples, it is prohibited. Ido not wonder at people going mad, and committing murder, under such con- ditiocs. A murder had been committed just before we reached Great Falls. The facilities for sly drinking are not to be numbered. Any stranger would wonder why there were so many drug stores in so thinly populated a place. Surely the whole of the inhabitants de not require constant pbysicking. No, but they want something besides, which the law siys they shall not have. " Kerosine "is the staple trade of these establish- ments; but all that is disposed of is not consumed in lamps. It was not until the gloaming fell that we could enjoy tolerable comfort, and that was on sufferance. The mosqui- toes were preparing for the Fourth of July, and did not , parade as expected. But the flies are at any time quite as I annoying, because they are always on the war path, and hang around scalps with the attentions of an Indian. We were promised a drive for the morrow that would compen- sate us for all we had suffered, and make up for the dis- appointment we felt. There was a gloriously breezy bluff, or headland, about ten miles away, where it was always cool, and where we could refresh as we wanted. Then the drive would lead through a splendid country, the scenery of quite an English character, with demi woods to shelter us from the heat, and where bays and inlets threw from their breasts the delicious airs with which only water could temper the influence of the sun. Alas! we were again doomed to disappointment. The drive was certainly such as we might obtain in the English lake district, if heaven's furnaces were in full blast. .But who would care to drive from Bowness to Ambleside if Windermere was dry? When we reached Dover we fouud the tide just about its lowest ebb. The sea had taken up its carpets, and gone out towards the Atlantic, leaving a muddy floor for us to get our breezes and inspiration from. But we drove on to Dover Point, three miles further on, and no one need be surprised at the horse finding the stables without being shown. The equine nature has something of the human about it. We sought our stable as well. But where was the promised breeze? Gone with the tide, we were in- myrs Foli. HEALTH. formed, and would not return without it. former has been dealt with. It was not the fault of the place that the tide was out. It could not be answerable for the moon's ruling. It was merely the accident of the time. But the Great Falb l—cardlog, and spinning, weaving and bleaching,—great as are the works that man has constructed there, and they are great, as we saw from passing through them, they are not to compare with the ideal I had formed of the place. Bat the train is now due that is to carry us to within a few miles of the Canadian frontier, and our Scowls friend, his wife and two children, are all agog for a delightful out- ing, only thsy Is4ep Out of the sun as well as they can. We are on the spin agalo, away, away, for long miles we go, the Ibis of cars wriggling like a mighty snake; but our faces require Oar handkerchiefs all the time. When tired and sleepy, and as dusty and gritty as a smithy floor, we are informed that we are at the depot bearing the name of Wolf bro' Junction. Here we lunched oil etticken pie, which was more like an English dish than anything I had tasted in the States, INear the station I was introduced to a small wooden shanty where a newspaper is printed and published, the proprietor being the editor and reporter, and his young I wife compositor and paragraphist. Which of the two was I the engine to drive the machine I had not the temerity to enquire. But it was a most compact little place' and ap- peared to be furnished with everything neces.sary for work- ing a "news mill" on a small scale. Being Monday, it was, as is usual on a weekly, a slack day, and the whole of the staff were going out, both of them. I was very much in- terested with this model office, in which everything was kept in such order as only a woman knows how, or has patience to see to. None of the compositors smoked or drunk My readers should have seen the editor, as we found him, He was still in his war paint; and Crasoe could not have been better furnished with arms and ammunition than he was. His waistcoat pockets were crammed with pencils, pens, scissors, gum brush, pipe with tobacco ashes dribbling Out of the bowl, a six-inch rule, and things editorial we could net make out. We were kindly received, and we had , as much fan out of him ag Pit sun could ext Met. 15 Aii aboard !" Another long whirl and we are at North Conway, in the very lap of the White Mountain region. " Jumping Jehosphat !" exclaimed the deacon, as he "dumps " himself upon the platform, "Something with the lid off again !" If it was hot at Great Falls, they must have turned the reflector of a Dutch oven on the face of the Barnum-white-elephant mountsins. Seat ourselves anywhere? No, let us walk abroad until our mortal candles are melted to the wick, Hear what the Advance man has to say : " North Conway was hotter than Hades with the lid off. It fairly toasted itself in a red-hot bed of sand. Not a breath of air was stirring. " Is this a pleasure resort?' whispered Brierley, suddenly taking his hand from a heated fence rail upon which he had thought to rest, wearily. "Upon our assurance that it was so, and that it was one of the prettiest and most romantic spots in the whole mountain range, a spot which, for its command of craggy peaks, snow clad hills, embowered vales, winding roads, lovely views, darling little lakes and wondrous echoes, had not its equal for charming attractions, he could only say: " How soon does the train start for Fall River? How soon can you get out of this oven? Do you think we've money enough in the gang to buy me a cake of ice to- sit upon?' "We took him to see our old friend Pitman, who dosed the sufferer with citrate of magnesia, acid phosphate, ice water and fans, until he really began to see that kindness and desperate remedies were quite equal to the task of , making him forget that it was the seventh paper collar he I had just wilted in a day that was not even yet above half ' over. And then he trudged across the great Sahara of red- hot sand which lay between us and the station, and got on board and started for Boston, a long and weary ride, in which we indulged in perspiration and wicked thoughts, and never ceased growling at the hest until we had got our bath at the Massachusetts House, and kindly Charley Baker was telling 1 the pretty waitress to put big lumps of ice in our evening cup of tea." We were enticed into a " drugg,ry," and 'prescribed for. The rest—perspiration and a desire to pull a cloud over us. ' Three thousand feet of mountains, not at all white, ex- cept where a stone crops out of the bush that clothes the flanks of this seemingly interminable range! Wild enough I was the scene, which would be a thousand times wilder when draped in the snows of winter. But now—oh for a lager, and a return train! I need not describe these mountains, even if I could. Everybody has paisted such excrescences on the face of nature either on paper or canvas. The same with rivers which, looked upon from a utilitarian point of view, are merely drains to these mountains. But I would not suffer such commonplaceism to interfere with the soul's apprecia- tion of these wonders. They are mountains and streams to me still,—the same that my boyhood worshipped, and gilded my youth with a halo of poesy. But they were not revealed to me with the thermometer at 96 in the shade, and an engine panting and growling near.—From Great Britain Over the 5e4," by BAIN BRIERLEY.

PRESCOL RURAL SANITARY AunfoßirY. A meeting of the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present Messrs W A Meadows (chairman), J T Hall, J Griffiths, W Tyrer, W Newsome, J Kenwright, Leatherbarrow, Rev T Chambers, and S H Hartley (clerk), —The minutes of the last meeting were confirmed.. THE REPORTED SMALLPDX AT HALE—In reply to Mr Kenwright, the Clerk said the cost of the burnt clothing of the persons who were reported to have suffered from small- pox at Hale was over £9.—Mr Hall remarked that Dr Cooper had made a statement that the man was suffering from smallpox when he was not. He thought Dr Cooper should be called upon to give some explanation after the expense which had been entailed.—The clerk was instructed to write and ask Dr Cooper for an explanation. THE CHARGE AGAINST THE MEDICAL OFFICEI9.—The Local Government Board wrote enclosed copy of a letter from Mr W Law with refence to the proceedings of Dr E F Hall, the medical officer of health. Mr Law wrote stating that a case of smallpox had not been reported or properly cared for, and as it seemed that the Guardians ignored the charge and appeared desirous of screen- ing their sanitary medical officer, he (Mr. Liw) asked for a sworn enquiry in the cause of justice, as he was in a position to prove the case. After some desultory discession it was decided that that authority should join with the Guardians in asking the Local Government Board to make a full inquiry into the allegations made by Mr. Law. THE SEWERLGE OF ECCLESTON.—The Clerk read a letter from Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, of Tunbridge Wells, who stated that they had had a conference with their clients and solicitors on the subject of the sewerage of the Eccleston district, and they had full instructions to take all such steps as might be advisable to further the provision of proper pub- lic sewers. They asked whether the Rural Sanitary Authority meant to adopt the report of Messrs. Goldsworth and Twist, and undertake forthwith the suggested works or any part thereof. If not, their clients would prefer a corn- plaiut to the Local Government Board under the provisions of the 'Public Health Act, as the present state of matters could not be allowed to exist.—The clerk was instructed to ask the Local Government Board to hold an inquiry into the matter, and see what portions of the report of Messrs Golds- worth and Twist should be carried out.—Mr Newsome ex- pressed the opinion that the general body of ratepayers in Eccleston should not be called upon to pay rates Tor the ins- provement of private property. • ESTIMATE OF EXPENDITURE —The Clerk stated that the estimate cf expenditure for the half-year ending the 25th March, 1885, was as follows :—Salaries £215, other ex- penses, printingokc. £6O, Eccleston scavenging £l5, Hale £4O, Rainhill £274, Whiston £219, total £s4B.—The esti- mate was adopted. THE SANITARY CONDITION OF HALEWOOD SCHOOLS.—The Rev T Chambers said there had been a case of sickness amongst the children attending the Halewood schools and the medical officer and sanitary inspector had reported that there was something wrong with the closets and drains. Certain alterations were necessary, and he asked the Authority if it could not be made a town- ship matter. The alterations were for the benefit of the children and the township generally, but the managers of the school were unable to carry out the. repairs as they were altogether without funds.—The Clerk said he did not think the Sanitary Authority could legally carry out the repairs; but they could run the risk of being sur- charged to any amount expended in the work if they deci- ded to proceed with it. They, however, had to look to the owners of private property to put their property in a sanitary state.—Mr Hall expressed the opinion they could not make it a township charge —Mr Tyrer expressed him- self to the same effect.—The Rev T Chambers: We have no funds to do it —Mr Tyrer: Suppose you were compelled to do it or close the schools.—The Rev T Chambers: We should have to close the schools in hot weather.-1t was ultimately decided that the Authority should proceed with the work. SURVEYOR'S REPORT.—The Surveyor (Mr Twist) re- ported that he had arranged with Mr Fraser, district high- way surveyor, to carry out the alteration in the sewers near the New Inn, Ditto's, and the work was being proceeded with. The effluent water from Rainhill sewage farm con- tinued satisfactory. New drains and a sewer were being constructed by the owner of eight houses in Duke-street, Ditton, and a cesspool provided until such time the Author- ity cause the much needed sewer to be made on the high- way reported upon a short time ago. The ditches in Hall- lone, Ditton, remained very unsatisfactory, and be would as a temporary measure suggest to the Authority that they should give him instructions to get them cleaned out. Several owners of property situated in Halewood, Tarbock, Cronton, Bold, and Rainhill had had their attention drawn to sanitary defects, and he had every reason to hops that without directing their especial attention to them he would be able to get the improvements made. He submitted plans of cottages for Colonel Gamble, about to be erected in Hard-lane, Windle, which were according to bye-laws.— The report was adopted. THE HEALTH OF THE TOWNSHIP.—Dr. E. F. Hall (medical officer) reported that the health of the district con- tinued satisfactory. There bad been a few cases of diarahoea, but nothing of a serious character. He had had a complaint from Mr, Dainteth objecting to all the cottages in his neighbourhood using his pump, and he was going to take steps to stop them from doing so. Their only supply would then be f:om a public-honee which was decidedly objectionable, and moreover it was some distance from the cottages, which number about 18. There were two owners, one of whom he was informed was quite willmg to share the expense of getting the Widnes supply. This was all the business.

'VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT WARRINGTON. On Saturday, the annual inspection of the Ninth Lane shire (Warrington) Ride Volunteers took place, the inspec ing officer being Colonel Thackwell, commanding officer ef the Slit and 40t1e Regimental districts. In the afternoon the corps assembled at the Armoury, and afterwards marched, headed by the band, to Mr Cross's field in Arpley, where the inspection was made. The officers present were Lieut.-Coi. Greene!! (commending), Major and Adjutant O'Leary, Captains Bolton, Litton, Briggs, Ridgway, Widdows, aod Thompson ; Lieutenants Gooch and Buckton ; and Surgeons Gernalland Watkins. There were also present 35 non-cem- missioned officers, and 426 rank and file. In the field the I battalion was put through is variety of evolutions by Colonel Greenall and tlae oftice of higher rank in the presence of :.! the inspecting officer. In all or Coeg ovements the men moved with commendable steadiness and smartness, and the marches past were well done. In his address, the Inspecting Officer complimented the corps upon the way in which it toad gone through the various manoeuvres. He thought it was A that Warrington could not supply a larger and stronger regiment, although what there was was very good indeed, as the men pretefit.ed a smart and soldier-like appear- ance. He should have very ingeh pleasure in reporting favourably of them to headqtiarterti. He exhorted the officers to attend the drills regularly, and tbsts set the men a good example, which be was sure would be follovd, Greenall also subsequenly addressed the corps. Tney heZ.4: be said, done their work very steadily that day. During the previous week the attendance at drill had been satisfac- tory, though not so good in proportion as last year This falling off, however, he attributed to the fact that Bank Holiday was included in the week, for the attendance on that evening had been very small, and bed consequently brought down the average considerably. He was pleased to m.ntion that he had recommended Captain Litton, who had been associated with them for a number of years, for the post of honorary major; and also that Captain Bolton, who had eerved with them for 15 or 20 years, would shortly be presented as major. He had likewise applied that Dr. Wet- loins should be appointed SS major to the corps, and he hoped this application wou'd be considered favourably. The name of Lieutenant Gooch had not been left out of the list for promotion to a captaincy; and finally the name of Ser- geant Hutchinson, who was the only member of that corps who had served 25 years in it along with himself, had beer.' sent in for promotion as quarter-master sergeant, aergeant ilutchinsou's cervices were well wino reeognition, and he hoped the sergeant's good example would be one that the members of the corps would try to imitate. Colonel Green- all further alluded to his accident of the previous week, and expressed his thanks for the sympathy he had received from the members of the corps. Alluding to the remarks of the inspecting officer as to the strength of the corps, he said the great difficulty at Warrington, and places similarly situated, was to get a sufficient supply of good officers. He thought if they could only get plenty of officers of the right stamp, they might have a regiment a thousand strong. In conclusion he thanked the drill instructors and others for their services during the past year. The corps afterwards marched back to the armoury.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. ENTHUSIASTIC MEET„ING LAST NIGHT IN MANCHESTER. A meeting for the purpose of obtaining an expression of opinion as ta the necessity of connecting Manchester with the sea b:e a ship canal Was held last evening in the Free Trade Hell, Manchester. There was a very large attend ance, and the meeting was most enthusiastic in its support Of the scheme. The chair was occupied by the Mayor of Manchester (Mr. Goldemidt), and there were also on the !platform Mc. Jacob Bright, M.P., Mr. R. Leake, M P., Mr. W. IL Houlde•vorth, M.P., Messrs. W. H. Whittle, H. Bode ington, B. L. Green, Reuben Spencer, J. C. Fielden, Dr. Mackie (Warelegton), and numerous others. The GLEAM/dal said that of the many meetings held in that halt eearcely any had been of greater importance than that of that night. (Hear, hear.) Tee severe contest in Pariterneet hid intensified the interest felt in the project of the Ship Canal by a large majority of the citizens ef Man- chester and tee committees by which it was surrounded. Therefore as the chief magistrate of that city he could net hesitate to take the chair on that occaelon. (Loud applause.) It would be admitted by everybody that the contest had been most ably carried on, and with an energy and perseverance which such an im- portant CauSe merited, and if the promoters had not met with success they certainly deserved it. (Hear, hear.) The principal consideration for them would be whether a Ship Canal from Menchester to tho sea would be an advantage to thet diee ict. (‘ Yes.") lie believed very few, if any, Would deny that. (Hear, hear.) He saw around him many who were the Leads of municipal Corporations and Local Board-2, and they, like himself, did net commit the Local Authorities to any course of action, because it would be for each Loma Aathority, in its own chamber, and its own way, to tilseuss any suggestion which might be the outcome of that Ineetime. (Hear, hear. He was sure they would beart;ey agree seith him that the procedure in reriiament I itt elation to works of that land wee anythlng but eatisfac- tory. (Hear, hear, and loud epplause.) There ought, he ' said, to be one jeint committee, the members of which should be chosen from the House of Lords and from the House of Commons. (Hear' hear.) This would not only save expense and time, but woald secure a verdict which would have the confidence of all parties concerned. (Hear, hear.) He trusted that during the next seseioa of Parliament they might be more success- Ertl, and that a tribunal would be found which would bring the great question to a satisfactory solution in accordance with the almost unanimous with of that community. (Loud applause). Mr. ADAMSON, who was remitted with long continued ap- plause, the audience rising to its feet and waving bats and handeerchiefs, said he felt that if he had returned amongst them brokenhearted he should have felt it mended by their cordial reception and applause that night. (Hear, hear.) He belt the impression when the bill was thrown out by the Com- mons committee, that when the Lancashire men heard of that report he could at any rate calculate on their sympathy and auppert. feetid applause.) They had a. meeting of the subscribers to the canal that afternoon and an unanimous resolution was passed that the citizens of Manchester and the district would not b 3 sat upon by Liverpool or any other place. (Loud applause.) He believed that the reeolution of the sabscribem was now stronger than ever it had been before—(applause)—and he thought that with their support they should be sure to go on and conquer in the long run. But there were some doubtful spirits, and they hardly knew where to find them. The great ring of the railweys—the railway shareholders—was hidden almost behind every door, and they never knew when they were to find an enemy to put his foot down to stamp them out of exigence. Bat he hoped the encouragement they would receive from them would enable them to break up that rail- way ring and destroy for ever the conferences that raised up their heads in favour of the freights between Liverpool and Manchester. The greatest enemy they had in the - House of Commons was the solicitor for the Bridgewater Canal; but he (Mr Adamson) trusted that that gentleman would get his deseft. and that when they got their Ship Canal the poor little stinking Bridgewater Canal would perish. (Lasghter.) With regard to the ways and means, he salt, the membera of the committee and the public had contributed largely, but the time was coining, and they had invited the Corporation of Manchester to become joint promoters with them, as well as other boroughs in the dis Pict. Let them hive the au- thority of thLSJ bodies in their favour, and they would go to Parliament with ten times the force they had before. (Applause.) They had submitted their views to the Cor- poration and ohe Mayor of Manchester, and they were not only received with great courtesy, and he believed that everything they had submitted would be considered with great attention, and if he could interpret their good looks and ensiles ha Was sure it meant they intended to support them. (Elea., hear.) If they did not he should be disap- poiubel, and he believed they would be disappointed. (Hear, - tear.) Was it right for the Liverpool Corporation to fight against the Bill wiru borough funds and all its iefluence, and th tt they should not ask the Manchester Corporation to tea thcin ? (Hoer, hear.) Referring to the schemes at present under cuisideratiou, he said that which ever side of the river they went they did not intend to interfere with the estuary. (Hear, hear.) He concluded by proposing the followinz reeeluthen :—" That this meeting hereby ex- presses its opinion that the necessity for the construction of the Seip Canal to Manchester has been proved, and pledges itself to support the Provisional Committee in its continued aft olds to obtain the necessary powers from Piffle- meat to carry on such an undertaking in such a manner as they may deem meet eff mtatel." (Loud applause). Mr. floineeswartne, M P., who was received with loud applause, sec:ailed the reeelution. He said he supposed they were aware that he was rather a heretic on the subjmt of the naval, anti although heretics when converted aneele the best of people, still sortie little of his heresy continued with him. lie had reehy a sincere and hearty sympathy with the object that Mr. Adamson and they had in view, and he was sure they would allow him to express his own opinions ia his own ways, fairly and straightforwardly. (Hear, hear.) Ile did not, however, know that he had very mach to any that they would not agree with. It appeared to him that taking a practical view of that question that there were three conditions which it was essential should be kept to view by those who were going to devise the Ship Canal. In the first place he thought it Was any essential condition of any scucessful scheme. that they shoe! not injure or run any risk of injuring the es- tuary of the Mersey. He sail this because the success of a Ship Can it depended on the nominjury of the estuary, and the mentent they did injure it, or run the risk of injur- ing it they damaged the probable success of the canal. The neat con titian was that the canal they constructed should be one that would not raw:mire any very great expense in order to maintein it. They ought not, he continued, to en- coareze the Utopean idea that they were going to en ikc Manchester into a paradise, or into a greet port like Liver- pool or Lenden. The other condition of success was that the schema must commend itself net merely to the people who dreamt bat to commercial man whose capital they wanted in order to carry it out. He believed that the rejec- tion of the former scheme was the very best thing that could hove happened. ("No, no.") He said this because, as Mr Adeenion. himself had told them, he believed that the fresh erehemo which would be produced would be in many ways suortdor to the Orin that had been abandoned. (A p- phase.) All he could say was that if Mr Ademeon and his friends could not advise one that WAS better than the one that had been ateeniotted he knew he would not brim; it before the Houle of Commons. He did net believe, however, that the Tenney which had been spent WAS money lost, but that it would be like bread cast upon the waters, and they should see it after many days. (Laud applause.) Mr. beet) Bright, M.P., who was received with loud ap- plauss, supported the resolutiou. He said that when the bill was rejected last year there were failings in the public mind es to what should be done, but the great difference be- tween this year and last was that the edacetion of the pub- lic mind wife regard to that great object was much more complete and universal. (Hear, hear.) Another influence at Work this sear was that the feeling of self.resp.-ct of the people of Manchester had been aroased. Lancashire men were cet, accustomed to put their hands to anything which was ri,riat or capable of easy defence without being success- ful. (Applause.) They were not accustomed to be beaten, and if he were not mistaken the Lancashire men Ind made I up their minds not to be beaten. (Loud applauee.) Men whom defeat did not dishearten and who were stronger after a second repulse than after a first were very near to victory. (Applause.) It was his opinion, after much intercourse with his fellow men, that those who had open minds and who had gone carefully into the evidence were now almost every- where free to admit that that would he a profitable invest- ment. ( Applause.) After referring to the local, the coast- ing, and other traffic which the canal was likely to open out, he said the protnoters were engaged in a struggle with great veated interests. In this struggle nrivate individuals had "Rae great sacrifices, and the tontest in one respect was not fair. He thought no one would deny that the contest between private citizens of Menchewer and Salford and other places and the pulelic bodies of Liverpool and other public bodies was an unequal one. (Heir, hear.) He wanted to know whether the public bodies of Mancheeer, Salford, and other places would any longer stand aside. ("Na," and loud applauee.) That would not be his ideal of municipal duty, and he was glad to hear from Mr. Adamson with regard to the temper and prcbable intentions of the great Town Coun- Cil of Manchester, (Applause) He could not understand the rationing which applauded a Town Council for supply- ing pieures and bochs, and the next moment condemaed a Town Cmecil if they took part in ppening a great highway to 3,-.a by which every man, woman, and child in that city would he benefited. (Loud applause.) The resolution was then carried amidst greet enthusiasm. Mr. R. Spewoeft next moved, "That in view of the great expense -incurred by the private subscribers in their repeeted atteenete to obtain a Bill for powers to construct the Ship Canal. thha meeting; largely composed of ratepayers of the city of Manchester, urges the Corporation to contribute to the edit of the renewed application to Parliament, and trusts that the other municiwel corporations of the district will also aid in raising a sufficient fund successfully to carry on the etreeele for the Bill." (Loud applause.) They ex- pected, Mr. Spencr said. that the Manchester Corporation would contribute £15,060 or £23,001, and he did not think -the Corporations of Salferd, Stockport, Warrington, and other places would come short f their duty when the time arrived. Some persons had said that corporations had not power to contribute for such a purpose, but he was legally advised l that they hod. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. PLATT (Oldham) seconded the adoption of the reso- lution, which was carried enthusiastically.

Votes of thanks afterwards brought the proceedings to a close.

At a meetiog of subscribers and others interested in the Manchester Ship Canal scheme, held at Manchester yeszer- day afternoon, it was stated that the total income to the ' end of July amounted to £lOO,lOl, and the expenditure £86,651. It was resolved to persevere with efforts to obtain Parliamentary sanction to the scheme. MEETING OF THE MERSEY DOCK BOARD. At the meeting of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, on Thursday, Mr T D Hamby, the chairman, presiding, Mr Baring said that owing to the enforced abaence of the chairman last week he had till now deferred making a few remarks in regard to the recent Parliamentary proceedings. Those proceedings embraced the final record of perhaps the most important episode that ever happened in the history of the trust. It was not his intention to go into the Canal Bill or to dilate upon the vicissitudes and troubles which the Board had had to encounter in connection with it, ex- cept to say that whatever fear or anxiety they had endured had been ranch allayed by the coneciousness that the con- duct of the campaign was under such excellent generalship as that of the chairman. (Hear, hear.) He asked the Board for a unanimous vote of thanks ,to the chairman, solicitor, secretary, and general staff for the eminent services which they had rendered in connection with the Menchester Ship Canal Bill.— Mr. Littled ale seconded the motion, and trusted that now the Genii Bill was for the present, at leaat, out of the way, the Board would give their most anxious attention to the removal of every just ground of complaint which the manu- facturing iodustries of Lancashire and elsewhere might have by a very large redaction in charges, and that the railway compenies would co-operate.—The rnotion was adopted by acclamation.—The Chairman said he wished to thee!: Aii members of the Board, and especially the members of the Parliamentary Committee, for their co-operation. It had " been said that if a scheme Lea been brought forward which did not at el.: eiiect the estuary, then, apart from the conei- f.eratton of any particular c mditione, they would be dis- posed to look on at the Parliamentary proceedings, leaving the scheme, if it were carried, to find its own level financially and commercially. They must now wait to \ see whet would Come next. If another proposal was to \be submitted to Parliament, they must know exectly what it was before they could determine what their duty might be. (Applause.)

SINGULAR RIOT AT POOLE—Active rioting occurred on Thursday at Poole. Mr Norton, who initiated a raid open publicans, was mobbed upon applying for summonses, and an attempt was made to throw him into the breakwater. He escaped with difficulty, and remained in his house guarded by vdice while the crowd burnt his effizy, broke his win • dows, and threatened to fire his timber yard. Great excite- ment prevails. FRAUDS ON WARRINGTON TRADESMEN.-01 Monday. at the Warrington B.rough Police Court, Albert Furness, a discha,ged soldier and a native of Warrington, was brought before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Councillor Monks, on two charges of obtaining goods by false pre- tences, viz :—One suit of clothes, value 30s, from Messrs. Hammond and Co., Manchester Clothing Company, Horse- market-street, and one pair of boots, value 9s 9, from Mr Charles Sudlow, shoemaker, Winwick-street.—The Chief cc nstable (Mr Hunt), in stating the case, said that on Wed- nesday, the 6'h ina, the defendant went to the Manchester Clothing establishment and tendered a note purporting to have come from his brother, Josiah Furness, who was a householder and property owner, askins; that the bearer should ho supplied with a suit of black clothes. The clothes r. ere supplied to him, and he soon after Dawned them at the shop of Mr Morton. Subsequently he went to Mr Sudlow's and obtained a pair of boots in the same manner.—Evidence was then called proving the fact of the prisoner having oh• tamed and then pawned the articles, and Josiah Furness, the pris mer's brother, swore that he had neither written the notes made use of by the prisoner, or given his authority for his named to be so used.—Prisoner, who reserved his de- fenc., was committed to the Quarter Sessions on both charges.

div.head: IRE EXAMINER SATURDAY. AUGUST Di, 1884.
div.p: IRE EXAMINER SATURDAY. AUGUST Di, 1884.
RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

UNJUST SCALES AND WEIGHTS AT RUNCORN. Before Mr W Bankes and Mr G L Davies, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, George Duateevand, coal dealer, Halton-road, was charged with being in posseasioa for use for trade of a weighing machine which was unjust —The defendant pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Leah said on the sth August he visited the defendant's coal yard, and there found a weighing machine, which he allowed the man in charge to clean. He tested the machine, and discovered that it was 6 ounces against the purchaser. Further inves- tigation showed that there were attached to the scale two pieces of lead and a piece of iron, which mid be easily re- moved, and on taking them away the scales were 101bs loz against the purchaser.—The defendant, who said he was under the impression thee). etal was secured to the machine, was fined 10e and costs 93 6.1.--John Ellis, coal dealer, Canal-street, was proved to be in posses4on of a scale which was Ilb 14pz against the purchaser when certain loose pieces of metal were removed, and of two 561 b weights which were respectively Paz and 4.iz light.—to the first case a fine of Is and costs 93 61, and in the second case of 103 I and costs 93 61 was inapo3ed.--Joseph Ackerley, coal dealer, Mill-street, was convicted of having in his possession 1 a scale which was B,z against the purchaser —Defendant, who explained that the scale was on sloping ground, was fined 103 and costs --A similar peralty was imposed on Benjamin Williamson, coal dealer, Queen-street, who was in possession of a machine which, when Superintendent Leah first tested it, was I.b against the purchaser. When several pieces of loose iron had been removed the scales were 71bs against the purchaser.--John Saunders, marine store dealer, Granville-street,'was summoned for having in his possession five 561 b weights which were false and Un- just—Defendant pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Leah said he found in the defendant's shop five 56,1) weights which were light, es follows :-11b, soz, Ciz, 2iez light. A 51b weight was 2 ounces light--Defendant said he beught the weights with the business six months ago, and had intended having them examined on Thursday. He exdleined that he only purchased with the weights in question, selling by means.of others, and he must, there Sore, have been a great loser by their ineorree:ness.-- Alfred Santley, marine store dealer, Water-street, was fined 103 and cost for being in possession of a scale which was 5 ounces against the purchaser.—Defendant explained that part of the scale was made of iron and part of wood, and the hot weather had affected the wood.
