div.p: Xtttero to lite gditor.
A MARRIAGE WIFE LOCKED DOORS.

Sir,—A few days ago, so I am informed, a marriage WRS celebrated at the church of St. John the Baptist, Earles- town, the doors of the church being closed and locked during the performance of the ceremony. lam told that this was done by the ordet of the Vicar (the Rev. T R. Matthews), and I should like to know whether such a thing is legal— whether or not any clergyman has a right to order the closing of the church doors daring the celebration of any portion of the Bmk of Common Prayer, or any portion of the common services of the Church of England. Perhaps the Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar of the parish, will kindly enlighten me upon this point 7—Yours, rte., Earltstown, August 11th, 1884. INQUIRER.

div.head: MR. W. RHODES ON THE CO-OPERtITIVE MEETING.
div.p: MR. W. RHODES ON THE CO-OPERtITIVE MEETING.

Sir,—ln your report of the disorderly annual meeting of the Runcorn Co-operative Society, and the scene which fol- lowed when the ballot was demanded for the election of secretary, I am reported to have mounted the steps of the platform, and gesticulating in an excited manner, delivered a speech to Mr. Watson. I contra hot this, and here state that I never even attempted to make a speech to any one from the platform steps. Referring to the charge made against me by Mr. Watson of giving two or three checks to ono person, this is a deliberate untruth. I challenge this gentleman or any other perms present at the meeting to come forward and prove this assertion. I have been con- nected with this society from its formation, but have now retired in disgust therefrom without a stain upon my char- acter. Will you please insert this in your next issee, and oblige, yours respectfully, WM. RHoDES. 42, Wellington-street, Runcorn, August 120, 1534.

div.head: MR BOTTOMLEY AND MR HOWES.
div.p: MR BOTTOMLEY AND MR HOWES.

Sir,—l am not surprised that you are unable to find room in your paper to reproduce the whole of the wretched farrago of nonsense contained in Mr Howes's last letter to the Tersda7e Mei eury. Any other man would be ashamed of the quirks, and quibbles,and paltry Subterfuges put forth ty Mr Howes in the correspondence in the Barnard Castle paper, but the repre- heap his ign ranee of this champion of Liberalism evidently knows no bounds. He now makes two statements in the Examiner that I will take as specimens of his usual style cd argument (?) In order to discredit one if possible, he endeavours to lead your readers to believe that that my state- ment, that I had never heard of his acceptance of my chal- lenge when I wrote to ths Teesdale Mercury, was untrue and insinuates that his acceptance had appeared at that time. Now, sir, on his own showing, his letter was written on Thursday, July 3rd, and therefore could not appear until July 9th, as the paper only comes out on the Wednesday. He admits my letter was written an July 8 b, and allowing for time for postage, I could not possibly see his letter until July 10th. So much then for his first endeavour to naislead. He then asserts that no reply has been received to his letter of July 3-d, accepting the challenge. Your readers will perhaps be surprised to learn that correspon- dence has since been passing between the local secretaries, and Mr Howes, and myself, and that the 18th and 19th of September have been finally settled upon as the date for the debate to take place, and th it this has been announced in the local newspapers.— Verbose sap.—Yonrs faithfully, J H BOT rOMLEY.

P.B--The Editor of the Exami,ter will sea from the above how uneilled for and ungentlemmly was his remark about " impudently " ehirkinz this discussion. 121, lienshaw-street; Oldham, August 7ch, 1881.

div.head: WANTED A PHILANTHROPIST.
div.p: WANTED A PHILANTHROPIST.

Sir,—With the view of attracting the attention of sonas of those good people who S 3 kindly look after the wants of cattle, I ask you, Mr. Editor, to allow me a little of your space. I feel confident that I have but to state to the public that the Warrington Water Works Company, in their anxiety to pay a dividend, or else large salaries to their officials, are perpetrating a gross and shameful injustice to about 500 workmen, to cause the benevolent to open their purses to the widest extent. Cattle can have drinking troughs pro- vided them, nay the very dogs in the streets come in for their share of attention, but the workmen employed at Messrs. Rylands' are debarred from these blessings. I sup- pose this is because cattle have a market voice; workmen, when done with, can be pushed aside and fresh ones take their plan. For some three or four years the Water Com- pany have insisted upon levying a kind of black mail upon employers. The latter have rebelled, and the consequence has been that the workmen—working in the midst of red hot furnaces and in mills, the atmosphere of which is dense with particles of lime dust—have been literally without a drop of clean water tea slake their p imbed throats. I think the facts are, as follows : The Water Company agree to supply firms with wator at ad per head ; in addition to this they claim the right to charge an additional water rent for office purposes, water closets, &e , or a lump sum of .C 5 in the case of Messrs. Ryland& Now it so happens that the firm in question want nbee of the company's water for the purposes named, it being already provided. Nose the less for this fact, the Water Company insist upon the £5, this being neither more nor less than a fine upon Messrs. Rylauds because they pump the water used for manufactur- ing purposes out of the river. Now this is what I call harrassing the trade of Warrington, and the next time our worthy Mayor has to respond for the Town and Trade " I hope he will state this as one recta= why oar trade is "paralysed." Bat we have rather a humorous side to this subject ; two men come dailveinto the works, one of whom must have car- ried in as much water as would float the Ore at Eastern. These two men sell pop to the workmen e 11. per bottle ; whether they pay for the water or not I cannot say ; that is Mr. Ross's business At all evente. our employers are wil- ling to pay 61. per head for their workpsople to have a sup- ply of clear water. This would mean that each man ought to drink five hundred gallons of water a year, which is simply ridiculous. More than this, meat of the men PaV water rates, being householders, and I am told that if they venture to carry their cans full of water into the works they are liable to an action at law on the part of the Water Company. Well, I suggest that Mr. ROSS looks ab out for the undersigned any day aliceut one o'clock, and he shall have the opportunity of trying his hand at this busineks. What the workmen want is a drop of water to drink while at work, and if a scheming manager like Mr. Ross et ande in the way he most be sat on.—Yours, ate.,
WEIITHAV.
THE VACCINATION QUESTION.

Sir,—Many of your readers will be pleased to notice that you have opened the columns of your excellent journal to the above important and irrepressible public question. May I venture to contribute a few facts bearing upon.the cm- troVersy, in the hope that others may be induced to investi- gate what one of our distinguished physicians, Sir Andrew Clark, of London, pronounced at Steinway Hall, a short time ago, to be "one of the most important questions now engag- ing the attention of thoughtful miods.,' Vaccination was claimed by Jenner to afford immunity against smallpox for life, and a credulous Parliament at the inatigation Of certain Royal personages, believing, or pretending to believe, this promise (for dehrmstration was impossible) voted Jenuer an award of £30,000! Faith in that protection which Jenner Claimed for a perilous operation is now aban- doned, even by the most ardent vaccinators. The advocates of vaccination have never been able to show thaPthe opera- tion has reduced the death-rate in the general mortality from all causes, and it is remarkable that epidemic years, , both of smallpox and cholera, are usually years of a I diminished mortality. The smallpox hospital returns show that from 75 ta 100 per cent. of all who are attacked by smallpox have received the protective vaccine inoculation. Mr. Matson, the medical director of the Highgate Smallpox Hospital, reported that in 1871, or 950 cases 870 bad been vaccinated. The Lancer for August 27th, 1881, furnishes the following particulars of the 43 cases treated for smallpox in the Bromley Hospital between A pril 25th and June 29th, I 1881 :—" Of confluent smallpox there were 113 cases, of die- crate 14, of modtfied 13. All the cases had been vaccinated —three re-vaccinated; two of the confluent CAVA died." Wherein, then, is the advantage conferred by the operation? That vaccination does not mitigate smallpox is also proved by the returns of the me ropolitan and continental smallpox hospitals, the average mortality to cases being now admitted to be as high as existed previous to the Jennerian era, viz, about 18 per cmt. That vaccination is a hazardous opera- tion is now allowed by the leading Press of the day. Corn- , menting upon the deith of four, and serious injury to five children, officially admitted as due to vaccination at Norwich, June, 1882, the Times says:—"There carf be no doubt that vaccination has been the channel for the commu- nication of disease- of a very grave character." The St. James's Gazette declares that "what happened at Norwich has been happening at a greater or less degree for years." The Methodist Recorder says:—" In the presence of such facts, compulsory vaccination cannot he defended." How terribly destructive to human life this -vaccination has proved to be may be learned by referring to Parliamentary Returns, No. 433, dated 1877, entitled "Vaccination Mor- tali,y." and No 392. Session 2.1880, entitled "Infant Mor- tality," where it will he seen how children are yearly being vaccinated into untimely graves. Posterity will read these piinful records, which men pass be "as the idle winds" with unspeakable surplice, and chronicle the facts in proof of the barbarism of the nineteenth century. For further particu- lars on this "burning question," venture to refer your readers to the publications issued by Mr W Young, 114, Victoria-street, Westminster, London.—l am, yours faith- fully, WILLIAM TEBB, National Liberal Club, London, August Bth.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

Sir.—What shall we do with the House of Lordsbe- coming the univeisil cry. R.iforrn it, or abolish it—which is to be done? It is obvious that something will have to be done with it in order to progress with remedial legisla- tion, because its chief function appears now to be a direct blocking of all useful measures. It never initiates any use- ful measures itellf, but impedes and postpones all measures sent from a Liboral House of Commons. Let us have a dissection of this house alandholders. Exclu- ding tha six Royal dukes whose politics:are not specified, or nine peers who are minors, it appears to consist of 503 members. Of these five are of uncertain politics, while 278 are Conservatives and 220 Liberals, giving a Conservative majority of 58. Now arises the great evil, and which makes me, a working-man, feel that it is time to have a look at the doings of these men, and see whether they are promoting my interests or theirs. On land questions this Liberal minority is merely mythical, as was proved by the rejection of the Government Bill to check those cruel evictions which were taking place in Ireland. This Bill was brought in in the session of 1830, and only 51. of the so-called Liberals .voted in its favour, whilst a host of them voted in the
A SCHOOL BOARD FOR GREAT SANKEY. RATEPAYERS' MEETING LAST NIGHT.

The Local Government Board having issued an order for the formation of a School Beard for the district of Great Sankey, which contains a population of about 2,000 persons, a meeting of ratepayers, called by circular, was held in the National Schoolroom, Great Sankey, for the puspose of nominating five candidates for the Board. Thera were about 14 (*sons present, and the Rev. C. E. Vernon wae voted to 'the chair.—The Chairman explained that it was advisable, if possible, that a contest should be avoided, and they were met that evening to agree meon the nomination of five per- sons to constitute the School Board. The Chairman ex- pressed his regret that the attendance was so limited, and several gentlemen pr2sent complained that the notice calling the meeting was issued at a very late period.—Mr. Hatton thought Mr. Sutton as returning officer had been guilty of, neglect —Mr. Jeans said the meeting was called merely as a matter of courtesy, pure and simple, to. agree if possible to nominate only five persons. Each person present could go away and nominate any ratepayer he pleased.—Mr RAgway then nominated the Vicar (the Rev ES Jackson), and Mr Jeans seconded the proposal.—The Chairman remarked that Mr Jackson had informed him that he would not stand.—Mr Ridgway replied that the Vicar was always reedy to:do his duty, and when he saw that It was the unanimous wish of the meeting he would allow the nomination to stand. It was essential the vicar of the parish should be on the Board.—The Chairman observed that the Vicar would no , doubt be glad to do all he could.—Several ratepayers also expressed a strong wish that the Vicar would stand.—The following nominations were then made: The Rev E Jackson, proposed by Mr J C Ridgway, seconded by Mr W D Jeans; Mr JO Ridgway, proposed by Mr James David- son, seconded by Mr W J Hatton; Mr W D Jeans, proposed by Mr J Dignum seconded by Mr James Turner; Mr W J Hatton, proposed by Mr .1 C RiJgway, seconded by Mr W D Hughes; Mr G Grange, proposed by Mr H B Mr Jeans suggested the advisability of nominating two or three other gentlemen so that if any of those now named could withdraw if they wished. He should be glad to nominate Mr Turner. He added tint he should not feel in- clined to stand if the vicar withdrew, and Mr Ridgway ex- pressed a similar sentiment. —Mr Kerfoot said they seemed to have met simply be support the vicar.—Mr Jeans and Mr Ridgway denied this, and the former added that he should be glad to nominate Mr Kerfoot.—Mr Kerfoot replied that he would not play second* fiddle, and Mr Turner echoed the statement. A • ratepayer said he would propose Mr V;.rcion if be would stand. —Mr Kerfoot: Mr Vernon is not a ratepayer. The proposer: That doesn't matter.—Mr. Kerfoot: Oh!— Mr. Jeans said as this was the first election the ratepayers as a whole ought to deoide who should form the School Board.—Mr. Ridgway approved of this course, and Mr. Ker- foot said he and Mr. Turner would be willing to stand if that course were taken.—Further nominations were then made in en informal manner as follows :—Messrs Thomas Kerfoot, W. D. Hooghton, James Turner, and Mr. Cook, it being understood that the nominations would be made in due form at Mr. Sutton's office this kSiturday) morning. After some further conversation the meeting terminated%

majority against it of 282. We can soon see through this by tooktng at the fact that out of these 509 peers, 438 are landholders possessing land amongst them to the extent of 14,251,132 acres, with a rental of £11,872,333: It is owing to the action of this House of Lords that so mach crime and bloodshed have existed in Ireland since the Liberal Government have been in power. Mr. Gladstone commenced by giving attention to the Irish land queation, but we find that this honse of hereditary legislators, of many of whom it may be said that— , The midwife laid her hnd on his thick skull With this prophetic bieivisiN—Be thiut dull determined to prevent a Liberal Achninstration from accom- plishing that which was just and right. In 1871 a bill was passed by the Liberate for the Abolition of Purchase in the Army. The Lords refused to pass it, and Mr. Glad- stone carried it over their heads to the Queen and thus it 1.)..c fine law. If we look back to history, we find that Crom- well in his parliament passed a resolution to the effect that, whatever was pissed in th it house would become law, whether the coosent of the House of Lords was with it or not. In order to show how the lords have treated legisla- tion for Ireland, I will just give you sonic of the bills which the unappointed chamber or assembly have rejected, delayed, or mutilated in the last fifty years : Mr Brownlow's Bill for the Drainage of Bogs and the Reclamation of Waste Linde.

the Tenant's Compensation Acts of 1845 and 1853, the Land &Cs of l SOO 1870, arid 1581, tho Compensation for Distur- bance Bill of 1880, the Arrears Act of 1882, every Irish Fran- chise Bill, Registration Bill, and Municipal Reform Bill, the Catholic Emancip ition Bill, the Tithe B:11, the Church Disestablishment Bill, the Penal Laws Repeal Bill, the Catholic Marriage Bill, and a host of others. Oily a few days ago (since, in fact they rejected the Franchise Bill). they threw out by a majority of 69, or 110 to 41 votes, the Poor-law Guardians Bill, "I trust," said the Chief Secre- t iry for Ireland, during the disenssion as t.) the immorality and corruption of .Irish offl3ials and Irish public b)ards, "the Poor-law Guardians Bill will be turned into an Act this session, for besides the fact that it would confer bene- . tits on Ireland, some of the controversies which have been entered upon at length would be closed at or.ce and for ever." The Lords v,ry soon settled it, and thus once more proved themselves to be the real enemies of Ireland. I should like in my next letter to Saw more on this Bill— what it is, and what a just bill it would have been if pas- sed!or the peasantry of Ireland. _ _

There are five different classes of peers :-1. By virtue of hereditary right. 2. By creation of the Sovereign. 3. By virtue of office, viz, Bishops. 4. By election for life, viz Irish Peers. 5. Be' election for duration of Parliament, viz, Scotch Peers. If you will allow me, I will continue this ktter and say something upon these differtnt classes of Peers in your next issue. flaping you will arent me space. I rem lin yours, &c, A YOUNG RADICAL. Widnes, August 6, 1884.

div.head: "STAND FIRM, MOSES."
div.p: "STAND FIRM, MOSES."

Sir,—Sir Wilfrid Lawson was very happy in his apt illus- tration of the position taken by the Tories in the House of Commons. Not daring any longer to oppose the Govern- ment lest their obstruction tactics should become too glaring, they now egg on their big brothers in 'another place." Reading the speeches of Tory orators just at present is very much like reading "The Essence of Parliament" in Punch. Indeed, I think our comic friend ought to make seizure of the whc le of Lord "Random's " speech at Pomona and give especial prominence to the lavish apologies his lordship felt compelled to offer for having so often done those things he ought not to have done. His lordship quite recently underwent a Viioll9 and sudden political conversion. Find- ing the men of Birmingham required something stronger 1 than the 1.000 voters of Woodstock, his lordship quickly put himself in order, and not only swallowed the Franchise pill, but also, while his brother Tories were declaiming against its extension to Ireland, ne insisted upon that pill being swallowed also. Now, what do we see? Something that must gladden the eye of every Radical. The Tory party " pic-nicing " at Pomona, their battle cry being " The bill, the whole bill, and nothing but the bill !" Why, the Rods and the Tories will have to shake hands yet; their only trouble will be—Who sliall be leader ? As for measures, I never yet had ten minutes . - .
conversation with a Tory working-min but I found him more extreme in his views than what the usual run of R icli-
cab are. On this important natation of the Franchise, the Tories are in this predicament—rho leaders hate the bill most heartily, but they know it would never do to go to the . .

. , country with a tale of this sort ; therefore ihev have dragged to the front the redistribution question. The poor blind Tory working-man in his eagerness to supprt his party, accepts a cheap trip ticket—idmitting the bearer to either Belle Vise or Pomona—and wondering, while he is jour- neying, what it is all about. Here arn I, save this bcfog4eci Tory, going to support the bill the Liberal Government has carried to the door of the House of Lords, and here is Lord Salisbury with a caucus of lords behind him that won't let it pass. The whole question to the Tory mind is about as clear as mud.
Mr. Gladstone in the Rouse of Commons, and Lord Gran. villein the H iuse of Lords, arc pledged to bring. in a Re-

distribution Bill. Upon what lines it will be drawn none of us know. But Lord Salisbury comes to the front and says, "Mr. Gladstone, we have the strongest faith in your sin- cerity, but we found that the last time we Tories pissed a Reform Bill and a jerrymandering Redislribuiion Bill, that it worked very well for LI", and we intend to du ',bp like again if possible." This is the whole secret of the fresent turmoil. So far as the Radical party are concerned, their strongest wish and desire is that the House of Lords will, like Moses, stand firm, and then we shall have the greatest conflagration ever seen. Have we not Lord Salisbury's word for it that there requires more "pressure." Let him but stand firm, and he shall have such an amount of pressure as he little dreams of. The Duke of Portland says tho Lords were "all made by the will of God." I wonder if he includes the Doke of Marlborough, Lord S. Leonardo, an 4 the Earl of Aylesford, and one or two others that could be mentioned, beciuse if so he might just remember that Charles I was "King by Divine right,"• and yet his head rolled off. If

our Tory friends woUtdonly b 1 honest to their convictions we should soon settle this question. How can the Lords possibly be in favour of Redistribution when they upheld rotten boroughs until threatened with a swamping creation
of peers? They resisted the progress of religions liberty,be• cause the privileged Church was an outwork of the privi- leged class. They resisted the extension of Habeas Corpus . .
an-a of personal liberty.
They, resisted the btilot; they
resisted the abolition of-the slave trade, and the Reform of Criminal Law. Borstlll7'B Bill for the abolition of the

death punishment in cases of petty theft was thrown out by the Lords, and among the 32 who voted in the majority were seven bishops. But to enumerate the faults and crimes of this huge caucus would be wearying. Mr Chaplin tells us that to appeal to the country now would mean for the Liberal pasty "absolute damnation." Well, we have known our Tory friends to prophecy before now, notably so when their late leader issued his famous letter to the Duke of Marlborough urging the selection of "man of light and leading." The country interpreted his advice not exactly to his liking, and now we are coolly bidden by this master of jibes and sneers to appeal to the country. So far as War- rington is concerned it had better be put (di a bit, as I notice that our Tory friends are not quite prepared with a candi- date. A recently-held Tory caucus meeting having selected Mr Adamson, found oat after their separatioh that he was a Liberal, so they had to fall beck upon the "4:31-,•and Old Man" from Walten. EXCURSION FROM lAMBI TO Borcros.-1 sebo'ars, teachers, and friends of the Lymm Nonconformist Sonday Schools had their ennui' trip on Monday, the place ellec- tud being Buxton. The party numbered about 400, and the weather beinedn,, had an enj 'gable day. The scholars were in charge of the various superintendents and teachers. Two long trains were engaged for the occasion, and the trip was taken advantage of by many not personally connected with the schools. RUSIIBEARING.— Lymm rnshbearing commenced on Sat- urday and was continued until Tuesday, the OCCASIOG being considered a general holiday in Lyrnea and the surrounding dis•ricts. None of the observances fermerly characteristic of rushbearing day were carried out, and the proceedings were simply of the nature of an ordinary pleasure fair. The neighbourhood of the Cross was stocked with a miscella- neous collection of stalls, swing boats, round-abouts, and the Usual accompanirrrents of a fair, and a gold business was apparently transacted. There were also a number of stalls and shows erected on a vacant piece of ground near the railway station, but the centre of the village. presented the most animated appearance. Though the business of the fair was necessiiily suspended on Sunday the visitors were numerous, the weather being fine, and the pretty walks round and ahont the village were admired by many in- tent on spending a day of quiet enjoyment in the aim- try. On Monday, the principal day of the fair, the village was crowded during the afternoon and evening, and merri- ment reigned supreme. The various hostelries were exten- sively pitronised, but good order prevailed throughout the day. After Monday the business of the fair considerably ,jecreaiied, and the village has now resumed Its usual quiet appearance. On Sunday the Primitive Methodists of Ly.nrn held an open-air service near the Cross, which was well attended.

COLLIEVY ACCIENNT NEAR 041111411 : FOUR LIVES LIST. -A frightful accident occurred on Thursday morning at the Albeit Colliery, Chamber Lane, Hol!Inwood, near Oldham. A fall of roof occurred about six o'clock, by which fear men named James Leach, John Wright, Eli Greaves, and Joseph Leach, belonging to Rollinwood and F:ailsworth, lost their lives. The pit has previously been remarkably free from accidents. Greaves and Wright are married, and leave Widows and children. It seems that tho men were in waggons, :ind had gone about three hundrel yards along the trainway when a mass of stone, measuring about three yards long and eight Inches thick, loosened and fell. Orient the men, seeing the danger, tried to jump out, but too late to avoid !,eing ornahed about the head. 40seph Leach was badly cut ablut the head, but thn ininrieeenf the others are of an Internal character.

ACTIVITY IN THE CHESHIRE SALT TRADIA—The export returns compiled for last month recorded the triskest busi- ness transacted in July, with one solitary exception, for the past seven years. Trade had been larguishing all summer, and the stocks of salt in hand were heavy, hut the enor- mous export last month of 127,998 tons against 103,878 tons for the corresponding mouth last year has greatly re- duced them.

THE WELSH IN WARRINGTON.-4'Or Some titne past the Weleh residents of Warrington and neighbourhood have felt the need of a building in which to conduct religious cer- vices in their own language and according to their accus- tomed forms. Occasionally services have been held and sermons preached in Welsh in rooms lent for the purpose, and at a recent service there were about 80 people present. It was thought desirable by those interested to secure if, possible a room in a building in John-street, belonging to the Corporation, in which to conduct services, and at th 3 last meeting of the Warrington Town Council Mr Dixou submitted a resolution to the effect "That Messrs W 14 Pritchard and E Williams, of White-street, be allowed the dSO of the tapper room of the building in Johti-strect on Sundays for the next six months, at a rent to be arranged afterwards" Some discussion took place en the resolution, touching the advisibility of letting the room for denomina- tional purposes, it being contended by some of the members that it was against the rule to take that course, although the power to do so might rest with the Corporatios, but niti- I motels, the resolution was passed by nice votes to seven. It other preliminaries are satisfactorily arranged, he holding of services will be commenced with no more delay than is absolutely necessary, although the promoters cannot see ' their way to having a resident Welsh minister for some time, or, at any rate, until they feel that the plan is more firmly intablished. tioweyer, it is hoped that it will not be difficult to get a regular supply of ministers in the mean- time, and we see no reason Nay tica services ellould not prove a permanent success.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The appointment of Prince George 4 Wales to be a Knight of the Garter is gazetted. The Duchess of Edinburgh joined her children at Birch- all Glenrnuck, near Banger, on Friday afternoon. On Friday morning there was another land subsidence at Northwich. A boy and horse were engulphed but after- wards saved.
The men employed in Itioenoffeven slate qulrries, Fes- tinoig, struck work on Friday against a threatened reduc- tion of 5 per cent in wages. The slate trade is reported to be very flat.

At Ayr, on Friday, a girl named Alice Malone was re- manded on the charge of placing obstruction on the railway at Muirkirk, whereby four trucks were thrown off the line The prisoner confessed her guilt. The rernains of the late Bishop Claughton were conveyed to St Paul's Cathedral on Friday morning, where service was performed by the Bishop of London. The body was afterwards removed to Elton for interment. IMPRISONMENT 0 ANTI.NACCINATORS.—FO Ur men are now in Leicester goal undergoing terms of imprisonment for refusing to have their children vaccinated. 'Toe vacci- nation officer has reported that he cannot carry out the law, there being about twelve hundred persons waiting to be summoned, while over two-thirds of the children born are unvaccinated. The Vaccination Acts were a dead letter, and there liad not been a single case of smallpox in twelve months.

FRIGHTFUL STABBING AFFRAY IN IRELAND —A terrible stabbing affray took place on Friday at Kingscourt, County Cavan, which, it is feared, will have fatal results. A butcher's assistant named Galloly quirrelled with two men whose names have not yet transpirei and attacked them in a furious manner with a large butcher's knife, inflicting such fearful wounds that neither are expected to recover. Two policemen who were on protection duly in the neigh- bourhood pursued Gralloly, and, after an exciting chase of over a mile, succeeded in coming up with him, knocked him down with their rifles, and lodged him in the police barracks. The dying men's depositions have been taken.

div.head: SERIOUS FIRE IN LONDON: SEVERAL PERSONS INJURED. _
div.p: SERIOUS FIRE IN LONDON: SEVERAL PERSONS INJURED. _

A serious fire broke--MTIC;b-o—ui ten o'clock on Friday morning on the premises of Messrs. Hodgson, envelope makers, Little Trinity.lane, Upper Thames-street, London. The fire was caused by the bursting of the gas-engine bag. The dimes spread with fearful rapidity, and the forty or fifty workpeople on the premises were placed in great dan- ger of their lives. Most of the employs are women, and some could only escape by jumping from the windows. In this way many were injured, and one man was removed to the hospital. The firemen were speedily convinced that no efforts could save Messrs. Ilodgson's warehouse, and they directed their attention to preventing the fire from spread- ing, but the adjoining roof of Messrs. Foot Brothers' ware- house caught fire. The fire was mainly kept to Messrs. Hodg- son's, where it broke out, but the buildings on either side have had portions of their roofs burnt off, and the contents were damaged both by Eire and water.

div.p: EX fRAORDINARY DEATHS FROM BLOOD POISONING.

ST PETEIISBCIRG, FRlDAY.—nree persons have died in the neighb)whond of this city from blood poisoning, caustd by the sting of flies which had prevbusly settled on cattle infected with rinderpest. TEIE CHOLERA.
TOULON, FRIDAY.—There were three deaths from cholera here last night, two of which occurred in town and one in the suburbs. Among the victims is Lieutenant Berte, of the French nary.
A Central News Marseilles telegram, dated Friday fore- noon, s i7s :—Nine deaths from cholera occurred during the past twenty-four hours. The weather is cooler, rain having fallen.

div.head: SOUDAN EXPEDITION.
div.p: THE SOUDAN EXPEDITION.

CAIRO, FRIDAY.—The whole expeditionary force will be pushed fmward to Wady Haifa as soon as possible, and will proceed thence to Semuelo, on the way to Dongola. There is ample provision of dahabiehs for the transport of troops aoove and below all the cataracts, and the small boats from England are considered useless.

Major General Wilbraham Lennox is gazetted to the com- mand of a brigade in Egypt and Colonel Christopher Barnes to the command of the Royal Artillery in Egypt. REPORTED DEFEAT OF THE FRENCH AND RE-CAPTURE OF TAMATAVE. (Exchange Company's Telegram.) PARIS, FEUDAL—According ts Le Matin, a telegram has just baen received by the French Government stating that during the absence of Admiral Miot, who had gone with the fleet to occupy Volemtr, the Hovas, under the command of Colonel Willoughby, had attacked and re-captured Tama- tave. Part of the French garrison, it is added, Weal mas- sacred.

_ _ (Reuter' s Telegrams.) PARIS, FRIDAY.—There is no foundation whatever for the report published by Le 31atin this morning that th 3 Gover- ment had received a despatch front Nladag,ascar stating that the liovas on the 3rd inst attacked the French garrison of Tamatave and took possession of the place. The Minister of Marine has received, via Mozambique, despatches from Admiral Mist, dated Tamatave, 9th last, reporting the condition of all the French posts in Mid 'gas car to be satisfactory. The Central News Paris correspondent says :—The French- Government have to-day received art official despatch an- nouncing that Tam at we was re-taken by the Hovts on the 3rl inst. The enemy numbered 10,000 and were commanded by Colonel Willoughby. The French garrison escaped to their ships after being driven out of the fortifications. The news has created an immense sensation here.

I THE ALLEGED CA.NNIBALISSI BY ARCPW EXPLORERS. NEW YORK, FETDAY.—lntelligence received from Re chaster (Nov York) states that the exhumation of the bo iy of Lieutenant Eislin4bury, of the Greely expedition, bas caused a profound sensation, and is regarded as affording full proof of the charges of cannibalism against the expedi- tion. Other bodies will also be exhumed.

The "New York Times" publishes a sttternent to the effect that the reports made to the Navy. Department by the officers engaged in the Greely relief expedition show that starvation drove the survivors of the Greely party to canni- balism. It appears that after their food supply was exhaus- ted in February they were kept alive on human flesh. , When the rescuing party discovered them at Cape , Sabine, the first attention was given to two , men lying insensible from cold and privation. One was wild with delirium ; and as they lifted him he slid, " Don't let them shot me, as they did poor Henry. Must Ibe killed and eaten as Henry was? Don't let them. Don't." The rescuers reported this mittsr to Commander Schley, who, after investigation, felt satiefi d thee the poor felloW was @peeking the truth, and that some of the men who per- ished bed been stripped of their flesh to keep their surviV- log camrades alive. He, therefore, instructed two or three gentlemen, among whom was Dr. Ames, surgeon of the I Bear, to make a careful examination of the evidence and to I put their conclusions in writing. This was done, and the reports are now before the Navy Department. Lieutenant Greets, was decidedly unwilling to have the bodies of the ' • , buried dead disturbed. He thought it wise, as they bad been , buried so long, to let them refuels in their Arctic graves. Commander Schley did not agree with him, and the bodies were dug out from their graves Most of the blankets con- tained nothing but heaps of white -bones, many of them , picked clean, and the remains could be identified only by Ithe marks on the blankets. On making inquiries Coin. , mender Schley discovered that many of the 17 men said to have periehed from starvation had been eaten by their famishing comrades. It was their last re:ort. It was ' reported that the only men who escaped the knife were three or fonr who had died of scurvy. The amputated limbs of some men who had afterwards perished were eagerly de- voured as food. Charles Henry, above referred to, Wag a German, without any American relatives. Driven to des- pair by hunger, Henry saw an opportunity to steal a little more than his share of the rations and made the attempt. He was diecovertd and shot for this crime. In the pub- lished official report the death of this man is set down as having occurred on June oth. When the body was found his heads and face, though shrunken, were intact and recog- nizable. But nearly everywhere else the skin Ifad been stripped from him and the flesh picked from. the bones. Even his heart and lungs had been eaten by his comrades. One rib was found to have been shattered by a bullet, and to another a smell fragment of lead wate,attached. The bullet-bole was found in the skin. The body was in this. condition when it was interred in Cypress Hill Cemetery, Brooklyn, last S tturclay. A great sensation has been caused by this reported cannibalism, and an official inquiry will probably be ordered into the matter by Congress.

. • • THE PREMIER AT HAWARDSN.—The Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone arrived, with Mrs. Gladstone aod Miss M. Glad- stone, at Chester Station on Tuesday night, shortly after quarter-past seven o'clock, en route for Hawarden, where, it is expected, he will remain for a fortnight previous to pro- needing to Scotland. A Scotland-yard detective accord' paniPd the train from London, and proceeded to Hawardco. Mr. Gladstone attended prayers on Wednesday morning 14 the Parish Church,. Hawardeo, and afterwards walked through the village. Ile looked remarkably well. 00 Thursday Mr. Gladstone was present at the annual show 01 the Hawarden Horticultural Society, held in Hawardso Park ant delivered a short speech in responding to a vote of thanks accorded to Mrs. Gladstone for distributing the awards to the successful exhibitors. In doing so he inci- dentally referred to a wish expressed by one of the audience that he might pass Vie Franchise Bill, and said he could assure those whom he W 49 then addressing that that glib' ject lay very near his heart. He believed, too, it lay very near the hearts of the people of the three kingdoms, and that when the bill was passed everybody would feel it was time ts forget the old squabbles which had taken place about it, emsidering it an act of justice and wisdom which would make the nation stronger, more united, and more attached than ever to the Throne and to the laws•of the land.

NEW YORK, MONDAY.—A severe earthquake shock oc- curred here yesterday afternoon, extending along the entire coast of the States of Main and Maryland, and was felt eastward as far as the Alleghenies. The shock lasted from 10 to 15 seconds. Concordant accounts have been received from all the chief cities in the zone of territory affected. The severity ef the shock was greatest at Hartford, in Connecti- cut, where several persons were thrown down and bruised. No fatalities, however, occurred anywhere beyond that a man in the Hartford gaol died of fright. SPAIN. MADRID, TUESDAY.—King Alfonso this morning pro- ceeded to Pamplona, and met with a most cordial reception. He reviewed the garrieon, and was subseqaently present at a bull fight. THE TRANSVAAL. The Transvaal Volkraad having ratified the convention •t-e concinnea wirn the British Government tics ap•a , commission will, it is expected, be appointed to define a iron- tier line between the Tramsvad and Bechuanaland. Ml.• Mac- kenzie, British Minis'er, in Bechuanaland, has gone to Cape- town to confer with Sir Hercules Robinson. THE TRANSVAAL AND ZULULAND. DURBAN, WEDNESDAY.—The Chief Urmayamana has agreed to the boundary marked out by the Boers of Zulu- land. According to trustworthy intelligence received here M. Joubert, President of the Transvaal, has been elected Pre- sident of the ceded territory in Central Zululand. PERU. NEW YORK, TUESDAY —A dispatch from Lima states tha General Caceres, who recently proclaimed himself provi- sional president of Peru, has informed the diplomatic body in that city that he has assumed supreme power. POST-OFFICE ROBBERIES IN AUSTRIA. VIENNA, WEDNESDAY.—Some sensation has been caused here by the discove yof two fresh Post-office robberies. A letter containing 15,000 florins has been abstracted while in transit between Vienna and Lembarg ; while on the Pestb- Vienna line a whole mail bag has disappeared containing valuables and registere letters, including a number of cheques, to the amount of 80.000 florins, which had been posted to Vienna by the Pesth Savings Bank. THE GHEELY EXPEDITION: THE ALLEGED CANNIBALISM. WAsarteeircost, WEDNESDAY—Mr Chandler, Secretary of the navy, has been interviewed with regard to the acts of cannibalism alleged to have been committed by the sur- vivors of the Greely expedition. Mr Chandler stated that no such report wan in possession of his department, and he declined to expressany opinion as to its veracity, and refused to discuss the subject further. NEW YORK, Wxn:Ygsnev.—Thts New York Times to-day reaffirms the accuracy of its allegations regarding the Greely expedition, and hints that Dr Pare' was shot by his com- rades. The paper says that one of its reporters yesterday saw a score of officers and seamen of whom not a single one denied the story of cannibalism. SWITZERLAND' GENEVA, WEDNESDAY.—Two young girls were assassi- nated last night at Martigny, in the canton Valais. The police are endeavouring to discover the perpetrators of the crime. A severe hail storm occurred yesterday in the canton vraud, causing considerable damage it'the vineyards. EXPLOSION AT A POWDER MiLL : TEN LWES LOST. KAser (RUSSIA), lIIUDBDAY.—A powder mill exploded here this morning, setting tire to five adjacent buildings. Tex workmen were killed.
